## 7\. The working-with-me template

This section is the complete content of the template: one Sŏn spine shared by all three founders, with a short seat-specific preamble for each. A founder can fill it in unaided from what is written here. Every founder's actual answers are blank. This is the container.

It is not a formatted fillable artifact. That packaging is gated on the document methodology (`86ajgn2z5`).

### 7.1 Before you start: instructions common to all three

**Who reads this.** Your two co-founders read the full version. The two leads, when seated, read the issued version (section 7.6). Assume the reader knows the concept and does not know you.

**How long.** As long as it takes to be specific and no longer. A weak document is long because it is vague. Two to four pages is the expected range.

**Do these three exercises first, alone, before writing anything.** They take an afternoon. Their outputs feed prompts C, F, and G, and without them those prompts get answered from self-image rather than evidence.

*   _The values exercise._ Imagine yourself at eighty, looking back at your working life. Ask what gave it meaning. Write the ten values that show up. Cut to five. Cut to three. For each of the three, write the specific activity that tells you that you are working in accord with it, one positive outcome of holding it, and one trade-off it costs you. The trade-off is the part that matters; a value with no trade-off has not been thought through. Name values as activities where you can ("I do not ship a thing I would not put my name on") rather than as single words, which say less than they seem to.
*   _The work style placement._ Two axes: introverted to extroverted (do you gain energy from people or from being alone? do you talk to think or think to talk?), and task-oriented to people-oriented (do you reach first for the problem or for the people in it?). The four corners have working names: Analyzer (introverted, task), Director (extroverted, task), Collaborator (introverted, people), Promoter (extroverted, people). Place yourself three times: at work in an ordinary week, at home, and under load (the last week before a deadline, or a bad service). The three placements are usually not the same, and the differences are the useful part. This is shared vocabulary, not a verdict. It does not decide what you can do.
*   _The strengths inventory._ List the three or four things you are best at. For each, split what it is made of into skills (tactical things you can do: build a model, write a brief, run a pass) and capabilities (the broader ability to deploy those skills in a situation you have not seen before). Mark each as innate (as easy as breathing; you never had to learn it) or acquired (you built it, and you can say when). Then, for each strength, write the sentence: "This strength is also a weakness when..." and finish it honestly. Then write what guardrail, if any, you have built against that.

**Rules for the writing.** These are the house's standing rules and they apply to this document.

*   The customer is the customer. Never "guest."
*   No em dashes. Use commas, colons, semicolons, or a new sentence.
*   Sentence case for every heading.
*   No daypart code names. Say early morning, lunch, dinner, late night.
*   No financial figures. If a figure is needed, say it lives in the model.
*   No brand facts from memory. If you cite the canon, cite it.
*   No performed conviction. Not "I am committed to," not "I believe in," not "my goal is." Say what you do.
*   Profanity is spoken. It does not go in the document.

**How to answer well, in general.** Specific over categorical. An example over an adjective. The thing you would rather not write is usually the thing the reader most needs. Where you do not know the answer, write "I do not know yet" and move on; prompt K collects these. A blank is more useful than a performance.

**What a weak document looks like.** It describes the founder the writer would like to be. It uses words from a leadership book. It has no trade-offs. It says "collaborative" without saying what happens when a decision is needed by Friday. It contains nothing the other two founders could not have guessed.

### 7.2 Preamble for Brandon: concept, operating systems, experience, public voice

Your seat is the origin of the operating concepts and the public voice of the house (WP p.03). Most of what is in the record started as something you thought. That is the seat's strength and its specific hazard, and the record names the hazard itself: systems get built for how the founder thinks (WP p.17). So three prompts carry more weight for you than for the others.

Prompt B (what lives in my head) is, for your seat, the concept: which parts of it are in the record and the canon, and which parts are still only in you. Be exact. The record is long, and it is easy to assume it holds everything; it does not hold the reasons behind many of its decisions, and the leads will need those reasons when they extend a system you designed.

Prompt D (how I decide) should address a thing the others will notice: you hold the concept, so a decision in your domain can feel like a decision about the whole house. Say where your domain ends. Say what you want to be consulted on in the kitchen and the model, and what you do not need to know.

Prompt I (how to reach me) has a public-voice dimension the others do not have. The brand engine runs on the public voice, and that is your seat (WP p.03, p.30). Say what that does to your availability, and what happens to the concept when you are producing.

One thing the seat does not decide: you may be the person most often in the room, but the room's tempo is the canon's and the table's (section 2). Your document should say how you intend to be present on the floor without becoming the integration layer the leads are meant to be freed from.

### 7.3 Preamble for Dominic: capital, financial architecture, technology build

Your seat is the model and the machine (WP p.03, p.05). The record says the most common cause of restaurant failure is the controllable set, undercapitalization and weak controls, and that your seat is the answer to it: "The financial rigor is not a slide prepared for the raise. It is a founder" (WP p.05). It also makes you the owner of the stack the record calls the nervous system (WP p.21). Three prompts carry more weight for you.

Prompt B (what lives in my head) is, for your seat, the model's assumptions and the stack's mesh: the connections between tools, the ones that are built rather than bought, the reasoning behind bought-versus-built (WP p.21 to 22). The record says the house should run without either founder's memory. Say what would break in the model and the stack if you were unreachable for a month.

Prompt D (how I decide) should address how the other founders get a read from your domain without a figure being asserted outside it. The concept founder and the chef will need to know whether something is affordable, and they will need it at the speed of a decision. Say how you want to be asked, what form your answer takes, and what you need from them to give it. Say also how a stack decision that changes how the floor works gets made, because that is a seam the record does not resolve.

Prompt C (how I work) has a question the others do not face: your domain did not come from hospitality (WP p.05). The service metronome (section 2) and the floor are not your native ground. Say how you intend to learn them, how much of the room you want to see, and what you do not need to be taught.

### 7.4 Preamble for the chef partner \[Chef-gated\]

_This preamble is written to a person who has not yet been identified. It is a prompt, not a description. Nothing here is filled in on their behalf. Whether it is read before or after the partnership is signed is open and is decided by Session 7._

You are joining as an equal founding partner, not as a hire. The record is explicit about why: two founders own everything outside the kitchen so that the culinary seat can be a founding one, "freed from carrying the rest of the business alone" (WP p.03, p.05). The two founders' documents have been written before yours. Read them first. Then write yours on the same spine, so that the three are comparable.

Three things the house already holds that your document should answer to, not repeat.

First, the record's kitchen structure is strands, not levels: Station Leads own domains, Chef on the line and Chef on prep are execution roles and neither is a promotion from the other, and the Steward is a tension node, not a support role (WP p.11). Your seat owns culinary execution during service and culinary direction overall, and the record distinguishes the two (WP p.10). Prompt A is where you say how you read that structure and what in it you would change.

Second, the canon's culinary framework, Mahk, holds that taste is memory, that the kitchen must hold a point of view, that the chef can articulate what each dish is reaching for, and that the Mahk standard is a hiring criterion (canon 01; canon, what remains). Prompt A is also where you say how you hold that.

Third, and this one the two founders owe you plainly: the record currently holds two accounts of your seat. The white paper says the chef partner "owns the culinary vision as an equal founding partner" (WP p.03). The canon says "the brand owns the culinary identity. The chef executes within it" (canon, what remains). These were written at different times and they are not the same statement. Your document is where you say how you read the difference. The three of you resolve it together; the two founders have filed it as a decision to make before you are seated, and it is routed to the session that writes the founding documents.

The rest of the spine applies to you exactly as it applies to them. You have not met the people you are writing for. Write it anyway; it is part of how you meet them.

### 7.5 The spine

Each prompt has four parts: what it asks, what it is really asking for, how to answer well, and what a weak answer looks like. The answer space is blank.

* * *

#### Header

Name. Seat. Date written. Version. Who has read it.

* * *

#### A. My seat and its edges

**The prompt.** State what you own, in a paragraph. Then state where your domain ends: the three or four decisions nearest your edge that belong to someone else, and who. Then state what you are accountable to: the outcomes your domain is judged by. If a job description exists, point to it and do not repeat it.

**What it is really asking for.** Not a role and its goals. Co-founders with separate domains do not need each other's goals; they need each other's edges. This prompt asks for the border, drawn from your side, so the other two can draw theirs and the three maps can be compared for gaps and overlaps.

**How to answer well.** Name the edge cases, not the center. Everyone knows the concept founder owns the concept. What the others need is: does the concept founder own the uniform wear test, or the Maitre d? Does the capital founder own the choice of reservation platform, or the concept founder, because it shapes the arrival? Does the chef own the beverage program's food pairings? Write the ones you are unsure of; those are the ones that matter.

**What a weak answer looks like.** A title and a list of responsibilities copied from the record. No edges. No mention of anything you are unsure you own.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### B. What lives in my head

**The prompt.** List what you know that the house depends on and that is not yet written anywhere the house can read it. For each item: what it is, what would break if you were unreachable for a month, and by when it will be in the system.

**What it is really asking for.** This is the code-bearing principle applied to you. The record says the house is built so it does not depend on either founder's memory (WP p.05 to 06). This prompt is the audit of how far that is currently true. It is the most important prompt on the spine, and it is the one a standard version does not have.

**How to answer well.** Be concrete to the point of discomfort. "The concept" is not an item; "the reason the host stand was removed and what replaces its functions" is. "The model" is not an item; "the labor assumption by daypart and where it came from" is. Include relationships: the vendor who returns your call and no one else's, the consultant whose number is in your phone. Include reasons, not just decisions: the record holds many decisions and fewer of the reasons behind them, and the leads will need the reasons when they extend a system.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "Most of it is in the white paper." Or a list with no dates. Or a list that flatters the writer by being long and vague.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### C. How I work

**The prompt.** Your three work-style placements (at work, at home, under load) and what the differences between them mean for the people around you. Whether you talk to think or think to talk. How you take in information best: reading, hearing, seeing, doing. What gives you energy and what drains it. Your hours, and which service periods you will and will not be physically present for. Where you do your best thinking and where you do your worst.

**What it is really asking for.** The operating conditions under which you are good, so the others can create them when they need you to be good, and recognize when you are not.

**How to answer well.** Use the placements from the exercise but do not stop at the label. "Director at work, Collaborator at home, Director-under-load with the people-orientation gone entirely" is a useful sentence because of the last clause. Say what the others will see, not what you feel. Say the daypart truth: a founder who will not be in the building at seven in the morning should say so here, because the morning will otherwise assume they might be.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "I'm a mix of all four." No hours. No statement about presence by service period. A list of preferences with no consequences attached.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### D. How I decide

**The prompt.** In your domain: what you decide alone and tell no one; what you decide alone and tell the others after; what you want to be consulted on before deciding; what you consider a joint decision. What you need in order to decide: data, a conversation, a walk, a night, a prototype. How fast you decide, and what happens when someone needs a decision faster than that. How you change your mind and what it takes. What a decision from you looks like: is it written, is it spoken, how do the others know it has been made.

**What it is really asking for.** The rule the record does not hold. There is one joint decision in the record (lunch, WP p.36) and no general rule. This prompt asks each founder to state their own draft of the rule from inside their domain. The three drafts are then the input to the founders' decision-rights rule, which the three of you set together and which this document does not set.

**How to answer well.** Give the four categories real examples from your domain. Say the uncomfortable thing about your speed: if you decide slowly and the house will sometimes need fast, say what the others should do (ask for a deadline; decide without you; escalate). Say how you want to hear that a decision of yours has consequences in another domain, because that is the seam the record leaves open.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "I'm collaborative and like to talk things through." No categories. No speed. No account of what the others should do when your process is too slow for the moment.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### E. How I disagree, and how to disagree with me

**The prompt.** How you raise a problem with another founder's work. How you want to hear that you are wrong: in what form, in what setting, from whom, how soon. What you do when you are angry, and what the others should do about it. What "going meta" looks like with you: the conversation about the conversation. What you will never say in front of the team, and what you will.

**What it is really asking for.** The internal application of Principle 3. The record establishes honesty outward: name what is open, transparency first, be direct about what happened. It says nothing about how three equal partners tell each other hard things. This prompt is where each founder supplies their half of that, so the exchange can be built on three stated preferences rather than three guesses.

**How to answer well.** Tell a story. "The last time someone told me a system I built did not work, here is what I did in the room and here is what I did the next day." Say the setting: some people can hear it in a group and some only alone; some in writing and some only in person. Say what you do under stress that the others should read as stress and not as intent. If you go quiet, say so. If you get loud, say so.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "I welcome feedback." "I'm direct." No story. No setting. No account of what you look like when it goes badly.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### F. My strengths, and what each costs

**The prompt.** From the strengths inventory: your three or four strengths, each split into skills and capabilities, innate and acquired. For each, the sentence "this is also a weakness when..." completed. For each, the guardrail you have built, or "none yet." Then: which of these strengths does the house currently depend on in you personally, and which has been moved into the system.

**What it is really asking for.** Two things. The standard one: a strength is also a weakness, and a founding team that knows this can staff around it. The Sŏn one: a founder's strength that the house depends on personally is a memory failure waiting to happen. The last question in the prompt ties the strengths inventory back to prompt B.

**How to answer well.** The "also a weakness when" sentence is the whole prompt. "I read people well" becomes useful only when it continues "...which means I sometimes decide about a person before the evidence is in, and I have built the guardrail of asking one question first." Distinguish innate from acquired honestly; acquired strengths are the ones you can teach, and the house will want to know which those are.

**What a weak answer looks like.** A list of strengths with no costs. Costs that are secretly strengths ("I care too much"). No mention of what the house depends on you for.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### G. My three values at work

**The prompt.** From the values exercise: three values, each with the activity that tells you that you are working in accord with it, one positive outcome, and one trade-off. Then: where you expect your values to collide with the other founders' or with a house decision, if you can see it now.

**What it is really asking for.** Not the company's values; the canon holds those. Yours. The reason is practical: when a founder is a blocker, it is usually a value being defended without being named. If the three of you can say "I am holding this because of X," you can negotiate at the level of the value rather than the level of the decision.

**How to answer well.** Activities over words. A value stated as a word ("integrity," "excellence") is nearly useless; the same value stated as what you do ("I do not open a daypart until the one before it is steady") is a decision rule the others can work with. The trade-off is mandatory and it should be a real one you have paid.

**What a weak answer looks like.** Three words from a list. No trade-offs. Values chosen because they sound like a founder.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### H. What I look like under load

**The prompt.** What zero bandwidth looks like in you: the behaviors the others will see before you notice them yourself. What tips you into it. What helps and what makes it worse. What you want the other founders to do when they see it. What you will do when you see it in them.

**What it is really asking for.** The cooling system applied to the founders (Principle 6). The record measures the team's bandwidth and not the founders'. This prompt is the founders' own leading indicator, written by hand until a better one exists.

**How to answer well.** Observable signals. Not "I get stressed" but "I stop answering messages and start answering only the ones from outside the house." Say what the intervention is, and give the others permission to make it. Say the thing you do under load that damages the house (the decision made too fast; the message sent to the whole team; the shift you take that you should not), so the others can catch it.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "I handle pressure well." No signals. No permission granted.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### I. How to reach me

**The prompt.** Which channel for what: what is urgent and how to mark it; what is for information only and how to mark it; what waits. Expected response times, honestly. Hours, and the hours you are not reachable. During a service period you are working, what reaches you and what does not. What you will read and not answer, and how the others should read your silence.

**What it is really asking for.** Reachability, not cadence. The founder cadence (when the three of you meet, and for what) is a joint decision and is designed in Session 4; do not set it here. This prompt is the individual layer under it: how a message finds you.

**How to answer well.** Adopt a convention and state it. "FYI in the subject means no reply needed" is the kind of thing that saves a hundred small frictions. Be honest about response time; a stated eighteen hours that is kept is worth more than a stated two hours that is not. Say what does not reach you during service, because a founder on the floor at dinner cannot be the escalation path for the model.

**What a weak answer looks like.** "Text me anytime." No conventions. No statement about service periods.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### J. What I need from each of you, and what you can expect from me

**The prompt.** For each of the other two founders, by name or seat: the two or three things you need from their domain to run yours, in what form, and how often. Then, for each: what they can expect from you, stated as commitments you will keep rather than qualities you have.

**What it is really asking for.** The standard version of this prompt is a manager telling reports how they will be supported. Sŏn has no reports at this level. This is the peer version: three people with separate domains stating their dependencies on each other. The three answers, read together, are a dependency map of the founding team.

**How to answer well.** Be specific about form and frequency. "I need a read on whether a floor change is affordable, in a sentence, within a day" is answerable. "I need financial support" is not. For what the others can expect from you, write things that can be checked: "You will hear about a concept change before the team does." Not "I will be transparent."

**What a weak answer looks like.** Generalities. Needs stated as complaints. Expectations stated as virtues.

> _(blank)_

* * *

#### K. What I do not know yet

**The prompt.** The prompts above you could not answer honestly, and why. The things about how you work in a house that does not exist yet that you will only learn when it does. The date you will revisit this document.

**What it is really asking for.** Principle 3 applied to the document itself. A founder who has never run a room at this scale, or never worked with these two people, does not know some of the answers. The house is built to name what is open. So is this.

**How to answer well.** Short. Honest. Dated.

**What a weak answer looks like.** Empty, because everything above was answered with confidence.

> _(blank)_

* * *

### 7.6 Issuing the spine to a lead later \[Team-filled\]

When the Operations Lead and the Maitre d are seated, each founder issues a shorter version to them, and each lead is asked to write one on the same spine for the founders and for each other. The issued version keeps prompts A, C, D, E, H, I, and J, with J rewritten for the lead as reader. It omits B, F, G, and K, which are for the partners. The lead's own version adds one prompt the founders' version does not need: how they will discuss development and progression with the people in their domain, and how they want to be included in the team's work. That prompt is written when the leads exist and is not drafted here.

* * *

## 8\. Specifications

For each instrument the material recommends: whether Sŏn uses it, what it must contain, what it must do, what it must refuse to do. These specifications are what the downstream clusters consume when the instruments are built. No instrument is built here; instrument production is gated on the document methodology (`86ajgn2z5`).

### 8.1 The values exercise

**Does Sŏn use it.** Yes, as a founder self-instrument, completed alone, feeding prompt G of the working-with-me document. Later, as a lead self-instrument on the same terms. \[Recommended\]

**What it must contain.**
*   The eighty-year-old prompt: looking back at a working life, what gave it meaning.
*   The reduction: ten values, then five, then three.
*   For each of the three: the activity that signals working in accord with it; one positive outcome; one trade-off.
*   The why-and-story frame: why this value matters to you and one example of it appearing in your life.
*   A note that values are best stated as activities or decision rules rather than single words.
*   The example list of values, as examples only.

**What it must do.**
*   Produce three values each with a real trade-off.
*   Be completable alone in under two hours.
*   Keep the full working private by default; only the three values, activities, and trade-offs export to the working-with-me document.
*   Ask, at the end, where the writer expects their values to collide with another founder's or with a house decision.

**What it must refuse to do.**
*   Derive company values or a mission from the founders' shared personal values. The standard exercise offers this as an option; Sŏn declines it. The record and the canon carry the company's intent; the founders' personal values are theirs and are not aggregated into a mission.
*   Rank one founder's values against another's.
*   Treat a value as a verdict on the person, or use it in any performance conversation.
*   Require the values be named with words from the canon's forbidden lexicon. The canon governs brand voice, not a founder's private vocabulary, but a value stated as an activity avoids the problem and is a better answer regardless.

### 8.2 The work style grid

**Does Sŏn use it.** Yes, as shared vocabulary among the founders and, later, the leads, with the explicit caveat that it is not deterministic and does not decide what a person can do. Placement is done three times: at work, at home, under load. \[Recommended\]

**What it must contain.**
*   The two axes, each stated as a question: introverted to extroverted (energy from people or from solitude; talk to think or think to talk), task-oriented to people-oriented (reach first for the problem or the people).
*   The four working names: Analyzer, Director, Collaborator, Promoter, each with a two-sentence description of what it is good at and what it is worse at.
*   The three placements: at work, at home, under load.
*   A Sŏn-specific addition: the strand question. The record's two strands require different intelligences, the outward-facing relational and expressive under load, the inward-facing architectural and timing-precise (WP p.10 to 11). The grid asks which strand's intelligence the writer recognizes as their own, and whether they hold both.
*   The caveat, printed on the instrument: a preference is not a limit, and the grid is never used to stereotype.

**What it must do.**
*   Give three people who work in separate domains a common vocabulary for their differences within one conversation.
*   Surface the under-load placement, which is where founder collisions actually happen.
*   Feed prompt C of the working-with-me document.

**What it must refuse to do.**
*   Be used in hiring, in role assignment on the floor, or in any progression decision. The question of how work style demand differs by daypart, and whether service pressure selects for some quadrants over others, is owned by Sessions 5, 6, and 8 (`86ajgnhh3`). This page notes one refinement for those sessions as an input, not a conclusion: the claim that service selects for Directors and Promoters describes the outward-facing strand; the inward-facing strand, architectural and timing-precise, is where the Analyzer's intelligence lives in service, and the record's strand structure already reserves that place. The scarcity claim is therefore about one strand, not about service.
*   Be treated as an assessment with a score.
*   Replace the strand structure. The strands are the record's vocabulary for the floor; the grid is a vocabulary for individuals.

### 8.3 The strengths inventory

**Does Sŏn use it.** Yes, as a founder self-instrument feeding prompt F, and later for leads. \[Recommended\]

**What it must contain.**
*   Three or four strengths, named.
*   For each: the skills it is made of (tactical, binary: can do or cannot) and the capabilities (the broader ability to deploy skills in an unfamiliar situation).
*   For each skill and capability: innate (as easy as breathing) or acquired (built, and when).
*   Two Sŏn additions. The trade-off column: "this is also a weakness when..." completed for each strength, with the guardrail built against it or "none yet." The dependency column: whether the house currently depends on this strength in the writer personally, or whether it has been moved into the system.

**What it must do.**
*   Produce, for each strength, its cost and its guardrail.
*   Distinguish what the writer can teach (acquired) from what they cannot (innate), because the learning platform will want the teachable ones.
*   Tie back to prompt B: every strength the house depends on personally is an item for the knowledge-transfer list.

**What it must refuse to do.**
*   Become the competency map for any floor position. The documented competency requirements per position belong to the progression structure (WP p.11) and are specified in Session 8 and built by the learning cluster.
*   Compare founders to each other.
*   Record a capability without an example of it having been used.
*   Be used in any compensation or review conversation.

### 8.4 The management prerequisites checklist

**Does Sŏn use it.** Once, as the gap list in section 5, and then it is retired. It is not adopted as a recurring readiness test. \[Recommended\]

**What it must contain.** The mapping in section 5: each standard item, what it assumes, what the record holds, what is absent, and where the gap routes.

**What it must do.**
*   Route every gap to a session or to counsel.
*   Hand off, rather than resolve, the items owned by existing carryovers: founder job descriptions (Session 2), the 1:1 (Sessions 4 and 12), levels and ladders (Sessions 8 and 13), compensation philosophy (Session 13), the review instrument (Session 13).
*   Name the assumptions Sŏn has replaced by design: a manager above, ladders and levels, the desk-native 1:1, the periodic feedback event.

**What it must refuse to do.**
*   Score Sŏn. Absence of a standard structure is not a failure where the record has replaced it.
*   Be re-run against Sŏn without translation. Sessions 3 and 4 produce Sŏn's own definition of "the operating system is running," and that definition replaces this checklist.
*   Imply that ladders and levels are a prerequisite. Whether a single house needs them is open (`86ajgnj4e`).

### 8.5 The working-with-me document

**Does Sŏn use it.** Yes, for all three founders, on one spine with seat-specific preambles, and later for the two leads in a shorter issued form. \[Recommended\] The timing of the chef partner's exchange is open and routes to Session 7. \[Founder-gated\]

**What it must contain.**
*   The header: name, seat, date, version, who has read it.
*   The eleven prompts of the spine (section 7.5), each with its four-part guidance printed on the instrument so the writer does not need this page.
*   The common instructions (section 7.1), including the three prerequisite exercises and the standing rules.
*   The seat-specific preamble for the writer's seat (sections 7.2 to 7.4), with the chef partner's preamble marked chef-gated and containing the record's two accounts of the seat.
*   An open-items section (prompt K) and a revision date.

**What it must do.**
*   Be completable by a founder alone, from the instrument, without a facilitator.
*   Make legible to a person in a different domain: the writer's edges, decision mode, disagreement mode, load signals, reachability, and dependencies.
*   Move the writer's self-knowledge and their unrecorded house knowledge (prompt B) into a document the house can read.
*   Produce three comparable documents, so the founders' edges (A), decision drafts (D), and dependencies (J) can be laid side by side and the gaps and overlaps found.
*   Support a shorter issued version for leads (section 7.6) without rewriting.
*   Be revised on a stated date and when the seat changes.

**What it must refuse to do.**
*   Be a job description, a contract, a performance instrument, a scorecard, or a statement of company values.
*   Set the founder cadence or the decision-rights rule. It collects each founder's draft of the second (prompt D) as input to a joint decision.
*   Assert brand facts or financial figures.
*   Perform. The master register applies: present without performing. No performed conviction.
*   Be filled in on anyone's behalf. The chef partner's is written by the chef partner.
*   Use the daypart code names, the word "guest," or em dashes.
*   Be issued to the team below the leads. It is a founder-and-leads instrument.
*   Be packaged as a formatted fillable artifact before the document methodology exists (`86ajgn2z5`).

# S2: Founding documents, the operating charter, and founder decision rights

# Session 2: Founding documents

**Program:** Scaling People translation. **Source:** Claire Hughes Johnson, _Scaling People_, Chapter 2, "Founding documents," book pp. 70 to 83; workbook pp. 11 to 22. **Seat:** Organizational Systems Architect. **Status of every position in this page:** recommended, founder-gated, chef-gated, or team-filled. Nothing here is final. Nothing here is landed.

**How to read this page.** Each numbered position carries exactly one mark. _Recommended_ is the team's position, ready for ratification. _Founder-gated_ needs input the team cannot supply: values, intent, working style, or a vote among principals. _Chef-gated_ is left open for the chef partner. _Team-filled_ is populated once the team exists. Quotations marked WP are from the white paper by page; Canon is `brand-guidelines.md` by section; Deck is the brand and experiential guidelines deck by page.

**The governing constraint on this session.** Sŏn's mission, long-term commitments, and principles are decisions. They are not a synthesis of existing brand language. This page structures those decisions, surfaces every implicit answer the record already holds so it can be accepted or rejected deliberately, and argues. Where a candidate reading is available in the record, it is named as a candidate, its source is quoted, what accepting it would commit Sŏn to is stated, and it is marked open. No candidate is recorded as a draft.

* * *

## 1\. What she asks for

Her framework has three parts, and she gives them a house: founding documents are the foundation, the operating system is the structural beams, the operating cadence is the mechanical components. Founding documents "detail the plans for the entire enterprise, including the company's long-term goals and principles and your company philosophy: why and how you exist and operate." Their job is to make sure "the operating systems you put in place share a common purpose, flow from your objectives, and are guided by a clear company ethos from top to bottom." A secondary job: when values are explicit, "expectations are known to all," which "makes it easier to give feedback when someone isn't meeting expectations."

Four documents:

*   **Mission.** Why the company exists. "Descriptive and aspirational." Her test for descriptive: "another organization should not be able to have the same mission." Her test for aspirational: "it's unlikely a mission will ever be fully achieved." Every layer, team, division, company, has one, and each ladders up.
*   **Long-term goals.** "The bigger-picture ambitions we hoped to achieve or improve over a period of years." Stripe's fit on two pages and had not changed in eight years. Quarterly and annual goals ladder up to them, so they are "a necessary precursor" to the goal-setting the rest of her chapter builds.
*   **Principles.** The values that "establish the culture that enables you to work toward those goals." Her tests: "relevant, believable, enduring, and deliverable." Her warning: "too many companies make their principles so idealistic that they don't resonate with employees because they have no connection to how the company actually operates." Her drafting method: write down notable moments in the company's history and ask what belief prevailed. Revisit every year or two. What matters most is "ensuring that they are truly expressed in how we hire, reward, lead, and conduct ourselves."
*   **Team charters.** A page per team that states why the team exists, its long-term goals, "what others can expect from the team," key metrics, major risks and dependencies, and how to work with it. Her template (workbook pp. 15 to 22): mission, vision, customers, metrics, strategic importance, major risks, provided interfaces, dependent interfaces.

She also gives a timing rule that matters for Sŏn more than any other sentence in the chapter: founding documents "become an even more important touchstone when a company grows beyond about 40 or 50 people."

* * *

## 2\. The reframe: what a founding document is for in a house that does not inflate

Her documents organize arrival. Stripe went from a few hundred to thousands while she was there; the founding documents were the thing that let a person hired in year six hold the same purpose as a person hired in year one, without either of them ever meeting a founder. That is what "touchstone" means in her sentence. The documents replace founder proximity as headcount dilutes it.

Sŏn does not have that problem, and a charter written as if it did would be organizing a growth that is not coming. The record describes "roughly eight leadership lines running the full span of the day against fourteen running one dinner service, and a kitchen of two title-tiers instead of four" (WP p.22). The building opens near full size and stays there. Nobody at Sŏn will be more than one conversation from a founder for years.

So what varies at Sŏn, if not headcount? Four things, and each is a way for a company to stop being one company.

**The hour.** Four service periods run out of one kitchen under one name. The white paper names this the hard problem: "Keeping a restaurant coherent across the day is not obvious, and getting it wrong is common" (WP p.33). Its diagnosis of the peer that failed is precise: "A daypart added as an afterthought, without its own reason to exist and its own operating logic, becomes a worse version of dinner, however well it is executed" (WP p.34). A late-night team and an early-morning team can drift into two companies at one address without anyone hiring a single extra person.

**The domain.** Three founding seats own three domains, and the record's whole structural claim rests on domains that are "small, specific, explicitly defined, interlocking" (WP p.09). Where two domains land on one object, the record predicts what happens: "The absence of a clear path is where politics begin. Politics are a load-bearing structure problem" (WP p.11). Section 7 of this page finds one such seam already in the record.

**Time, and the order things arrive in.** "Dinner opens first and runs on its own for at least a quarter... Lunch and brunch sit further back still, not to be revisited until the restaurant has operated for a full year, and whether lunch is ever built at all is an equal decision among all three partners" (WP p.36). Decisions made while dinner runs alone will bind late night when it opens. A founding document is how a decision made in the first quarter reaches a service period that does not exist yet without being re-derived by whoever is standing there.

**The seat that has not arrived.** The chef partner will join a company that has already decided a great deal. A founding document is how the company tells that partner what was settled before them, what was deliberately held for them, and which is which.

And there is a fifth reason, the one that settles the question of whether Sŏn needs founding documents at all. The record has already spent them. The white paper's onboarding design reads: "Why comes before how. Orientation to the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard happens before operational training, because a person needs the reason before the mechanics" (WP p.20). The white paper also stakes the company on being "built so it does not depend on either founder's memory" (WP p.06). Sŏn's record already orients every new person to a mission and a set of values before their first shift, and already stakes the company on an organization that does not run on founder recall. Neither commitment can be kept by a mission and values that exist only in the founders' heads. The founding documents are not an import from her book. They are a debt the record has already incurred.

**Position 2.1 (Recommended).** Sŏn's founding document is a coherence instrument, not a growth instrument. Its job is to keep one company across four service periods, three founding domains, a phased opening, and a founding seat that arrives late. Every section of it is tested against one question: does this settle something that would otherwise be re-decided at a different hour, by a different domain, or by a person who arrived later? A section that does not pass that test is not founding material and belongs in the operating system (Session 3) or the cadence (Session 4).

**Position 2.2 (Recommended).** The working name for the document is the operating charter. "Charter" rather than "constitution" or "manifesto," because the document assigns and limits authority rather than declaring belief, and because Sŏn's voice rules forbid the manifesto register (see section 6.4). The name is provisional and Brandon may change it; the function is not.

* * *

## 3\. The standing problem: what governs what

Before the charter can hold anything, it has to have standing, and right now the record does not leave room for it.

### 3.1 Canon already claims the whole company

The deck's cover, marked GOVERNING, reads: "Brand and experiential guidelines. The source of truth for every decision made under this name" (Deck p.01). The text canon's preamble: "The six-tier authority hierarchy governs all decisions. Higher tiers override lower tiers without exception" (Canon preamble). The deck's closing page gives the only conflict rules canon holds: "When this document conflicts with a habit, the document wins. When it conflicts with itself, the higher tier wins" (Deck p.94).

Neither artifact states what happens when canon conflicts with a different founding document. Canon has rules for canon against habit and canon against itself. It has no rule for canon against a charter, because at the time canon was written there was no charter. The session brief for this work asserts a clean split: canon governs how Sŏn speaks, looks, and positions; the charter governs how the company runs, decides, and holds itself accountable. That is a reasonable split. Canon does not agree that it exists. A charter that simply appears beside a document claiming to be the source of truth for every decision is not a founding document. It is a competing claim, and the company would hold two documents each asserting supremacy, which is precisely the drift canon's own rule forbids: "A living document changes by versioned decision, never by drift" (Deck p.94).

### 3.2 There are three documents, not two

The operating agreement Brandon and Dominic have already worked on is the third. The team has not read it; it is not on this program's allowlist and it is a legal instrument. But its existence changes the charter's shape. An operating agreement governs ownership, capital, and the legal authority of principals. A charter that assigns decision rights among the same principals either restates the agreement, contradicts it, or must declare that it sits beneath it. Only the third is safe.

### 3.3 The relationship the charter must declare

**Position 3.1 (Recommended).** The charter opens with a standing clause that names its relationship to the two documents that already exist, in this shape:

*   _To the operating agreement._ The operating agreement governs ownership, capital, and the legal authority of the principals. The charter governs operating authority. Where the two touch, the operating agreement wins, and the charter is amended to match. The charter does not restate the agreement's terms.
*   _To the brand canon._ Canon governs how Sŏn speaks, looks, positions, and is experienced by the customer. The charter governs how the company runs, decides, compensates, and holds itself accountable. Each cites the other and neither restates the other. Where a single decision falls under both, a seam rule states which governs.

The structure of that clause is the team's to recommend. Its content is not fully the team's: the seam rule (what happens when a canon rule and a charter rule bear on one decision) is exactly the question section 4 lays out, and it is founder-gated.

**Position 3.2 (Recommended).** Canon must be amended, by versioned decision under its own rule, so that "the source of truth for every decision made under this name" is scoped to the decisions canon actually governs, and so that canon states its relationship to the charter in the same words the charter uses for canon. Two documents that describe their boundary differently are already in conflict. This is a change to a governing document; whoever holds versioning authority over canon makes it.

**Position 3.3 (Founder-gated).** Who holds versioning authority over canon, and who holds it over the charter. The record does not name a canon owner. Canon's sonic governance names Brandon at Tier 1 for a sub-system; nothing names an owner for canon itself. Brandon is "the origin of the operating concepts" (WP p.03) and the canon reads as his; but the charter cannot record that as a decision. What the team can say: the charter must name the versioning authority for both documents, and the chef partner's relationship to canon versioning is part of the chef-seat question in section 9. Until the chef is seated, the interim authority must also be named.

**What breaks if this stays open.** Every downstream session writes positions that cite canon or the charter. If the boundary between them is unstated, Session 3's operating system, Session 5's hiring criteria, and Session 13's compensation architecture will each quietly pick one, and the company inherits three different answers to which document governs.

* * *

## 4\. The authority hierarchy conflict

The two canon artifacts, both on the allowlist, both declaring themselves closed and governing, state materially different six-tier hierarchies. Verified against both source texts.

| Tier | `brand-guidelines.md` section 02 (Version 1.0) | Deck pp. 32 and 93 (Version 3.0) |
| ---| ---| --- |
| 1 | Cultural Frameworks (Jaeyeonmi, Ma, Mahk) | Cultural frameworks (Jaeyeonmi, Ma, Mahk) |
| 2 | Positioning + Playground Philosophy | Company non-negotiables (no exploitation, toxicity, or disposable people; employee-first) |
| 3 | Jeong + Nunchi (service philosophy) | Positioning and philosophy (the three qualities; Playground, Jeong, Nunchi) |
| 4 | Brand Architecture | Architecture and identity |
| 5 | Voice and Tone | Executional systems (voice, type, color, space, sound, service, digital, photography) |
| 6 | Persona Profiles | Persona profiles |

The material difference is tier 2. The deck ranks the company's people commitments above positioning, philosophy, architecture, and every executional system, with override authority. The text version does not place them in the hierarchy at all; it states them in section 01 as a standalone block and never ranks them. The deck also carries a sentence the text version lacks: "The company protects four things in order, and the order is the decision. FIRST Bandwidth / THEN Joy / THEN Retention / THEN Results" (Deck p.04). The white paper agrees with the deck's spirit: "Bandwidth, then joy, then retention, then results. This is the metabolic sequence... This is mechanical, not aspirational" (WP pp. 12, 16 to 17).

### 4.1 Why this is the load-bearing question for a charter

For a brand document, tier 2 is a placement detail. For an operating charter, it is the whole question. Under the deck's hierarchy, "no disposable people" outranks a brand or service decision, and a service protocol that treated a person as disposable would be wrong by rule. Under the text version, the same commitment sits beside the brand system, and a conflict between them has no stated resolution. "The order is the decision" converts a sequence into a tiebreaker: when bandwidth and results conflict, bandwidth wins. Adopted into a charter, that sentence has operating consequences. A short-staffed night is answered by reducing covers rather than thinning the floor. A profitable service period that consumes the team's bandwidth is cut or restructured before it is defended on results. Those are real commitments with real costs, and they are why the question cannot be settled by picking the more recent version number.

### 4.2 The three rulings available

A founder can rule in one sitting by choosing one of these. Each is stated with what it commits Sŏn to.

**Ruling A: the deck's hierarchy governs; the text canon is out of date.** Commits Sŏn to: the people non-negotiables and the protection order as tier-2 rules inside canon, overriding brand and service decisions. The text canon is re-versioned to match. Consequence: a brand document holds the company's labor commitments and its operating tiebreaker. That is workable, but it means the charter's people section restates canon rather than owning the commitment, and it puts the chef partner's relationship to labor commitments inside a document about brand.

**Ruling B: the text canon's hierarchy governs; the non-negotiables move out of canon entirely.** Commits Sŏn to: canon as a brand document with no people tier, and the non-negotiables and protection order living only in the charter. Consequence: the seam rule in section 3 must then say the charter's people commitments override canon's tiers, or the commitments lose the override authority the deck currently gives them. The deck is re-versioned to remove tier 2.

**Ruling C: the non-negotiables and the protection order are the charter's highest tier, and canon states that all six of its tiers operate beneath them.** Commits Sŏn to: a single top tier shared by both documents, held in the charter and cited by canon. Consequence: canon's tier 1 cultural frameworks, which currently have "veto power over any downstream decision" (Canon 01), would sit beneath the people commitments. That is a substantive change: it means a decision that satisfies Jaeyeonmi, Ma, and Mahk but treats a person as disposable is wrong. The deck already implies this by ranking non-negotiables at tier 2 with veto over everything below but not over tier 1; ruling C moves them one step further. Both artifacts are re-versioned.

The team's observation, offered as argument and not as the ruling: ruling C is the only one of the three that is consistent with position 3.1 (canon governs the customer-facing company, the charter governs how the company runs) and with the white paper's claim that the metabolic sequence is "mechanical, not aspirational." Under A the operating tiebreaker lives in a brand document; under B it loses its override; under C it lives where operating commitments live and canon defers to it. But C also asks whether the cultural frameworks are outranked by anything, which is a question about Sŏn's identity, and that is not the team's to answer.

**Position 4.1 (Founder-gated).** Which hierarchy governs, and where the company non-negotiables and the protection order sit relative to canon's tiers. One of rulings A, B, or C, or a fourth Brandon supplies. Filed as a founder decision below.

**Position 4.2 (Founder-gated).** Whether "the order is the decision" is adopted into the charter as an operating tiebreaker, with the consequences named in 4.1 stated and accepted. The record holds it in the deck and the white paper; the text canon does not carry it; adopting it is a decision about how Sŏn will trade bandwidth against results on a real night.

**Position 4.3 (Recommended).** Canon exists in one version of record. The text canon (1.0) and the deck (3.0) have drifted from each other on a load-bearing point, in violation of canon's own rule. Before the charter cites either, they are reconciled by a versioned decision that names one artifact as the canon of record and the other as a rendering of it. This is filed as a document work item. The charter, once it exists, cites canon by version.

## 5\. The operating charter: specification

This is the core deliverable. Downstream clusters build the document from it. Each section states its purpose, what it must contain, what it must do, what it must refuse, where its content comes from, and what breaks if it is wrong or missing.

### 5.1 What the document is

One document, short, declarative, in Sŏn's voice. It states what the company is for, what it protects and in what order, who owns which domain, how decisions are made and how deadlocks break, what it commits to its people, how its service periods stay one company, what it refuses, and what is still open and who closes it. It is read by the founders, by every lead, and by every new person before their first shift. It is not customer-facing; "The parent company is not a brand and is not named in customer-facing contexts" (WP p.36). Investors read the white paper. The white paper argues; the charter states.

### 5.2 Design rules for the whole document

**Position 5.1 (Recommended).** Seven design rules, each derived from a failure already visible in the record.

1. **Commitments and owners, never tools or addresses.** Both canon artifacts point to their record of truth at a ClickUp document that is now archived and excluded from this program; the canon also states the Surface-and-Zone Baseline Document lives there. The white paper names Airtable as the data-layer hub; Airtable is no longer in use. Two governing documents, written within the last year, already carry dead references. A founding document names the company's commitments and who owns them. It never names a tool, a vendor, a system of record, or the address of another document. Those live in the operating system, where they are expected to change.
2. **Every statement is settled, held, or deferred, and says which.** Canon's own discipline, "Every decision in this document is closed unless marked \[HELD\] or \[DEFERRED\]," extended with the four marks of this program. A held statement names who closes it: founder, chef partner, or team. A deferred statement names the condition that opens it.
3. **Versioned by decision, never by drift.** Canon's rule, adopted. The charter records its version, the date of each change, and who made it. It names, in its own text, who has authority to version it (position 3.3).
4. **Sŏn's voice rules apply.** No "we believe," no journey, no founder hero narrative (Canon 09). The forbidden lexicon applies. Sentence case. "Customer," never "guest," "in any internal communication" (Canon 01). No code names for service periods; time of day only. See section 6.4 for why this is an asset.
5. **No figures.** No percentage, threshold, or dollar amount appears in the charter. The compensation percentage is "still being finalized" (WP p.20) and the white paper carries "no ask, no terms, and no figures" (WP p.02). Figures live in the compensation architecture and the operating system, where they are versioned on their own cadence.
6. **Never assert the unproven.** "The discipline is to never assert the unproven, to a customer or to a reader" (WP p.36). The charter does not name future brands, the membership tier, or any concept that has not opened. It may state that the connective layer is built to hold more; it may not say what.
7. **Cites, never restates.** The charter cites canon by version and the operating agreement by title. It does not copy their content. A restated rule drifts from its source the day the source is versioned.

What the charter refuses, as a standing list in its own text: to describe tools; to name future brands; to carry code names; to carry figures; to restate canon or the operating agreement; to record a proposal as a decision; to describe any founder's interior qualities, strengths, or working style (those are the founders' own to write, Session 16).

### 5.3 Sections, in order

**Section 0: Standing.** _Purpose:_ give the charter authority. _Must contain:_ the relationship clause to the operating agreement and to canon (position 3.1), the seam rule once ruled (position 4.1), and the versioning authority (position 3.3). _Must do:_ make it impossible for a reader to hold canon and charter as competing claims. _Must refuse:_ to claim authority over anything the operating agreement governs. _Source:_ structure from the team; seam rule and versioning authority from the founders. _If wrong or missing:_ every downstream document picks its own answer to which governs; section 3.3 names the consequence.

**Section 1: What Sŏn is for (mission).** _Purpose:_ her mission, in her sense: why the company exists, stated so that no other organization could hold it and so that it is never fully achieved. _Must contain:_ one statement, and a note of which entity it belongs to (see 6.1). _Must do:_ be true on opening day when only dinner runs, and still true when the layer holds more. _Must refuse:_ to be a positioning line, a thesis about compounding, or a description of the restaurant alone. _Source:_ Brandon, with the record as input (section 6.1). _If wrong or missing:_ every daypart charter (section 11) and every team goal (Sessions 3 and 4) ladders up to nothing, and the onboarding sequence the white paper commits to has no "why" to deliver.

**Section 2: Long-term commitments.** _Purpose:_ her long-term goals: the ambitions over years that quarterly and annual goals ladder up to. _Must contain:_ a short list, stable across years, stated without figures. _Must do:_ give Sessions 3 and 4 a parent for every metric and goal they set. _Must refuse:_ to carry a target value, a date, or a future brand name. _Source:_ Brandon, with the record's candidates in 6.2. _If wrong or missing:_ the operating system sets goals with no parent, and the goals drift toward the lagging indicators the white paper explicitly rejects.

**Section 3: Company non-negotiables.** _Purpose:_ the three refusals and the operating philosophy. _Must contain:_ "No Exploitation Ever / No Toxicity Ever / No Disposable People. Employee-first operating philosophy" (Canon 01). _Must do:_ state whether these outrank canon's tiers (position 4.1). _Must refuse:_ to soften any of the three into an aspiration. _Source:_ the record; the ranking from the founders. _If wrong or missing:_ the company's clearest existing commitment has no operating home.

**Section 4: The protection order.** _Purpose:_ state whether "bandwidth, then joy, then retention, then results" is a tiebreaker or a description. _Must contain:_ the sequence and, if ruled, the sentence that makes it a rule. _Must do:_ tell a lead on a short-staffed night what wins. _Must refuse:_ to be stated as a rule if the founders have not accepted its consequences. _Source:_ record; ruling from the founders (position 4.2). _If wrong or missing:_ the white paper's "mechanical, not aspirational" claim is unenforceable.

**Section 5: Principles.** _Purpose:_ her principles: how the company operates, stated so they are "deliverable." _Must contain:_ a short set, each stated as what the company does or refuses, each traceable to a decision already made or a moment already lived. _Must do:_ be the thing hiring scores against (Sessions 5 and 6), feedback references (Session 12), and reviews measure (Session 13). _Must refuse:_ virtue words; anything a competitor could claim unchanged; anything not expressed in how Sŏn hires, pays, or leads. _Source:_ Brandon selects and words; the record supplies candidates (6.3); the chef partner may add one or more from the culinary domain (chef-gated); revision after the first year of operation is mandatory. _If wrong or missing:_ every people session from 5 onward scores against an unstated standard.

**Section 6: The founding seats.** _Purpose:_ three job descriptions for three principals. _Must contain:_ per seat, the specification in section 7. _Must do:_ resolve the OS-surface seam and name who owns culinary direction overall. _Must refuse:_ to describe any founder's interior qualities; to describe the chef seat before position 9.1 is ruled. _Source:_ record for the domains; each founder for their own seat; founders jointly for the seams. _If wrong or missing:_ "Politics are a load-bearing structure problem" (WP p.11), and the record has already produced one seam.

**Section 7: Decision rights.** _Purpose:_ the rule the record has been applying without writing down, and the deadlock rule. _Must contain:_ the pattern in section 8, the classes of decision reserved to all partners, the deadlock rule, and the interim rule before the chef is seated. _Must do:_ let any lead know, before the event, whether a decision is theirs. _Must refuse:_ to list every decision; it states the rule and the reserved classes, and the operating system holds the instances. _Source:_ pattern from the team; reserved classes and deadlock from the founders. _If wrong or missing:_ the eight instances in the record stay instances, and the ninth case is judged during the event.

**Section 8: People and compensation commitments.** _Purpose:_ the founding commitments to the people who work here, stated as a philosophy that reaches cases the record did not anticipate. _Must contain:_ the list in section 10. _Must do:_ let Session 5 write a job posting and Session 13 build an architecture that both satisfy the same commitments. _Must refuse:_ any percentage, point weight, or premium. _Source:_ record; Brandon confirms the list; Session 13 builds the mechanics. _If wrong or missing:_ the compensation architecture is built with no stated philosophy to test against.

**Section 9: One company across the day.** _Purpose:_ the commitments that keep four service periods one company. _Must contain:_ the phased opening as a commitment (dinner first, alone for at least a quarter); each service period requires "its own reason to exist and its own operating logic" before it opens; lunch and brunch as held in reserve, with building lunch an equal decision among all three partners; the daypart charter (section 11) as the instrument by which a service period earns its opening. _Must do:_ bind late night to decisions made while dinner ran alone, and give the lunch decision a form. _Must refuse:_ code names; any statement that lunch will be built. _Source:_ record; the team for the instrument; the chef partner for the culinary logic of each period (chef-gated). _If wrong or missing:_ the failure the white paper diagnoses in its peer.

**Section 10: Structure.** _Purpose:_ the organizational commitments the operating system implements. _Must contain:_ code-bearing over load-bearing; "Authority lives in the domain. The person who owns the domain is accountable to its outcomes" (WP p.08); domain ownership "small, specific, explicitly defined, interlocking" (WP p.09); the two parallel leads, "Neither reports to the other" (WP p.10); "service authority distributed to the closest-to-customer position" (Canon 01). _Must do:_ state the commitments, not the org chart. _Must refuse:_ titles, headcounts, reporting lines; those are Sessions 3 and 8. _Source:_ record. _If wrong or missing:_ Session 8 designs structure against the white paper's argument rather than a stated commitment.

**Section 11: What the charter refuses.** The standing list from 5.2, in the document's own text.

**Section 12: Held and deferred.** _Purpose:_ the honest register of what is open. _Must contain:_ every held statement with who closes it and every deferred statement with what opens it. _Must do:_ make the chef partner's inheritance legible on day one. _Must refuse:_ to let anything held read as settled. _Source:_ every section above. _If wrong or missing:_ "a settled-looking answer to an open question is the tell of a deck that has not been pressure-tested" (WP p.22).

**Section 13: Versioning.** Version, date, author of each change, and the versioning authority.

**Position 5.2 (Recommended).** The section list above, in that order, is the charter's structure. The order matters: standing before content, commitments before structure, structure before the open register. Brandon may rename sections; the set and the sequence are the team's recommendation.

## 6\. Mission, long-term commitments, and principles: structuring the decision

This section does not write any of the three. It states what each has to do, what makes one wrong, what Sŏn already holds, and exactly what Brandon supplies.

### 6.1 Mission

**What it has to do.** State why the company exists in one sentence that no other organization could hold and that is never fully achieved. Be true on opening day and true when the layer holds more. Be the thing every daypart charter and every quarterly goal ladders up to. Be deliverable in the onboarding sequence the white paper commits to.

**What makes one wrong.** Her first test: if another organization could hold it, it is a positioning line, not a mission. Her second: if it can be completed, it is a goal. Sŏn's own test, from the record: if it asserts the unproven, it is out. And a fourth, from this session: if it describes the restaurant alone, it misdescribes the company, because "The restaurant is the proof of concept. The connective layer is the asset" (WP p.34).

**The prior question: whose mission?** The canon header names Future Nostalgia Hospitality Group. The white paper says the parent "stays in the background" and "Sŏn is the only brand the customer meets at the building" (WP p.36). Her test says the parent and the restaurant cannot share one mission. A charter for the restaurant is a charter for the proof of concept. A charter for the company must have a mission that is true before the layer has held anything but Sŏn, without naming what it will hold. This is the hardest constraint on the sentence and it is Brandon's to resolve.

**Position 6.1 (Recommended).** The charter is the company's, not the restaurant's, and the mission belongs to the entity that owns the connective layer. Sŏn's service periods sit beneath it with daypart charters (section 11). This is a structural call the team has standing to make; the sentence itself is not.

**What Sŏn already holds that bears on it, quoted, tested honestly.**

*   The positioning: "Korean restraint / Texas warmth / Polished but playful" (Canon 01). This is a positioning, a description of register. It passes her uniqueness test only weakly and fails as a mission because it says what Sŏn is like, not what it is for.
*   The canon's own example of longer-form copy: "Most restaurants are pointed at the plate. We are pointed at the relationship. The plate is how we earn the right to have one" (Canon 09). This is the nearest thing in the record to a mission sentence. Tested: could another organization hold it? Yes; relationship-over-product is a claim many hospitality companies make. What would make it Sŏn's is what the record adds around it: one address, four service periods, Korean food, employee-first, a layer that carries the customer across their whole day. The sentence as written is register copy, not a decision.
*   The white paper's thesis: "Three things can be built to compound... The organization, which compounds what the company knows. The customer, which compounds the relationship. The brand, which compounds earned attention" (WP p.06). This is an investment thesis. As a mission it is held by any company that read the same argument. It is the reasoning behind a mission, not the mission.
*   The opening line of the concept: "A restaurant, read correctly, is not a room that serves food" (WP p.02). A negation. A mission cannot be a negation.

**Candidate reading, marked open and awaiting Brandon.** The record's material converges on a mission about the customer's relationship with one company across their day, carried by an organization that does not depend on any one person, through Korean food at one address in Austin. Accepting a mission of that shape would commit Sŏn to: measuring itself by the relationship and the organization rather than the plate; treating the plate as instrumental ("how we earn the right"); and holding the sentence true when the layer carries brands other than Sŏn. It would also commit the mission to a claim about Korean food specifically, or leave that to Sŏn's daypart charters and keep the company's mission cuisine-neutral. That fork is real and it is the kind of thing this candidate cannot decide.

**Position 6.2 (Founder-gated).** The mission sentence, the entity it belongs to, and whether it names the cuisine. Brandon supplies: the sentence; the decision on entity; the decision on whether Korean food is in the company's mission or Sŏn's. The team supplies the tests it must pass and the candidate above.

### 6.2 Long-term commitments

**What they have to do.** Be the ambitions over years that Sessions 3 and 4 hang metrics on. Be stable enough that they read the same after eight years, as Stripe's did. Carry no figure.

**What makes one wrong.** A target value makes it a goal, not a commitment. A future brand name asserts the unproven. A lagging indicator (revenue, labor percentage, food cost) contradicts the record: "these exist because they have always existed. All lagging indicators" (WP p.22).

**What Sŏn already holds.** The record's candidates, quoted:

*   The three engines: an organization that compounds what it knows, a customer relationship that compounds, a brand that compounds earned attention (WP p.06).
*   The leading indicators the white paper commits to measuring: "Employee NPS: would you recommend working here, tracked regularly rather than annually. Cultural labor score: beyond hours and cost, how the team is actually doing. Customer recognition rate: whether the building is actually recognizing and remembering customers" (WP p.22).
*   The cultural measures: "retention rate, internal promotion rate, engagement results across psychological safety and values alignment, and participation in development" (WP p.23).
*   The structural commitment: a company "built to run without them" (WP p.06).
*   The coherence commitment: one company across the day, each service period with its own reason to exist (WP pp. 33 to 34).

These are unusually well-formed for long-term commitments because none carries a figure and each is already a stated intent. What is missing is selection and ownership: which of these are the company's long-term commitments, which are metrics that serve them (Session 3), and which are structural design (Session 8).

**Position 6.3 (Recommended).** Long-term commitments are stated in the charter without figures; every metric that measures them lives in the operating system (Session 3) and is set on the cadence (Session 4). The candidates above are the input list.

**Position 6.4 (Founder-gated).** The selection and wording of the long-term commitments. Brandon supplies which of the record's candidates are commitments and adds any the record does not hold.

### 6.3 Principles

**What they have to do.** Be "relevant, believable, enduring, and deliverable." Be expressed in how Sŏn hires, pays, leads, and conducts itself. Be the standard Sessions 5, 6, 12, and 13 score against.

**What makes one wrong.** Her warning applies with unusual force to a company that has not opened: principles "so idealistic that they don't resonate with employees because they have no connection to how the company actually operates." Sŏn has no operation yet. Her drafting method, "write down notable moments in the company's history," has no history to draw on. What Sŏn has instead is decisions.

**What Sŏn already holds.** The record is dense with principle-shaped statements, and they fall into registers that must not be confused:

*   _Refusals._ "No Exploitation Ever / No Toxicity Ever / No Disposable People" (Canon 01). These are section 3 of the charter and are not principles in her sense; they are limits.
*   _Operating tenets stated as mechanics._ "Authority lives in the domain" (WP p.08). "When something goes wrong, the first question is not who failed. It is what allowed this to happen... Management absorbs blame from staff. Post-mortems are private and process-focused" (WP p.17). "If it matters to the experience, Sŏn pays for it. Costs are not shifted to employees" (WP pp. 19 to 20). "There is no hierarchy of importance. Everything is treated as equally important" (WP p.20). "Advancement requires preparation, not permission" (WP p.16). "The discipline is to never assert the unproven" (WP p.36). "Employees are the users" (WP p.17). "Bought where the capability is settled, built where it is the edge" (WP p.21). These are principle candidates.
*   _Cultural frameworks._ Jaeyeonmi, Ma, Mahk. These are canon tier 1 and govern the brand system. They are not company operating principles and the charter cites them rather than adopting them.
*   _The playground test._ "Does this build or foreclose conditions for agency? If it forecloses agency without a documented reason, it violates the philosophy" (Canon 01). Stated for "customers, founders, and employees," so it crosses the canon-charter seam. A principle candidate.

**Position 6.5 (Recommended).** Sŏn's principles are drawn from decisions rather than from moments, because the company has decisions and no moments. Each principle in version one is traceable to a decision already in the record or a decision Brandon makes in ratifying the charter. Version one is marked pre-opening. A mandatory revision is scheduled after dinner has run alone for its first quarter, and again after the first full year, when the company has moments to test the principles against. That revision cadence is routed to Session 4.

**Position 6.6 (Founder-gated).** The set, the count, and the wording. Brandon supplies: which of the record's tenets are principles and which are operating rules that belong in Session 3; any principle the record does not hold; the wording of each. The team supplies the candidate list above and the register constraint in 6.4.

**Position 6.7 (Chef-gated).** Whether the culinary domain contributes a principle to the company set, distinct from Mahk, which governs the brand. Left for the chef partner.

### 6.4 Why Sŏn's voice rules are an asset here

Stripe's principles are largely virtues: Curious, Resilient, Humble, Macro-optimistic, Exothermic. They name a quality and then explain it. Sŏn's voice rules forbid that register outright. "No 'We believe,' no 'journey,' no founder hero narrative" (Canon 09). The forbidden lexicon rules out authentic, passion, thoughtful, intentional, community-driven, crafted, and most of the standard vocabulary of a values statement. Rule 1: "Copy never names its own effect." Binary test 5: "Could this sentence appear unchanged in a competitor's copy? Out."

That constraint does her work for her. Her failure mode is the principle that sounds good and does not connect to operation. Sŏn's grammar cannot produce that principle. A principle written under Sŏn's rules has to be a statement of what the company does or refuses, in subject-verb form, ending at its last load-bearing word, specific enough that no competitor could print it. "Management absorbs blame from staff" passes every one of her tests and every one of canon's. "We value humility" passes none. The company's voice rules are the deliverability test built into the sentence, and the charter is written under them without exception.

**Position 6.8 (Recommended).** The charter's mission, commitments, and principles are written under canon's voice rules and pass canon's six binary tests. A principle that fails test 5 is not a principle; it is a claim any restaurant could make.
