## 15\. Findings inside Sŏn's record

Thirteen findings, each a conflict, a silence, or two accounts of the same thing, found by reading the white paper and both canon artifacts against each other and against themselves. Each is written as what the record says in one place, what it says elsewhere or fails to say, why the difference bears on recruiting specifically, and who closes it. The six-tier hierarchy difference between the canon artifacts, the floor manager and Maitre d question, the data hub, and the period count are already open in the ledger and are not counted again; where one of them touches a finding it is named as adjacent. None of these is resolved on this page. Where a section above supplied a working answer, the finding says which position holds it and marks it as the team's reading, not the record's.

**15.1 One development marker, and a thesis that needs two.** In one place: "Cross-strand fluency, the ability to hold both at once, is the real development marker," "visible in the web as more connections and recognized in compensation as meaningful" (WP p.11), and its recognition is a named open item, "Compensation architecture, how cross-strand fluency is recognized and paid" (WP p.15). Elsewhere: the house is "one restaurant and one brand, one brand texture, met at different times of day" (WP p.33), late night "is dinner's own later register" (WP p.35), canon's fifth visual principle is "One system, four moods" (Canon v1.0, section 03), the service model holds "Same foundation, four registers" (Canon v1.0, section 08), and the deck says "Each daypart continues the one before it. None begins again" (Canon v3.0, p.18). Every one of those requires the same person to hold a different register at a different hour: the server whose jacket comes off at late night (Canon v1.0, section 08; Canon v3.0, p.81), the person at the window at seven and on the floor at seven. The record names no marker for that, and says nothing about whether it is recognized. Why it bears on recruiting: the seat sheet's service-period field (P10) is where a second period is recorded, one pool staffs the periods, and the first period expansion is the first succession event, so the dinner cohort is being hired into a fluency the record has not named. Who closes: Session 13 for whether it is recognized in compensation, Session 8 for its structural placement, and the founders on P62. Silence.

**15.2 The first thing a candidate is handed is the artifact Part I argues against.** In one place: the transparency sheet's first item is "the org chart" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: "The org chart calls them the most replaceable. That is not a cultural problem. It is a structural misread" (WP p.7); the web has "No top. No bottom" (WP p.9); and the artifact meant to replace the chart is an open item, "Visual design, the web rendered as a designed organizational artifact rather than a chart" (WP p.15). So the sheet names an artifact the record rejects, and the artifact the record wants instead is undrawn. Why it bears on recruiting: item 1 is the first thing a candidate reads, at the first interview, before any offer; a chart with a box above their seat tells them the opposite of Part I before their first day, and a lead candidate reading it will arrive with the General Manager's playbook the rubric is built to refuse (P55). Who closes: the record's author for the sheet's wording, and whoever the founders name for the visual design open item for the render; P32 holds the interim, the web from the candidate's node outward and a hand-drawn neighborhood, as the team's reading. Contradiction, with a silence underneath it.

**15.3 The mechanics are handed at the first interview and are not finished.** In one place: "The candidate receives a single sheet with everything needed to decide: ... the compensation mechanics" (WP p.18), "No surprises and nothing withheld." Elsewhere: the built-in compensation is "set at a defined percentage that is still being finalized" (WP p.20), and "the remaining open piece is the final percentage" (WP p.22). Why it bears on recruiting: this is a sequencing conflict and not only an open number. The leads are in the building at least six weeks before dinner's gate (S4 carryover C1), so their first interviews run months before the gate, and the record's own sheet cannot be handed as specified until the architecture is ratified. The compensation architecture is therefore on the critical path of the hiring timeline, and the record does not say so. Who closes: Session 13 for the architecture, the founders on P35 for whether a first interview may run while item 6 reads "being finalized," which is the record's own word (WP p.20), and Session 6 for placing the ratification on the hiring calendar. Sequencing conflict.

**15.4 The content approval framework has no class for a person who is not team.** In one place: green-light content is "behind-the-scenes, team, food, community," strategic review is "trend participation, competitive commentary, partnership announcements," and leadership review is "crisis response, strategic announcements, sensitive topics" (WP p.31). Elsewhere: the documented build names "a chef search" as content (WP p.29), and its method invites the audience "into real decisions" (WP p.29). A candidate is not team, may never be, and is not named in any class; "sensitive topics" is not defined to reach them, and "community" arguably reaches a follower-candidate. Why it bears on recruiting: the build is the talent brand's distribution (P17), the chef search is named material, and the class gap sits exactly where the record most wants to publish. Who closes: Brandon's seat as the brand cadence's owner (WP p.3, p.31); P19 adds one rule and I19 the record, as the team's reading. Silence.

**15.5 Canon governs every word and names no surface a candidate reads.** In one place: canon is "The source of truth for every decision made under this name" (Canon v3.0, p.1), the language constant applies "in any internal communication" (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.5), and the forbidden lexicon applies "in all contexts, no exceptions" (Canon v1.0, section 09). Elsewhere: the register matrix names six surfaces, the dinner menu, the lunch menu, short-form digital, longer-form digital, in-space copy, and correspondence (Canon v1.0, section 09; Canon v3.0, p.55), and none is a recruiting surface or any employee-facing surface. "You" is specified "in customer-facing contexts" (Canon v1.0, section 01), and a candidate reading a posting is not a customer in that moment. Canon's Korean terminology rule, "stands without explanation in all brand contexts" (Canon v1.0, section 04), does not say whether a document handed to a candidate is a brand context, and the terminology deployment rules are themselves deferred (Canon v1.0, What Remains; Canon v3.0, p.91). Why it bears on recruiting: every posting, every answer, and the transparency sheet are bound by rules whose register is not named for them, so the team read one (P22) and could only mark it held. Who closes: canon's owner, and the deferred terminology session. Silence.

**15.6 Inclusion mechanics, and no position on who the team is.** In one place: language choice "protects dignity" (WP p.17), the fourth read asks "whether the building is equipped to create the environment this person needs to succeed" (WP p.18), and engagement is measured "across psychological safety and values alignment" (WP p.23). Elsewhere: nothing. The record states no goal, no read, and no position on the composition of the team; canon's non-negotiables are conduct constraints, not composition ones (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.4). Why it bears on recruiting: her chapter treats referral-driven homogeneity as first-order (Book p.172, p.181) and her workbook scores a recruiter on it (Workbook p.49); the record's own sources each narrow, the founders' reach, the referral, and a build audience that "self-selects at higher value" (WP p.29); and without a position the source-dominance read (P26) can report and cannot act. Who closes: the founders, routed to Session 11. Silence.

**15.7 The chef owns the vision; the brand owns the identity; the same person is a designation.** In one place: "the chef partner owns the culinary vision as an equal founding partner" (WP p.3), "The culinary vision is real and it is led by the chef partner" (WP p.37), and whether lunch is built "is an equal decision among all three partners, the chef partner included" (WP p.36). Elsewhere: "culinary identity belongs to the brand, not the chef" (Canon v1.0, section 02; Canon v3.0, p.33), "The brand owns the culinary identity. The chef executes within it" (Canon v1.0, What Remains), with the chef held as a hire (Canon v1.0, What Remains; Canon v3.0, p.87) and supplying "The dishes and the technique that execute within it" (Canon v3.0, p.89). Underneath both, the white paper places "The Chef Partner" among the functional designations one level below the management layer, owning "culinary execution during service, which is not the same as culinary direction overall," designations that "are not permanent elevations above anyone" (WP p.10), which is coherent for a partner in a code-bearing web and leaves "culinary direction overall" owned by no named seat in that paragraph. Why it bears on recruiting: it decides whether the third seat is recruited at all, whether canon's criteria are a scorecard or due diligence (P57), what a kitchen candidate is told they work inside, and who the kitchen's domain lead is in the hiring sense, since a nightly designation cannot open a seat. Who closes: the founders in the chef ruling (`86akh2qrp`, filed at `86akh3tw9`), and canon's owner for the wording. Contradiction, two accounts, with the designation as a third.

**15.8 The inward-facing floor strand has no domain lead.** In one place: below the management layer "the web is composed of strands, not levels," the inward-facing strand's output is "the operational sequence that makes the outward strand possible," and the customer "never feels this strand" (WP p.10 to 11); "In the kitchen, domain owners are Station Leads"; "In beverage, the Head of Beverage owns the program" (WP p.11). Elsewhere: for the floor, no domain owner is named for the inward-facing strand. The Maitre d owns "the how of the experience" and team development, the Operations Lead owns operational outcomes and reads the systems (WP p.10), and a runner's seat sits between them. Canon's uniform table names the runner as a role, "Quiet layer, no logo. Never the subject" (Canon v3.0, p.81), and names no lead for it; canon's floor manager "owns the room" (Canon v1.0, section 08; Canon v3.0, p.79), which is the adjacent open question. Why it bears on recruiting: every entry in section 12 that says "domain lead" is incomplete for runner seats, so no runner seat can be opened, decided, or given a practical in range until this closes (12.8, P64), and the sheet's field 3 for those seats reads as held. Who closes: the founders on P64, with Session 8's structure. Silence.

**15.9 The last round for the seats hired first has no pre-opening form, and no stated reads.** In one place: "For leadership and salaried roles, the final round is a dinner in the room, which is evaluation and recruitment at once" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: the two leads are hired before there is a room, since the leads' review must run six consecutive weeks before dinner's gate (S4 row 21, carryover C1), and the chef is upstream of the menu that is upstream of the room (P58); the record gives the dinner no pre-opening form for exactly the seats it names it for. The same sentence names what the round is and not what it reads, and a stage with no stated reads is the instinct read the record rejects two pages earlier ("reads competency rather than instinct," WP p.17). Why it bears on recruiting: the record's own last round for its most consequential seats cannot run as written for any of them. Who closes: the founders on P37 for the substitute; P45 supplies the reads as the team's reading. Silence.

**15.10 There is no seat inventory, and three lists of what seats exist.** In one place: the white paper names seats in prose, Operations Lead, Maitre d, Lead Host, Chef Partner, Head of Beverage, Station Leads, Chef on the line, Chef on prep, Steward, server, runner, host (WP p.10 to 11), and "roughly eight leadership lines" (WP p.22), with role naming an open item (WP p.15). Elsewhere: canon's uniform system names five roles, floor manager, hosts, servers, bar, and daytime (Canon v1.0, section 08), and the deck names five different ones, Maître d', server, floor manager, bartender, and runner (Canon v3.0, p.81), dropping hosts and the daytime role and adding the runner. No artifact holds a list of seats as a structure artifact, and "daytime" is a seat for a period without a ratified charter. Why it bears on recruiting: P14's range forbids opening a seat that is not on the inventory, P60 requires every inventory seat's competency requirements to exist before the cohort arrives, and row 36 cannot hold, all against a list that does not exist. Who closes: the founders on P15 for the owner, Session 8 for the structure, and the role naming session the record already names. Silence, with three accounts.

**15.11 Creators are offered a seat at a training day, and training days are where the cohort's practicals run.** In one place: creator access includes "a construction tour, a private tasting, or a seat at a training day" (WP p.31). Elsewhere: the practical is "in a real environment" (WP p.18), and pre-opening the only real environment is the training service, so the cohort's practicals run there (P42); canon forbids spectacle during dinner service (Canon v1.0, section 06), and P18 forbids a camera on any assessment stage. The record grants the access and says nothing about candidates being present at the day it grants access to. Why it bears on recruiting: a creator at a training day is a camera on a practical, and a candidate assessed in front of a creator has been treated as content before the decision. Who closes: Brandon's seat as the brand cadence's owner, with the Maitre d; the team's reading is that a training day with a creator present carries no practical, and it is filed as a work item rather than decided here. Silence.

**15.12 Format choice as a qualification filter reads against the record's own first principle.** In one place: "Respect for time is the first principle," the candidate chooses "the format, phone, video, or in person," and "Language choice protects dignity" (WP p.17). In the next paragraph: "Format choice does double duty as a qualification filter. Someone exploring options chooses a phone screen. Someone serious chooses in person. Someone with a transportation constraint chooses video" (WP p.17). Read as a filter, the sentence scores the candidate with a transportation constraint below the one without, in the record's own words, and scores a phone choice as low seriousness for the high-volume seats where the record itself mandates a phone screen (WP p.17). Why it bears on recruiting: if format is a score, the record's most inclusive mechanism becomes its least, and the seats it affects most are the high-volume ones. Who closes: the record's author; P31's table reads format as the candidate's own signal and never a bar, as the team's reading, and 12.3 forbids a decline on it. Internal tension.

**15.13 Interviewers are trained, and nothing trains the first ones.** In one place: "Interviewers are trained, because asking a good question and reading the answer is a learned skill, not an instinct that arrives with a title" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: the training infrastructure is the learning platform, on which "Any qualified team member can create training modules" (WP p.19), and the platform does not exist before the team does. Pre-opening the founders are the only interviewers, then the two leads, and nothing in the record trains any of them; the first hires of the house are made by untrained interviewers under the record's own definition. Why it bears on recruiting: row 44 requires a training record before any stage runs, and I21 requires one for every partner before the first stage, which the record cannot supply. Who closes: Session 6 for the training's content, and the founders for how they are trained before the platform exists, which the team routes to Session 6 as a carryover. Sequencing silence.

Thirteen findings: six silences, three contradictions or two-account conflicts, two sequencing conflicts, one internal tension, and one silence carrying three accounts. Session 1 found two, Session 2 three, Session 3 four, Session 4 six; the count here is what the read produced and is not a continuation of that line. Three of the thirteen (15.3, 15.9, 15.12) sit inside or beside the Talent acquisition section (WP p.17 to 18) and would have surfaced from a narrow read of it. The other ten would not: 15.1 needs Part I, Part V, and two canon sections read together; 15.2 needs pages 7, 9, 15, and 18; 15.4 and 15.11 need Part IV read against Part II; 15.5 needs both canon artifacts read whole; 15.7 needs pages 3, 10, 36, and 37 against canon's architecture tier, its held items, and the deck's gate table; 15.8 and 15.10 need the seat lists across all three artifacts; 15.13 needs page 18 against page 19. A session that pulled the Talent acquisition section and stopped would have held the candidate-facing system as decided and missed that the record cannot yet run it.

**P69 (Recommended).** The thirteen findings are filed as stated, each routed to who closes it. None is resolved on this page; where a section above supplied a working answer it is the team's reading and marked as such in the finding. 15.11 and 15.13 are filed as new items: a work item for training days with creators present, and a carryover to Session 6 for how the first interviewers are trained before the platform exists.

Count by mark: Recommended 57; Founder-gated 11; Chef-gated 1; Team-filled 0. Total 69. Nothing marked final or landed.

Two things about the count. Chef-gated carries one position because the kitchen is gated whole by the chef ruling (P57) rather than seat by seat, and every kitchen item on this page, the sheets, the sourcing, the practicals, and the decision-rights entries, sits under P44 and P58 rather than under its own mark. Team-filled carries none because recruiting precedes the team; what the team fills once it exists, the languages the process is available in, the trained interviewer pool, the pool's first entries, lives inside the instruments as fields and not as positions.

What the founders must close before the recommended positions can be acted on, in the order the hiring timeline needs them. First, the chef seat ruling (P57), because the timeline places the chef first and every kitchen row, sheet, and entry waits on it; until it is filed, dinner's gate cannot open (row 59). Second, the hiring partner (S4 P4), because that seat runs the burst, opens the first seats, and decides the first packets, and P49 turns on it. Third, the seat inventory's owner (P15), because without an inventory no seat can be opened in range and row 36 fails. Fourth, whether a first interview may run before the compensation mechanics are ratified (P35), because the leads' first interviews fall months before Session 13 can close the architecture; with it, the pre-opening substitute for the dinner in the room (P37), because the leads' last round has no other form. Fifth, the practical's employment form, at least in its interim (P43), because no practical runs without it. Sixth, the inward-facing floor strand's domain lead and the hosts' lead (P64), because no runner or host seat can be opened until they are named. Then the three that do not block a hire but shape one: the candidate-facing register before a posting goes live (P22), whether a referral is paid (P25), and whether a search firm is used for the two leads (P56). The interim two-partner decision rule, open in the ledger, decides the one entry this page could not complete, a disagreement between partners about a lead seat pre-opening. Whether the house states a position on the composition of its team (P26) is routed to Session 11 and does not block the cohort. Everything else on this page can be acted on the day Brandon ratifies it.

# S6: Hiring, the interview loop, and the scorecard

# Session 6: Hiring

This page is the Sŏn answer to the Hiring section of Chapter 3 (Book p.193 to 215), with the Chapter 3 workbook read for its interview framework and rubric, its sample questions, its written exercise, and its candidate review framework (Workbook p.43 to 77). It is written to be run from. A person who has not read the book can read this page and know what happens once a candidate is in a seat's pipeline: what each stage asks, who asks it, what counts as evidence, what is written down, how the decision is made, what the candidate is told, and what the process refuses to conclude about a person.

Every position on this page is numbered from P1 and carries exactly one mark. (Recommended) is the team's position, ready for founder ratification. (Founder-gated) requires input the team cannot supply. (Chef-gated) is left open for the chef partner. (Team-filled) is populated once the team exists. Nothing on this page is final. A recommended position is a recommendation until Brandon ratifies it, and a founder-gated position is argued to the ceiling one founder can reach and then marked for what Dominic, the chef, or the team must close.

Vocabulary follows the ledger and Session 5. "Operating system," unqualified, is the human system of strategy, accountability, and cadence; the software is "the stack" or "the OS surface." The customer is the customer, in every stage and every document. Service periods are named by time of day. A "seat" is a node in the web with a domain, a strand, and documented competency requirements; the "seat sheet" is the sixteen-field artifact that opens it (S5 P12); its field 8 is the assessment rubric this page fills (S5 P67). "The four reads" are competency for the strand at entry level, growth potential as self-directed mastery, cultural alignment as the non-negotiables plus comfort with distributed authority and the customer as customer, and what the building must supply for this person to succeed (S5 P5). "The packet" is the complete set of independently submitted scorecards on which the domain lead decides (S5 P46). Section 6 gives the four reads a second name, as the scorecard's four dimensions, because that is the form Session 13 inherits.

Financials are not a context source for this program. Her chapter carries salary bands, a compa-ratio worked example, a pay parity review, and the claim that compensation is a company's largest expense (Book p.199 to 202). None of it enters this page, as quotation, illustration, or range. Where a decision needs a figure, the page says the figure is not a context source and states the gap. Her line on page 214 that ends in profanity is referred to and not quoted.

Two tools are named because Brandon named them: Greenhouse is the applicant tracking system, retained over Rippling's native hiring module; Rippling is the single sign-on and human-resources layer. This page says, for every mechanism it places in a tool, whether it is configuration, a build, or to confirm. Nothing on this page asserts a tool feature as fact. No operating-system document names a data hub tool (`86akh5u6e`), and nothing here assumes one.

## 1\. Her ask, and what Sŏn already holds

### 1.1 Her ask

Her hiring section opens on a claim and a discipline. The claim: "interviewing is a skill that improves with practice" and is "best employed within a set process, with clear frameworks for assessment" (Book p.193). The discipline is small and exact: "a relatively simple framework for what all interviews should focus on, a clear sense of the tactical steps a candidate will experience, and a plan for how a decision is reached on making an offer" (Book p.193). She adds the candidate's side, that it is "critical to prep your candidates well," not by telling them the questions but by "setting them at ease" with the process, its length, the interview types, the dress code, and who they will meet (Book p.193).

Her process guidelines run as a list (Book p.193 to 194): a clear job description; decide who interviews; a ceiling of eight interviewers, "reduced to four or five" for entry-level and well-understood roles; trained interviewers; the rubric shared with every interviewer and "one or two elements of the rubric" assigned to each "to avoid overlap"; a kickoff for custom roles; a first round of three to narrow before the panel; a hiring committee or candidate review "to finalize your selection"; references checked by recruiter and hiring manager; the offer. Complexity "can flex up or down" with volume, and for high-volume roles "you may even be able to eventually forgo hiring committee meetings" (Book p.194).

Interviewing education: STAR as a framework; consistency as "the most effective interviewing tactic," meaning "the same questions of every candidate, while also leaving space in the interview to probe" (Book p.194); four common mistakes, not using the rubric, not interviewing for the capabilities the role most needs, assessing liking rather than success in the role, and over-prioritizing "the right candidate experience rather than the right trajectory and aptitude to learn" (Book p.195); the five things the best interviews suss out (Book p.195); her self-awareness and learning test, and the "I" versus "we" read (Book p.195); the three question types, situational, behavioral, and strict competency (Book p.195); working company values into behavioral questions without naming them (Book p.196); the written exercise (Book p.196); and the candidate experience as the one thing most candidates will ever know of the company (Book p.196).

Non-leader roles: scaled roles with a wide interviewer pool and a hiring manager or proxy, less frequent roles with "the same people interview all of the candidates" and a cross-section of functions on the panel (Book p.196); the Bar Raiser and Elevate programs, with Elevate's selection built from ATS feedback histories (Book p.197 to 198); the Stripe offer-approval channel with a twenty-four-hour turnaround (Book p.197); decision-making as consultative with the hiring manager as primary decision-maker and "checks and balances" such as executive or committee review (Book p.198); job level selection and everything that follows from it, which this page does not carry (Book p.198 to 202); candidate selection at Stripe with a live committee only on disagreement, newness, or uniqueness, the recruiter measured on funnel efficiency and hire quality, and the norm that "anyone on the hiring committee can veto a hire" (Book p.203); the four goals of whoever stewards the process, guard the candidate experience, really listen to interviewers, bring the organization along, decide for the company (Book p.204); the candidate review sidebar at full length (Book p.204 to 207); reference checking, with the rule that "Not making reference calls is a mistake," the lukewarm-reference rule, the percentile question, and seven behavioral reference questions (Book p.207 to 208); and the offer, verbal before written, nothing a surprise, documents automated early, the offer letter as a legal document, and the sell chat (Book p.208 to 209).

Leadership: transparency inside the company and its limits, layering, confidentiality for the candidate, the decision as the CEO's on a consultative process, the whole thing run as change management, the steps (two important people excited, stakeholders identified, a loop of stakeholders, deliberation as a feedback-collection forum, the announcement), the experience trap in the interview, hiring disagreements in both directions, and references and offers for leaders (Book p.209 to 215). Hiring internally: one candidate or several, no sham process, friction sussed out, external candidates met and said so, a lightweight internal loop with a feedback loop for the unselected, confidentiality, and the announcement (Book p.213 to 214).

The workbook supplies the worked form: one role's full framework, a recruiter screen, a team screen run in tandem with a written project, and four onsite interviews each with named competencies, named runners, a length, documented questions with situation, action, and result follow-ups, and a three- or four-column rubric with anchors (Workbook p.43 to 66); the sample questions with what each seeks (Workbook p.67 to 69); the written exercise with its twelve-point grading (Workbook p.70 to 72); and the candidate review decision-making framework in five steps (Workbook p.73 to 77). Pages 78 onward belong to Sessions 7 and 15 and are not read here.

### 1.2 What the record holds

The record's hiring system is two paragraphs long and Session 5 held them whole (S5 P1). "Interviewers are trained, because asking a good question and reading the answer is a learned skill, not an instinct that arrives with a title. Interviews are semi-structured with documented questions, and they assess specific competencies, cultural alignment, and growth potential rather than gut feeling. The goal is not only whether this is the right person, but whether the building is equipped to create the environment this person needs to succeed" (WP p.18). "For roles with a physical skill component, the second interview is a paid practical in a real environment. This replaces the stage" (WP p.18). "Speed is respect. When the skills and the alignment are there, the decision is made quickly and development starts immediately" (WP p.18). "For leadership and salaried roles, the final round is a dinner in the room, which is evaluation and recruitment at once" (WP p.18). "No one is ghosted" (WP p.18). Around those two paragraphs sit the commitments hiring runs inside: self-scheduling, language choice, format choice, the phone screen for high-volume roles, no unanswered applications (WP p.17); the transparency sheet at the first interview (WP p.18); "Employees are the users" (WP p.17); "Universal problems are not people problems. They are design problems" (WP p.17); labor as an asset in a tight Austin market (WP p.16).

The structure hiring reads against is Part I. New people "always enter at the outside edge" (WP p.9); the outside edge is "the most sensitive position" (WP p.9); "Every position has documented competency requirements visible to anyone" (WP p.11); the strands are "different jobs requiring different types of intelligence," not a promotion sequence (WP p.11); the invisible advocate auto-schedules the practical assessment and the ready-now pool holds the person with no open seat (WP p.11); "Advancement requires preparation, not permission" (WP p.14); functional designations "are not permanent elevations above anyone" (WP p.10); the two leads are parallel and "Neither reports to the other" (WP p.10). The record's performance system, which section 6 couples to, "develop\[s\] people rather than judge\[s\] them," reviews "every three to six months" on "development, growth, and the path forward rather than a verdict," under "no surprises," with feedback running "both directions" (WP p.19). Its training system is the learning platform, on which "Any qualified team member can create training modules and get paid for teaching everyone else," with "competency validation: no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19).

Canon's constraints hold on every word of it: the non-negotiables (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.4), the language constant "Internal communication included" (Canon v3.0, p.5), the playground philosophy's prohibition on "training systems that measure procedure execution without building toward judgment" and its requirement of "service authority distributed to the closest-to-customer position" (Canon v1.0, section 01), nunchi "Developed through mastery, exercised through judgment" (Canon v3.0, p.15), Mahk's requirement that "service speaks to a dish with felt knowledge, not recited description" (Canon v1.0, section 01), the five voice rules and six binary tests (Canon v1.0, section 09; Canon v3.0, p.53 to 54), and canon's one worked selection instrument, the photographer criteria with a cultural-fluency evaluation whose failure condition is a question the candidate asks (Canon v1.0, section 10; Canon v3.0, p.64).

### 1.3 What Session 5 already decided

Session 5 is this page's immediate upstream, and it decided most of what her chapter assumes a company still has to decide. The stages exist and are fixed by seat class: every seat takes application, first interview, decision, and answer; high-volume seats add the phone screen; physical-skill seats add the paid practical; leadership and salaried seats add the dinner in the room; domain-owner seats add an adjacent-domain second interviewer to the first interview; and pre-opening every seat adds the founder stage (S5 P38, P53; carryover `86akh7qdf`). The four reads are fixed and assigned per stage (S5 P5). Who may run each stage and who may not is fixed (S5 12.2). The scorecard's shape is fixed and it carries no free-text verdict (S5 I7 to I13). There is no hiring committee, no hiring meeting, and no recruiting seat; the decision is the domain lead's on a complete packet of independent scorecards, made the day the packet completes, with the answer sent the same day, and Greenhouse refuses a decision on an incomplete packet (S5 P46, P48; carryover `86akh7qkj`). A decline names a read or a must-have and nothing else. A lead who interviews at the first interview requires the second interviewer. A hole is held rather than filled below the bar, and the leads' review carries the hole as a slack question (S5 P46). The seat sheet is the one account of a seat and the invisible advocate reads the same document (S5 P11, P12). The transparency sheet is handed at the first interview and its item 6, the compensation mechanics, gates every offer (S5 P34, P35). Five instruments are refused, her work style grid, résumé review and the take-home, the hiring committee and meeting, her recruiter's loop and scorecard, and the bias-neutralizing copy tool (S5 I26 to I30). The readiness test stands at fifty-nine rows (S5 P65). Interviewer training is an obligation of the house with a training record on the person page, the stack enforcing it, and a re-training trigger when a scorecard returns without a named read (S5 P52, I21).

What Session 5 left to this page is exactly what her chapter is about: the inside of every stage. The documented questions, the anchors that say what evidence looks like at entry level, the interviewer training and its content, the calibration that keeps the read consistent, the practical's scoring, the scorecard's dimensions, the packet's reading, references, the offer, what hiring needs from levels, the leadership loop for the two leads and the third seat under each branch, the internal loop, and the hiring calendar placed against gates (carryovers `86akh7qdf`, `86akh7qey`, `86akh7qhr`, `86akh67gj`, `86akh3vbd`, `86akh3vrq`, `86akh5ut1`, `86ajgnhh3`).

### 1.4 How much is decided, and where she is refused

Honestly counted, her hiring section divides in three. About a third is absorbed nearly whole, because the record already asks for it and Session 5 already built the structure it runs in: trained interviewers, consistency, documented questions with probes, STAR as the probe's form, the three question types, values worked in without naming them, candidate prep, interviewer prep, the experience trap and its counter-questions, verbal before written, nothing a surprise, references for the seats where a reference can be read, the sham-process warning, confidentiality for a leadership candidate. About a third is refused, and refused as form rather than function: the hiring committee, the candidate review panel, the Bar Raiser and Elevate as seats or programs, the offer-approval channel, job levels and everything downstream of them, the veto as a standing right, the sell chat as a performed conversation, external validation interviews for an internal hire, and the "not sure" response. Section 8 works the functions inside the refused forms one by one and says where each lands. The last third does not apply because Sŏn does not have the thing it assumes: a recruiting function to steward the process, an organization to bring along, a person being layered, a board, ladders and levels to place a hire on, and a volume of hires and years of performance data to calibrate against.

The hardest inheritance is the one the brief names: Session 5 refused candidate review against a house of roughly eight leadership lines (WP p.22), and it refused the form. Her sidebar's mission, "a consistent, efficient, and transparent decision-making framework that seeks to control for bias" (Book p.205), is not a form. It is four functions, and a house that refuses the panel still owes each of them a home or an honest statement that it has none. Section 8 does that work and, where it finds an S5 position that should change, surfaces the conflict rather than overwriting it (section 8.4, section 19).

**P1 (Recommended).** Session 5's structure is held whole: the stages by class, the four reads per stage, the runners, the scorecard's shape, the no-verdict rule, the domain lead's decision on a complete packet, the five refused instruments, and the fifty-nine readiness rows. This page fills the structure and alters none of it. Every place it extends a Session 5 specification it says so by position number, and every place it would contradict one it stops and surfaces the conflict (sections 7.4, 8.4, 10.2, and 19) for Brandon rather than overwriting it.

**P2 (Recommended).** Her hiring section is absorbed for its discipline and refused for its forms. Absorbed: trained interviewers, the consistency rule, STAR as the probe structure, the three question types, principles worked in unnamed, candidate and interviewer prep, the experience-trap counters, references where a reference can be read, verbal before written, nothing a surprise, no sham process, candidate confidentiality. Refused, each with what does its work in section 17: the hiring committee and candidate review panel, the Bar Raiser and Elevate as seats, the offer-approval channel, job levels and their downstream, the veto as a standing right, the sell chat as performance, external validation interviews for an internal hire, and the "not sure" response.

## 2\. What an interview is for at Sŏn

### 2.1 Her five things, tested against the four reads

"The best interviews suss out how someone: Works with other people. Gets quality work done themselves. Motivates and develops themselves. Has or can develop the expertise needed for the role. Demonstrates leadership and resilience" (Book p.195). Five things, written for a company where a hire may be a manager and the interview is the whole assessment. Sŏn's interview is one stage among several, and its reads are fixed at four. The test is whether her five are already inside the four or whether one is missing.

Works with other people. In a load-bearing organization this is a personality trait. In a tensegrity web it is the structure itself: "The strength of the whole lives in the relationships between elements" (WP p.8), and the inward-facing strand's intelligence is "architectural and coordinated" (WP p.11), the outward-facing strand's "relational" (WP p.10). So working with others is not a fifth read; it is inside the first, because the strand's intelligence is a way of working with adjacent nodes, and inside the third, because "No Disposable People" (Canon v1.0, section 01) is a rule about how a person treats the people around them, including the steward and the runner who will never be above them.

Gets quality work done themselves. At entry level this is the practical's read for physical-skill seats, "procedure mastery and reproduction under load" (S5 P41), and the first read's evidence for every seat: a specific thing done, described specifically.

Motivates and develops themselves. This is the second read whole: "growth potential, read as evidence of self-directed mastery" (S5 3.1). The record's advancement system "favors the people who want it most" (WP p.11), and the interview reads for prior evidence of wanting something enough to have mastered it without being asked.

Has or can develop the expertise. "Has" is the first read at entry; "can develop" is the second read plus the seat sheet's field 7, what the house develops, which the interviewer does not score (S5 P12). Her "or" is exactly the record's split between the two horizons of field 6.

Demonstrates leadership and resilience. Leadership is not a read for an edge seat, because there is no altitude to lead from and a functional designation is "not a permanent elevation" (WP p.10). For the two lead seats it is competency for that seat, which S5 P55 defined as holding a domain without an apex, and section 3.5 gives it a question block. Resilience, read as holding up under load, is the practical's read, "reproduction under load," and the interview does not score it; a candidate can describe a hard night, and that description is evidence for the second read (what they learned) and the third (who they blamed), never a score for resilience itself, because the room is the only honest test of it and the practical is the room.

So her five map onto the four with one thing left over, and the leftover is deliberate: an interview at Sŏn does not read leadership at the edge and does not read resilience in a chair.

**P3 (Recommended).** Her five things are inside the four reads: working with others inside competency for the strand and the non-negotiables; getting work done inside competency and the practical; self-motivation is the second read whole; expertise present or developable is field 6's two horizons; leadership is competency for a lead seat only; resilience is the practical's load read and is never scored in an interview. No read is added.

### 2.2 Her self-awareness test, and the "I" and "we" read

"The best way to test for self-awareness is to ask a candidate how their colleagues would describe them. If they only say positive things, probe what constructive feedback they've received. Then ask, 'And what have you done to improve?'" (Book p.195). Eric Yuan's line beside it, that the number one thing is "Do they really want to learn?" (Book p.195), is the record's own bar for the second read. The three-part question is the best single instrument in her chapter for self-directed mastery, because its third part asks for an action the candidate took on their own account after hearing something they did not want to hear, and that is the behavior the invisible advocate rewards. It becomes the anchor question for the second read at every first interview, for every seat, in the same three parts and the same order (section 4.4).

"Watch for how much they use 'I' or 'we.' Too much 'I' is a flag that they may not be humble or collaborative ... Too much 'we' may obscure what role they played" (Book p.195). She prefers "we." At Sŏn the read is different in a specific way. The web's rigid anchor points are "domain ownership: small, specific, explicitly defined, interlocking" (WP p.9). A person who cannot say what they held is not describing a node; they are describing a team they stood inside. So "we" is the expected register and "what did you hold" is the required probe, every time, and the answer to the probe is evidence for the first read (did they own something specific) and for the third (did they credit the adjacent nodes). Her own example of the good answer, "It was my idea, but the credit goes to the whole team" (Book p.195), holds both. Her example of the less good, "I just did what everyone else decided" (Book p.195), fails distributed authority, because a person who will be handed a range and expected to act inside it has just said they wait to be told.

**P4 (Recommended).** Her three-part self-awareness question is the anchor question for the second read at every first interview, asked in her order. The "I" and "we" read is recorded as evidence, not scored as a trait: "we" is the expected register, "what did you hold" is the mandatory probe, and a candidate who can name what they held and credit the nodes beside them has given evidence for the first and third reads at once.

### 2.3 What an interview may conclude, and what it may not

An interview at Sŏn is one stage, run by a trained person, against a seat sheet, producing a scorecard with evidence against four reads. That sentence sets what it may conclude.

It may conclude that evidence for a read was heard or was not, against the entry bar the sheet states, and it may say what the evidence was. It may conclude that a disqualifier from field 9 was present, with the evidence. It may record, in the candidate's words, what the building must supply. It may recommend advance or decline, with the read named. That is all.

It may not conclude nunchi, because nunchi is "Developed through mastery" (Canon v3.0, p.15) and the house has taught the candidate nothing yet (S5 P6). It may not conclude Jeong, which "requires time, repetition, and memory" (Canon v1.0, section 01). It may not conclude presence, charm, energy, or how the room would feel about the person; those are the outgoing-profile distortion carryover `86ajgnhh3` warns about, and section 4.9 says what in the loop catches them. It may not conclude "fit," which is not a read (S5 P5). It may not conclude a level, a rate, or a place on any scale, because Sŏn has none (section 12). It may not conclude that the candidate can reproduce a procedure at tempo; only the practical can (S5 P41). It may not conclude anything about a competency the house develops (field 7); an interviewer who scores field 7 as absent has scored the house's own obligation as the candidate's failure. It may not conclude that the candidate will succeed in month six; the ninety-day plan and the check-in are where that is learned, and an interview that claims it has confused prediction with assessment. It may not read the candidate's format choice as anything (S5 P31, 15.12). And it may not conclude an offer, imply one, state a figure beyond the transparency sheet, or ask what the candidate earns elsewhere (S5 P40).

Two of those refusals are stricter than hers and are the record's. She allows an interviewer to weigh "the right trajectory and aptitude to learn" against experience (Book p.195); at Sŏn experience is not on the sheet at all, so there is nothing to weigh it against. She allows the founder's amorphous no on the candidate who is "just fine" (Book p.171); Session 5 removed it, and a no with no read is a re-training trigger (S5 P53, P52).

**P5 (Recommended).** An interview at Sŏn may conclude whether evidence for each assigned read was heard against the entry bar, whether a disqualifier was present, what the candidate said they need from the building, and a recommendation with a read named. It may not conclude nunchi, Jeong, presence, fit, a level, tempo reproduction, a developed competency's absence, month-six success, anything from format choice, or an offer.

### 2.4 Her four mistakes as the four failure modes

Her four most common interviewer mistakes (Book p.195) are, at Sŏn, the four failure modes the training names and the calibration read looks for.

Not using the rubric, "asking different questions of different candidates, and therefore never finding a way to benchmark an excellent answer." At Sŏn the question set is on the seat sheet's field 8 and the interview kit is configured from it; the stack shows the questions in order; the calibration read checks whether every question was asked (row 68). A scorecard with a blank question line and no reason is the tell.

Not interviewing for the capabilities most needed. At Sŏn the reads per stage are fixed and the anchors say what evidence looks like for the seat's strand. The tell is evidence recorded under the wrong read, or evidence for a competency the house develops.

Assessing liking instead of success in the role. This is the mistake the room produces: service pressure "selects hard for the outgoing profile" (carryover `86ajgnhh3`), and an interviewer the room rewarded will like the candidate the room would reward. The tell is a presence word on a scorecard, and section 4.9 makes the scan for them a check.

Over-prioritizing candidate experience over trajectory and aptitude. At Sŏn this one is structurally blocked, not trained against: the sheet refuses "A years-of-experience requirement" and "A credential where a competency is meant" (S5 P13), and no anchor names experience. An interviewer who reaches for it has nothing on the sheet to write it against. Her version of the trap in the leadership section, "the more experienced someone is, the better they probably are at being interviewed" (Book p.189), returns in section 13 with its counter-questions.

**P6 (Recommended).** Her four mistakes are the four interviewer failure modes the training names and the calibration read scans for: the unasked question, the misfiled read, the presence word, and the experience reach. The fourth is blocked by the seat sheet rather than trained against.
