## 17\. Instrument specifications

Specifications, never instruments. Nothing here is built, and no session builds any of it until the document methodology exists (`86ajgn2z5`). Each specification states what the instrument is, whether Sŏn uses it, what it must contain, what it must do, what it must refuse to do, where it lives and whether that is configuration, a build, or to confirm, who owns it and on what revision rhythm, and what it is gated on. Numbering is this page's own, I1 onward; Session 5's I1 to I30 are cited as S5 I-numbers. The instruments come in the order a candidate meets them: what they are told and what the runner is given, the kit and its anchors, the scorecard's layer, the practical's rows, the training and its records, the calibration and its notes, the decision's lines, the reference note, the offer, the calendar, the internal loop, the leadership and chef loops. The instruments her chapter proposes that Sŏn refuses come last, each with what does its work.

**I1. The interview kit.** What it is: the documented question set for one stage of one seat, generated from the seat sheet's field 8, with the questions in order, the probes each expects, and the read each question serves. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the record's "semi-structured with documented questions" (WP p.18) given a form, and it is what Session 5 said this page would write (S5 P67). Must contain, per stage per seat: the stage and the reads it assesses from field 8; the questions in the fixed order of section 3 (for the first interview: one background question, the first-read block for the strand or the section 4.8 block for a lead seat, the second-read block, the third-read block including the principle questions once P22 closes, the fourth-read block, the sheet walk-through, the candidate's questions); for each question, its type (situational, behavioral, strict competency), the read it serves, the mandatory probes ("what did you hold"; for lead seats "what did you specifically do" and "did it work"), and the STAR follow-ups it expects; for the adjacent-domain interviewer the section 4.7 block; for the phone screen the P10 items; for the founder stage the P14 questions; for the dinner the P14 prompts and silence; the kit's version and the sheet version it was generated from; and the languages the kit exists in. Must do: be generated from field 8 and change only when field 8 changes by versioned decision; exist in every language the seat's process runs in; be the source of the Greenhouse interview kit and scorecard template; be public on the seat sheet as the questions, without the anchors; be delivered in the prep note (I13). Must refuse: a question that reads a competency the house develops; a question about pay, current or past; a question that names nunchi, Jeong, or a principle by name; a question the anchors cannot be written for in the four-part form; her résumé walk; a question set that differs between candidates for the seat; a kitchen kit before the chef is seated and the menu exists (P19); a question that asks a candidate to name a person at a prior employer. Where it lives: the seat sheet's field 8 on the team home, a build; Greenhouse's interview kit configured from it, configuration. Who owns it: the seat's domain lead; kitchen kits the chef partner; revised with the sheet and at the mechanism reset. Gated on: S5 I2 and I7; P22 for the principle questions; the chef ruling for the kitchen.

**I2. The anchor set.** What it is: for every question in every kit, the three-level statement of what evidence looks like below the entry bar, at it, and beyond it, in the four-part form of section 4.2. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is what makes a documented question a read rather than a conversation, and it is what the calibration read measures scorecards against. Must contain, per question: the three levels, each stating what the account contains, the candidate's own part, what they did, and what they can say about what happened; for the fourth read, no levels and instead the three supply marks; for the practical, the rows of I4 in place of anchors; the version and date; and the worked examples for training (P42), written and not taken. Must do: read capacity in any domain at entry (P17); be the reference for every evidence line and mark; be revised only by versioned decision, first at the mechanism reset by the trained interviewers (P26), and every open candidate re-read against the new version; exist in the languages the kit exists in; be delivered in the prep note and never on the seat sheet. Must refuse: a presence word at any level (the lexicon in section 4.9); a years-of-experience anchor; an anchor that requires a fine-dining floor for any seat but a lead's, and for a lead's an anchor that names a house; nunchi or Jeong as an anchor; a fourth gradation; a numeric value; an example drawn from a real candidate. Where it lives: the team home beside field 8, restricted to trained runners, the Maitre d, and the leads; a build. Who owns it: the Maitre d for the standard, the domain lead for the seat, the trained interviewers at the reset; kitchen anchors the chef partner. Gated on: I1; the document methodology; P26 for the first revision.

**I3. The scorecard's dimension layer.** What it is: the layer every stage's scorecard shares, inside which Session 5's stage-specific fields (S5 I8 to I13) sit: the four dimensions of P33 as attribute groups, the marks, the flag, and the recommendation. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes, and it is the instrument Session 13's review rubric must be built against (P36). Must contain: per question, an evidence line; per dimension, one mark from does not meet, meets, meets with evidence beyond, or not assessed with a reason; for dimension 4, per item, can supply, cannot supply, or unknown; a disqualifier flag, none or named with evidence; a recommendation, advance or decline, with a dimension named on decline; the runner's name and training record reference; the sheet, kit, and anchor versions; the stage's date and length; for the first interview the transparency sheet version and language handed; for a paired or shadowed stage the pairing marked. Must do: be one template per stage per seat generated from the kit (P35); refuse submission without a dimension on decline; hide every other scorecard on the candidate until the runner's own is submitted; stay in Greenhouse permanently and unchanged after submission (15.3); be readable side by side at the calibration read; be the record the ninety-day read opens beside the person page. Must refuse: a free-text verdict field; a "not sure," neutral, or mixed value; a numeric scale or composite; a field for presence, manner, format, or fit; a field that writes to the person page or Rippling; an edit after submission by anyone; a score on a competency the house develops. Where it lives: Greenhouse, configuration, with the two-value recommendation and the "not assessed" value to confirm. Who owns it: the Operations Lead for the configuration, the Maitre d for the standard; revised only when P33's dimensions are revised, which this page recommends never, and Session 13 inherits. Gated on: S5 I7; P35's items to confirm.

**I4. The practical's scoring rows.** What it is: the rows that fill Session 5's scoring form (S5 I10), per seat, per station or section. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; a practical without rows is a stage with a paycheck (S5 8.4). Must contain: one row per entry-level procedure from field 6 for the station or section, each marked reproduced, reproduced with correction with the count, or not reproduced; the two universal rows, asked before guessing and cleaned as they went, with their marks; one load row marked held, held with a dropped step, did not hold, or not read, with the without-load mark from S5 P42; three people rows, the steward or porter, the downstream node, and the trainer, each with an evidence line and a non-negotiables mark; the debrief line in the candidate's words under procedure; the block's start and end and the hours told; the seat holder or mentor beside the candidate by name; the assessor's recommendation with the read named and, on a procedure decline, the rows. Must do: be scored during and immediately after the block (S5 I10); be public as rows on field 8 so the candidate is told what is scored (P30); be identical for a pool candidate (S5 P61); carry the shadow form beside it for an assessor's first practical (P28); feed the answer with the rows on a procedure decline. Must refuse: a composite; a row for presence, speed relative to the holder, or nunchi; a load mark on a without-load run; a row the candidate was not told; a row for a competency the house develops; a kitchen row before the chef is seated (P32). Where it lives: Greenhouse, as the practical's scorecard fields, configuration; the rows themselves on field 8, a build. Who owns it: the domain lead from the sheet; the Maitre d for the standard; kitchen rows the chef partner; revised with the sheet and at the reset. Gated on: S5 I10; P27's block; the chef ruling for the kitchen.

**I5. The interviewer training modules.** What it is: the thirteen modules of P37, as documents under the document methodology and, once the platform exists, as modules on it. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; the record's rule that interviewers are trained (WP p.18) has no content without it. Must contain: the thirteen modules as specified, each taking the check-in's unit of time; per module, what it teaches, the exercise the live session runs, and the written worked examples (I2, P42); the sequence in P38 (read, live session, observed stage, paired stage, solo) with the stage-specific additions (the shadow for assessors, the paired call for screeners); the re-training triggers and which module each returns the runner to; the currency rule (a season without a stage returns the runner to a paired stage); and the languages each module exists in. Must do: exist as documents before the first lead's first interview (P15, row 61); be taken on scheduled shift; be read at the live session by the Maitre d, pre-opening by a founder; be the reference the calibration read's notes cite; be revised at the mechanism reset with the anchors. Must refuse: an industry interviewing product's reads; a module that teaches a verdict; a worked example from a real candidate; a module that could be completed without a paired stage; a module that names nunchi as something an interviewer reads. Where it lives: the learning platform once it exists, a build; before it, documents on the team home or, pre-opening, the partners' page. Who owns it: the Maitre d from the seat's filling; pre-opening the founders under P39; the Operations Lead for modules 6, 7, and 13's compliance content with counsel; revised at the reset. Gated on: the document methodology; P39; S5 I21 for the record it produces.

**I6. The interim training record.** What it is: the versioned entry on the partners' page that stands in for Session 5's stack-written training record (S5 I21) for the founders and the first leads before the stack can write one. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes, if P39 is ruled as the team recommends, and only until the person page exists. Must contain, per person: the modules read with dates; the practice stages run, with dates and the consenting non-candidate noted as such and not by name; the paired read's date and who read it; the languages the person can run a stage in; the stages the person is trained for; and the entry's version. Must do: exist before the person's first real stage (row 61); be copied to the person page by the stack when the page exists, after which S5 I21 governs and this record closes; be readable by both founders; carry the P39 ruling's reference. Must refuse: a stage run before the entry's date; a practice stage on a real candidate; a practice scorecard in Greenhouse; a record that extends past the first Maitre d's seating without the Maitre d's own read of it; a record written for anyone but the founders and the first two leads. Where it lives: the partners' page; a manual entry. Who owns it: the founders; closed on the person page's build. Gated on: P39 (founder-gated).

**I7. The calibration read and its record.** What it is: the monthly read of every completed packet's scorecards by the Maitre d, its record on the partners' page, and the ninety-day outcome read per hire (P44, P41). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is where the functions of her candidate review that need a reader across packets land (P43). Must contain, per month: the packets read by count; the findings by kind (presence lexicon hits, unasked questions, misfiled evidence, developed competencies scored, off-sheet declines, per-interviewer mark patterns, the strand read, hires against and declines against, unevidenced flags); the interviewer count noted and the notes issued (I8); the re-training flags; the anchor or question revisions proposed for the reset; and, per hire at ninety days, one anonymized line per interviewer stating whether each dimension's marks corresponded to the person page's record. Must do: run monthly at the partners' domain read beside the candidate pulse (S5 P30), pre-opening by the partner who is not the hiring partner; run at ninety days per hire by opening the packet and the person page side by side and writing to neither; produce the record and the notes and nothing else; feed the mechanism reset; take one person's scheduled block. Must refuse: a candidate's name in the record; a decision reopened; a target or a figure; a meeting; a verdict on an interviewer; a scorecard edited; a merge of the two records; a claim of statistical significance. Where it lives: the partners' page for the record, a build; Greenhouse for the reads, with per-interviewer mark reporting to confirm and otherwise a small build. Who owns it: the Maitre d; pre-opening the calibrating partner; revised at the reset. Gated on: I3; P44; S4 P4 for the pre-opening owner.

**I8. The interviewer note.** What it is: the note the calibration read sends a runner when it finds something in their scorecards, her CR lead's feedback email (Book p.205) given a Sŏn form. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; transparency to interviewers is the function of candidate review that lands on the Maitre d (P43). Must contain: the runner; the finding by kind, from the four standing items (evidence unrelated to the anchor, a presence-lexicon hit, a developed competency scored, a narrow read filed under the wrong dimension) or the mark-pattern finding; the module it returns the runner to and the paired stage it requires; the date; and, for the ninety-day read, the line about the runner's marks against the outcome. Must do: go through the stack; cite the module; be written in the correspondence register (Canon v1.0, section 09); be kept on the runner's training record as the re-training line and nowhere else; go the day the read runs. Must refuse: a candidate's name; a verdict on the runner; a sanction; a note that does not name a module; "guest"; a figure. Where it lives: the runner's training record on the person page, a build; sent through Greenhouse or the team home, configuration to confirm. Who owns it: the Maitre d; revised with I7. Gated on: I7.

**I9. The dissent line.** What it is: the line the domain lead writes on a packet when deciding against any scorecard's recommendation (P50), including against a founder's competency concern (15.9). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is how a dissent is carried when there is no committee to carry it. Must contain: the runner's named dimension; the runner's evidence line; the evidence in the packet the lead read as outweighing it; the date; and, for a hire against a "does not meet," the P45 trigger's reference. Must do: be written before the decision is recorded; go to the runner the same day the answer goes; stay on the packet permanently beside the unchanged scorecard; be read at the calibration read; be attached to the leads' review line under P45. Must refuse: an edit to the scorecard; a reason not in the packet; a verdict on the runner; a line that names presence or fit as the outweighing evidence; a line written after the decision. Where it lives: Greenhouse, on the packet, a field to configure. Who owns it: the domain lead; revised at the reset. Gated on: S5 I14; P45.

**I10. The reference note.** What it is: the record of reference calls for lead seats, domain-owner seats, and the chef under Branch B (P54), an item in the packet and not a scorecard. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes, for those seats only; no edge seat has one (P53). This extends Session 5's packet (S5 I14) and is surfaced as such (10.2). Must contain: each person called, their relation to the candidate and the years, the candidate's consent to that person by name and its date; the documented questions in order (the percentile question in her ascending form; her seven adapted per 10.2; for lead seats the two lead-block questions) with each answer in the reference's words; the percentile and the 1 to 10 recorded as given; the caller's name; the date. Must do: be made between the first interview and the last round so the packet completes with it; be read fifth by the lead (P49); be read at the calibration read; stay in Greenhouse and never travel to the person page; be identical in questions for every reference for the seat. Must refuse: a mark on any dimension; a recommendation; a verdict; a call without consent by name; a back-channel without consent; a call to a current employer the candidate asked not be called; a decline resting on the note alone (P55); a note for an edge seat; a figure. Where it lives: Greenhouse, as a packet attachment or the bought surface's reference feature, to confirm. Who owns it: the deciding party per 15.5; revised at the reset. Gated on: ratification of the extension to S5 I14; the chef ruling for the chef's note.

**I11. The offer conversation and the written offer.** What it is: the aloud offer in P57's order and the written offer generated from the packet and the sheet (P58). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; her verbal-before-written rule (Book p.208) is the record's "No surprises and nothing withheld" (WP p.18) at the last step. Must contain, aloud: the seat by working name and strand; the sheet version and any change; the domain lead by seat; the range from item 8 read as what the holder decides; the start date and its conditions; the mentor's seat; that the written offer follows and matches; the open period (P60); an invitation to ask. Written: the same, plus the transparency sheet version, the service periods, item 6's content as ratified, the legal content the Operations Lead sets with counsel, and the pulse's question (S5 I16). Must do: be extended by the domain lead the day of the decision in the candidate's format, before the written offer; be written in the correspondence register; match aloud and written in substance; create the person page on acceptance (S5 P16) and open Rippling's onboarding; stand open five days, extended once to a stated date (P60). Must refuse: "welcome," "enjoy," "we're excited," or any performed line (Canon v1.0, section 09); a term not on the sheet; a figure this program generated; an offer while item 6 reads "being finalized"; an edge offer extended by a partner; negotiation of the range, the commitments, item 6, or the seat's name (P61); a chase after the open date. Where it lives: the conversation's record in Greenhouse, configuration; the written offer's generation in Greenhouse's offer templates or Rippling, to confirm; the legal content in Rippling. Who owns it: the domain lead; the Operations Lead for the legal content and the generation; revised when Session 13 ratifies item 6 and at the reset. Gated on: S5 P35; Session 13; the Operations Lead's counsel.

**I12. The stage-expectation note's content per stage.** What it is: the per-stage content of Session 5's stage-expectation note (S5 I15), which is her candidate guide (Book p.193) as the record's "tells them exactly what to expect at each step" (WP p.17). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes. Must contain, per stage: P7's list (what, length, who by seat, format and language confirmed, what the candidate will do, what is read and what is not, what to wear and what the house supplies, how and when they will hear, that questions are welcome); for the first interview the transparency sheet ahead; for the practical the hours, station or section, date, load state, the person beside them, and the pay's mechanism; for the dinner the room, date, and that nothing is decided at the table. Must do: be generated from the placed stage and go only when the stack has placed it; go in the candidate's language in the correspondence register; promise nothing the schedule does not hold. Must refuse: the questions or the anchors; a figure; "guest"; a promise about a service period without a ratified charter; an exclamation point; a stage length the house will not keep. Where it lives: Greenhouse, stage-linked templates, configuration. Who owns it: the Maitre d for the standard; Brandon's seat reviews the copy against canon until S5 P22 is ruled; revised with S5 I15. Gated on: S5 I15; S5 P22.

**I13. The interviewer prep note.** What it is: what a runner receives before every stage (P8). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; Session 5 made prep the house's duty (S5 9.2). Must contain: the seat sheet, current version; the kit (I1) and the anchors (I2) for the stage; the reads assigned; the must-haves and disqualifiers; the candidate's chosen language and format; the stage-expectation note the candidate received; the transparency sheet version handed if the first interview has run; the cumulative fourth-read answer; the runner's training currency. Must do: reach the runner on the OS surface before the stage, in their language; hide every other scorecard on the candidate until the runner's own is submitted. Must refuse: another runner's scorecard, recommendation, or conclusion; the phone screen's line beyond the must-haves marked; her "brief feedback" about the candidate (Book p.212); a candidate's résumé beyond the parsed must-haves for the phone screen; anything a prior runner concluded. Where it lives: the OS surface, a build; the scorecard visibility rule in Greenhouse, configuration. Who owns it: the Maitre d; revised with I1 and I2. Gated on: I1, I2; the OS surface's build.

**I14. The hiring calendar.** What it is: the ordered gates of P15 on the partners' page, each with a state and a date or "not yet." Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; carryovers `86akh7qhr` and `86akh67gj` require the calendar to run against gates and not dates. Must contain: the three upstream gates (chef ruling, hiring partner, inventory owner); the founders' training (row 61); the compensation architecture's ratification or P35's ruling, and the ratification's date ahead of the leads' offers (P16); the leads' sheets, first interviews, substitute dinner, founder stage, reference notes, offers, and start dates set to six weeks before dinner's gate (rows 21, 42, 56); the kitchen chain's links (row 59); the cohort's postings, stages, practicals per training service against the free holders and assessors, founder stages, decisions, offers, and start dates under S5 12.6; and for every gate its state and the row or position that names it. Must do: be read at the partners' review weekly; move a date only when a gate's condition changes; place practicals per training service against the count of seat holders and assessors free that day; show the six-week condition working backward from dinner's gate; feed rows 61, 68, 69, and 73. Must refuse: a start date chosen first and a practical scheduled to make it (S5 P42); a lead's stage before the founders' training record; an offer before item 6; a kitchen practical before the menu; a gate opened around a failed row; a figure; a date presented as a condition. Where it lives: the partners' page; a build. Who owns it: the hiring partner pre-opening (S4 P4), then the Maitre d for the cohort's stages and the Operations Lead for the gates' record; revised weekly at the partners' review. Gated on: S4 P4; S5 P57; S5 P15; P16.

**I15. The internal loop record.** What it is: the record of a seat filled from the ready-now pool (P69), from the pool read through the practical to the decision and the answers. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the record's internal succession made a run rather than a hope, and it is where the internal promotion rate (WP p.23) becomes real. Must contain: the seat and the reason it opened; the pool read's date and who surfaced on the track, by the stack; for each person, the dimension-4 conversation's answers, the practical's form (I4) scored in a real service, and for a lead seat the lead block's scorecard and the dinner's; the decision with the rows and dimension named for anyone not chosen; the answers sent the same day; each unchosen person's pool entry with the next practical's date; the announcement's content (the holder and the seat, no one else); and, for a seat opened externally, the sheet's record that the pool held no one on the track and, for a lead seat after dinner's first quarter, the partners' page line (S5 P60). Must do: run the pool read before any external source (S5 I24); schedule an internal practical without the seat on the floor's schedule (P72); write to the person page only the practical's date and rows; feed the internal promotion rate; be read at the calibration read. Must refuse: an interview that re-reads what the person page holds; external validation candidates (P70); a scorecard on the person page; a reference call for an internal candidate; a decline without rows named; a pool entry removed for not being chosen; a name in the announcement but the holder's. Where it lives: Greenhouse for the stages and the stack's pool (S5 I24) for the read, configuration and a build; the person page for the two entries. Who owns it: the domain lead per seat; the Maitre d for the pool and the standard; revised at the reset. Gated on: S5 I24; the training platform; the first tension loss after dinner opens.

**I16. The lead-seat loop.** What it is: the loop for the Operations Lead and the Maitre d, pre-opening and after, assembled from this page and Session 5 (P13, P24, P65, P67; S5 P55, P37, P53). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes. Must contain: the seat sheet with the record's definitions as fields 2, 5, and 6 (S5 P55) and the section 4.8 block as field 8; the first interview by a partner, or after opening by a partner and the co-lead, of sixty minutes, with the lead block, the second and third reads, the fourth read, and the sheet handed with item 6 filled or under P35; the substitute dinner pre-opening (S5 P37) or the dinner in the room after, with both partners' independent scorecards; the founder stage; the reference note with both partners each calling (I10); the decision by the partners on the interim rule; the offer by the hiring partner with the other partner present; the start date six weeks before dinner's gate for the first two. Must do: run confidentiality in full (P68); keep the six-week condition (row 56); place the compensation architecture ahead of the offer (P16); write the outside-hire line on the partners' page after dinner's first quarter (S5 P60); train the new lead as an interviewer before their first solo stage (P40). Must refuse: a search firm unless S5 P56 is ruled otherwise; a committee or deliberation forum; a sell chat; negotiation; the domain's nodes as runners without the reset's ruling (P67); an announcement to an organization that does not exist; a lead hired without a training record before running a stage. Where it lives: Greenhouse for the stages; the partners' page for the decision and the line. Who owns it: the partners; after opening the co-lead and a partner; revised at the reset. Gated on: S4 P4; S5 P35, P37, P56; the interim two-partner decision rule; P16.

**I17. The chef-seat loop under each branch.** What it is: the two loops of P66, one per branch of the chef ruling, of which one will run. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes, whichever branch is ruled; neither runs before the ruling. Must contain, Branch A: the operating-agreement negotiation's place; the founders' due-diligence questions on canon's two criteria (Canon v1.0, What Remains; Canon v3.0, p.89) and their written answers on the partners' page before the seat is offered (row 73); the cooking for the founders in a kitchen the candidate chooses; the experience-trap technique in the cooking; consent-only references as due diligence; confidentiality; the three written terms from S5 P57 as the negotiation's content; and nothing from the stage structure. Branch B: the seat sheet with canon's two criteria as scored rows in field 8 and the section 4.8 block adapted to the kitchen; the first interview with both founders and the sheet; the cooking as the practical scored on founder-built rows (S5 P57) including a people row; the substitute dinner; the founder stage; the reference note with both founders calling; the partners' decision on the interim rule; the offer with item 6 filled and no negotiation; the seat leaving the founding documents and the two record artifacts rewritten (S5 P57). Must do, both: run only after the ruling; show the search as the founders' search (S5 P18); precede every kitchen seat sheet, kit, row, practical, and hire (S5 P58); be run by founders who hold a training record (P39). Must refuse, both: a candidate shown before consent after the decision (S5 P19); a kitchen hire before the chef; a scorecard under Branch A; a negotiation under Branch B; a sell chat. Where it lives: Branch A on the partners' page and in the operating agreement; Branch B in Greenhouse. Who owns it: the founders. Gated on: S5 P57 (founder-gated); P39.

**I18. The count-filled answer.** What it is: the one template added to Session 5's answer set (S5 I15) by P49, for a packet that meets the bar after the seat's count has filled. Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; without it a candidate who met the bar would be sent a decline naming a read they met. Must contain: the stage reached; that the seat's count filled; the pool offered by name with the seat and a dated note (S5 I17); the pulse's question. Must do: go the day the packet completes; be written in the correspondence register; tag the candidate to the pool on a yes and surface them first when the count reopens (15.6). Must refuse: a read named as the reason; "unfortunately"; a softening second sentence; a promise of a date the inventory does not hold. Where it lives: Greenhouse, a template, configuration. Who owns it: the Maitre d; revised with S5 I15. Gated on: ratification of the extension to S5 I15.

The instruments her chapter proposes that Sŏn refuses, each with what does its work. Specified as refusals so that a downstream cluster does not build them by habit.

**I19. The candidate review panel.** What it is: the CR lead, reviewers, and admins who "meet multiple times per week to review feedback and approve or deny hire and no-hire recommendations and job level outcomes" (Book p.204), with the five-step framework (Workbook p.73 to 77). Whether Sŏn uses it: no (S5 I28, P46). Its functions are rehomed one by one in P43: framework application in field 8 and I1; scorecard verification in I3's shape, the lead's reading, and I7; outcome verification partially in the founder stage and the two calibration triggers (P45; S5 12.3); the decision standard in the ninety-day read; feedback to interviewers in I8; bias measurement as a pattern read (P47); the send-back as the incomplete-by-content re-run (P48); the admin as the stack. Leveling outcomes have no object. What does the job: I3, I7, I8, I9, P45, P48. Where the panel's one unhomed function lives: P46, founder-gated. Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I20. The Bar Raiser and the Elevate interviewer.** What it is: an outside-team steward on every panel with a veto (Book p.197) and a selected class of high-performing interviewers chosen by ATS history against outcomes (Book p.197 to 198). Whether Sŏn uses it: no. The outside-domain read is the adjacent-domain second interviewer for domain-owner seats and the founder stage pre-opening (P43), and after the reset for edge seats it is P46's question; the veto is the non-negotiable flag (P51); the selection method is the ninety-day calibration read (P41); every trained person is in the pool and there is no class (P40). What does the job: S5 12.2's adjacent-domain runner, S5 P53, I7, P51. Gated on: P46 for the post-reset edge read.

**I21. The offer-approval channel.** What it is: Stripe's per-function channels with a leader's twenty-four-hour approval and occasional veto (Book p.197). Whether Sŏn uses it: no (P52); it is a review from above. What does the job: the stack's refusals (S5 I14; S5 P35; S5 12.6), the two calibration triggers (P45; S5 12.3), and the same-day decision and answer (S5 P46, P47). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I22. Job levels, the salary band, and the compa-ratio as hiring instruments.** What it is: her Tables 3 and 4, the level placement at offer, the band, the target offer points, the compa-ratio, and the pay parity review (Book p.198 to 202). Whether Sŏn uses it: no, as hiring instruments (P62). Every hire enters at the seat's entry point; there is no placement; no figure enters this program. What does the job: field 6's two horizons and the fixed unlock period (S5 I2), the invisible advocate (S5 I24), and Session 13's entry pay rule, which is not a context source here. Levels and ladders as a structural question are Sessions 8 and 13's (`86ajgnj4e`). Gated on: Session 13 for the entry pay rule.

**I23. The veto as a standing right.** What it is: "anyone on the hiring committee can veto a hire" on conviction (Book p.203). Whether Sŏn uses it: no. What does the job: the non-negotiable flag with evidence, raisable by any runner at any stage, ending the candidacy, overridable by no one (P51; S5 12.3, 12.4). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I24. The sell chat.** What it is: a fifteen-minute call after the offer with a leader who shares enthusiasm and inspires (Book p.209). Whether Sŏn uses it: no (P59); the house does not perform for a candidate (WP p.25; Canon v3.0, p.27). What does the job: the transparency sheet and the documented build before the offer (S5 I5, P17), and an unscored conversation the candidate asks for, with the lead, the other lead, or a partner, inside the open period (P59, P60). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I25. External validation interviews for an internal hire.** What it is: meeting "a few external candidates and mak\[ing\] clear that you did so" to validate an internal choice (Book p.213). Whether Sŏn uses it: no (P70). What does the job: the pool read first and the external search only on an empty track (S5 P60, I24), and the internal candidate's real-service practical (S5 P61; I15). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I26. The "not sure" response.** What it is: the fourth ATS feedback value beside definitely, yes, and no (Book p.197). Whether Sŏn uses it: no (P35). What does the job: "not assessed" per dimension with a required reason, and the incomplete-by-content re-run when a stage assessed nothing on a dimension it owed (P48). Gated on: P35's item to confirm.

**I27. The back-channel reference without consent.** What it is: reaching people who worked with a candidate without asking the candidate, which she calls "risky" and does only with permission (Book p.215). Whether Sŏn uses it: no, without consent (P56). What does the job: her consent form, adopted whole, and the reference note's consent-by-name field (I10). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**P76 (Recommended).** The eighteen instrument specifications I1 to I18 as stated, each carrying what it must contain, do, and refuse, where it lives and whether that is configuration, a build, or to confirm, who owns it and on what rhythm, and what it is gated on. None is built here; all are gated on the document methodology (`86ajgn2z5`). Three extend Session 5 instruments and say so: I10 extends S5 I14, I18 extends S5 I15, and I6 stands in for S5 I21 until the stack can write a record.

**P77 (Recommended).** The nine instruments her chapter proposes that Sŏn refuses, I19 to I27, are refused as stated, each with the mechanism that does its work. The one function among them with no home after the mechanism reset, an outside-domain read on edge packets, is P46's and is founder-gated rather than quietly filled.

## 18\. Findings inside Sŏn's record

Ten findings, each a conflict, a silence, or two accounts of the same thing, found by reading the white paper and both canon artifacts against each other and against themselves with her hiring section as the question. Each is written as what the record says in one place, what it says elsewhere or fails to say, why it bears on hiring specifically, and who closes it. Session 5's thirteen findings and the ledger's open questions (the six-tier difference between the canon artifacts, the floor manager and the Maitre d, the data hub, the period count) are not counted again; where one touches a finding below it is named as adjacent. None is resolved here. Where a section above supplied a working answer, the finding says which position holds it and marks it as the team's reading.

**18.1 The hiring reads and the review's focus are named in two vocabularies, and the record never says they are one list.** In one place: interviews "assess specific competencies, cultural alignment, and growth potential rather than gut feeling" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: reviews "focus on development, growth, and the path forward rather than a verdict," and the team "weigh\[s\] in on management effectiveness, operational improvements, and culture" (WP p.19); advancement is "tied to demonstrated mastery" signed off in "a competency conversation" (WP p.19). "Cultural alignment" appears in the hiring paragraph and nowhere in the review's; "growth potential" at hiring becomes "growth" at review with no statement that it is the same thing measured later; and the documented competency requirements (WP p.11) are named as what advancement reads and not as what hiring reads. Why it bears on hiring: this is the seam Brandon's constraint closes, and the record has it open; a house that built its review from page 19 and its interview from page 18 would hire on three things and review on two others. Who closes: Session 13, with P33 and P36 as the team's reading, and the founders in ratifying the four dimensions. Silence.

**18.2 Two accounts of the advancement gate, and the hiring rule they contradict.** In one place: "When complete, the practical assessment auto-schedules with the appropriate domain lead ... No one's advancement waits on a manager's attention or judgment. The system is the advocate" (WP p.11). Elsewhere: "when a person is ready, they schedule a competency conversation with the appropriate lead and are signed off" (WP p.19). One account has the system schedule a practical; the other has the person schedule a conversation and a lead sign off, which is a judgment the first account says advancement never waits on. Underneath both: in the kitchen "domain owners are Station Leads" (WP p.11), and functional designations "are not permanent elevations above anyone" (WP p.10), so the "appropriate domain lead" who signs off a permanent competency may be a nightly designation. Why it bears on hiring: hiring separates the assessor from the decider (S5 P41, P46) and advancement, in both accounts, fuses them in the domain lead; the internal loop (section 14) runs the seat's practical scored by an assessor who does not decide, which is the hiring rule applied to advancement and is the team's reading, not the record's. Who closes: Session 8 for the structure and who signs off, Session 13 for the review's relation to the sign-off, the founders on which account stands. Contradiction, with a silence underneath.

**18.3 Everyone enters at the outside edge, and the leads are hired into the center.** In one place: "New people always enter at the outside edge. The web never acquires altitude, only reach" (WP p.9), with no exception written. Elsewhere: the Operations Lead and the Maitre d "sit at the center because that is where the most connections intersect" (WP p.9 to 10), the goal is that "the building rarely hires a manager from outside at all" (WP p.19), and pre-opening both leads and the chef are hired from outside into the center because there is no inside (S5 11.2). The record does not say what a lead enters at, what a lead's "reach" is on day one, or what the transparency sheet's "advancement path" (WP p.18) says to a person entering the center. Why it bears on hiring: the lead loop (section 13), item 7 on the leads' sheets, and the entry pay rule for a lead (P63) all need a word the record does not have; and "no altitude" is the record's structural claim, so the word cannot be a rank. Who closes: the founders, with Session 8 for the structure and Session 13 for what a lead enters at in the architecture. Silence.

**18.4 The language promise has no trained runner behind it at the first hires.** In one place: "a candidate whose first language is not English can interview with someone who speaks it" (WP p.17). Elsewhere: "Interviewers are trained" (WP p.18), the training is on a platform that does not exist before the team does (WP p.19), and pre-opening the only interviewers are the founders (S5 15.13), whose languages the record does not state. A first interview requested in a language neither founder holds has no trained runner, and the record names no interpreter, no interim, and no order of hiring that supplies one. Why it bears on hiring: language choice is the record's dignity mechanism and the cohort is the first population it is promised to; row 74 checks it and cannot hold whole until P39 rules. Who closes: the founders on P39. Sequencing silence. Adjacent to S5 15.13.

**18.5 Canon requires felt knowledge at service, and the strand definition does not carry it.** In one place: Mahk requires that "service speaks to a dish with felt knowledge, not recited description" and that "the room is slow enough that a customer is actually present" (Canon v1.0, section 01), and the language constant and lexicon reach every sentence spoken (Canon v3.0, p.28). Elsewhere: the outward-facing strand's intelligence is "relational and expressive and emotionally attuned under load" (WP p.10), with no culinary knowledge named; the record's training platform teaches it (WP p.19); and the menu it would be felt knowledge of is chef-gated and does not exist (S5 P44). Session 5 said Korean-cuisine fluency is not required at entry and the house trains it (S5 P27). Why it bears on hiring: the first read can score only the capacity for felt knowledge (P18's second question), and the cohort's actual felt knowledge of the menu cannot be taught until the chef chain reaches the menu, which sits ahead of the cohort's training on the calendar (P15) with no stated interval between the menu and the first service. Who closes: the chef partner for the menu, Session 7 for the training plan's sequence, and canon's owner for whether the strand definition gains the word. Silence.

**18.6 Blame the process has no hiring object.** In one place: "Universal problems are not people problems. They are design problems"; "when something goes wrong, the first question is not who failed. It is what allowed this to happen"; "Post-mortems are private and process-focused" (WP p.17). Elsewhere: the ninety-day plan "sets expectations and goals with regular check-ins and course correction" (WP p.18), and nothing in the record says what a hire that does not hold is, a person problem or a design problem, or where its post-mortem goes, or what in the hiring system is fixed when it happens. The record measures retention (WP p.23) and not the hiring system's part in it. Why it bears on hiring: without a loop from the ninety-day plan back to the packet, a failed hire is fixed at the person and the interview that produced it runs unchanged; the ninety-day calibration read (P41) is the team's reading and the record's silence. Who closes: the founders, and Session 14, whose subject includes low performers, for where a hire that does not hold is read. Silence.

**18.7 "Salaried roles" appear once, and the pay system has no place for them.** In one place: "For leadership and salaried roles, the final round is a dinner in the room" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: the built-in compensation "is distributed to the whole team, the culinary team included, on a point system weighted by the days each person works," "calculated daily" (WP p.20); "there is no hierarchy of importance" (WP p.20); and the record never again uses the word salaried, names which seats are salaried, or says how a salaried lead sits on a day-weighted point system that pays "the people who make the food" for "the nights they help fill" (WP p.20). Why it bears on hiring: the seat class that gets the dinner in the room is defined by a word the pay system does not carry (S5 P3, P36); the offer for a lead cannot state item 6 without it; and what a lead enters at (18.3) turns on it. Who closes: Session 13 for the architecture, the founders for which seats are salaried. Two accounts, one of them a single word.

**18.8 Cross-training crosses the chef's domain, and no one is named to sign it off.** In one place: "Cross-training is career development, not only operational insurance. A server who learns the kitchen becomes more valuable everywhere" (WP p.19), and "Each person ... develops outward, deeper into their domain and across into adjacent ones" (WP p.11). Elsewhere: kitchen domain owners are Station Leads and the kitchen is the chef partner's domain (WP p.11; S5 P44), the practical assessment schedules "with the appropriate domain lead" (WP p.11), and the record does not say whether a server on the kitchen's track takes the kitchen's practical, who signs off a competency held across two domains, or whether the receiving domain's lead or the person's own domain lead decides. Why it bears on hiring: the internal loop's cross-domain case (P69) puts the receiving domain's practical and lead in charge, as the team's reading; and cross-strand fluency, which is paid (WP p.11), is exactly the competency with two possible signers. Who closes: Session 8 for the structure, the chef partner for the kitchen's side, Session 13 for the pay. Silence. Adjacent to `86akh3wjw`.

**18.9 The Lead Host is collapsed by software in one place and owns the door in another.** In one place: "Reservations, identity, and the phone in software collapse a reservations manager and a lead host into one" (WP p.22), in the list of positions the code-bearing claim removes. Elsewhere: "The Lead Host owns the door and the host-stand function" as a functional designation (WP p.10); canon removes the host stand entirely, "Host stand removed. Credenza-scale storage at threshold" (Canon v1.0, section 08), and places the maître d' "at the top of the porch steps" as the arrival's first beat (Canon v1.0, section 06; Canon v3.0, p.68); canon v1.0's uniform table has "Hosts" and v3.0's has no host role at all (Canon v1.0, section 08; Canon v3.0, p.81). So the record collapses the seat, keeps it as a designation, removes its stand, hands its first beat to the Maitre d, and drops it from one uniform table. Why it bears on hiring: whether a host seat exists on the inventory, what its sheet's field 5 says the door is, and whether "Lead Host" is a seat to hire or a designation to assign, none of which the seat sheet can answer from the record; S5 P64 held the hosts' lead, and this finding is upstream of it, the seat's own existence. Who closes: Session 8 with the inventory (S5 P15), the founders, and canon's owner for the uniform tables. Two accounts, and a third in canon. Adjacent to the floor manager question and to S5 15.10.

**18.10 The record names leading indicators for the organization and none for the hiring system.** In one place: "Leading indicators, employee NPS, cultural labor score, customer recognition rate, are the nervous system's signal" (WP p.12), and "Sŏn measures what predicts problems before they compound" (WP p.22). Elsewhere: hiring is "a system" (WP p.17) and the only talent measures named are "retention rate, internal promotion rate" (WP p.23), both lagging for a hiring decision by a year or more; the record names no time-to-answer, no applications-to-hire, no share of hires reaching the first unlock, no ninety-day retention, and no measure of the hiring system's own conduct. Why it bears on hiring: the pipeline read (S5 I22) and the calibration read (I7) produce records with nothing in the record's measure set to feed; the mechanism reset will read the hiring system against measures this page and Session 5 named and the record did not. Who closes: the founders, with Session 17's assembly of the measure set; the pipeline read's four elements and the ninety-day read are the team's reading. Silence. Adjacent to `86akh2qzy`.

Ten findings: six silences, two contradictions or two-account conflicts, one sequencing silence, and one two-account finding carried by a single word. Three of the ten (18.4, 18.7, 18.10) sit inside or beside the Talent acquisition section (WP p.17 to 18) read against its neighbors on pages 19, 20, and 22, and would have surfaced from a read of those pages alone. The other seven would not: 18.1 needs page 18 against page 19 with Brandon's constraint as the question; 18.2 needs page 11 against page 19 and page 10; 18.3 needs page 9 against pages 10 and 19 and Session 5's pre-opening condition; 18.5 needs canon's Mahk section against page 10 and the chef chain; 18.6 needs page 17 against page 18 and page 23; 18.8 needs pages 11 and 19 against the kitchen's gating; 18.9 needs pages 10 and 22 against two canon sections and both uniform tables. A session that pulled the two hiring paragraphs and stopped would have found the language gap and the salaried word and missed that the record's own advancement gate contradicts its hiring rule.

**P78 (Recommended).** The ten findings are filed as stated, each routed to who closes it. None is resolved on this page; where a section above supplied a working answer it is the team's reading and marked as such. 18.1 is filed with the Session 13 coupling; 18.4 with P39; 18.6 to Session 14; 18.8 and 18.9 to Session 8; 18.7 and 18.3 to Session 13 with the founders; 18.5 to the chef partner and Session 7; 18.10 to the founders and Session 17.

Three things about the count. Team-filled carries one, the anchor set's first revision, because the anchors are the one instrument on this page that a first cohort of real answers will show to be wrong in places, and the people who will know are the interviewers who asked them. Founder-gated carries seven, and four of them (P16, P39, P46, P66) are the page's honest edges: a sequencing choice about the architecture, a pre-platform condition Session 5's instrument did not anticipate, a function her chapter argues for that Session 5's reset would leave homeless, and the third seat.

Where this page extends or reads against Session 5, listed once. P45 extends S5 12.3 with a mirror trigger. P54 extends S5 I14 with a reference note for three seat classes. P49 extends S5 I15 with a count-filled answer. P39 reads S5 I21's refusal of a hand-written training record as applying only once the stack can write one. Brandon ratifies each extension alongside the Session 5 position it extends, or refuses it, and nothing here assumes the ratification.

What the founders must close before the recommended positions can be acted on, in the order the hiring timeline needs them. First, the three upstream gates Session 5 already named: the chef seat ruling (S5 P57), the hiring partner (S4 P4), and the seat inventory's owner (S5 P15), because no hire runs without them and the chef ruling gates the kitchen chain whole. Second, how the founders are trained before the platform exists (P39), because the first lead's first interview cannot run until both founders hold a training record and rows 44 and 61 fail until they do; with it, how a first interview is run in a language neither founder holds. Third, the compensation architecture's place on the hiring calendar (P16), because the leads' offers cannot go until item 6 is filled and the six-week condition works backward from dinner's gate; with it, Session 5's P35 (whether first interviews run before item 6 is filled) and P37 (the substitute dinner), which the leads' loop cannot run without. Fourth, the third seat's loop under the branch the ruling chooses (P66), which follows the first gate directly. Then the two that shape the questions without blocking a hire: the principles version one (P22), after which the third read gains its principle questions by versioned change, and the incomplete decision-rights entries (P74), of which the runner and host seats' lead and the pre-opening partners' disagreement rule are Session 5's and the ledger's. Two are for the mechanism reset rather than now: whether an outside-domain read survives for edge seats after the founder stage ends (P46), ratified against the calibration read's first quarter, and the anchors' first revision (P26). And one is Session 11's with the founders: bias measurement's data (P47). Everything else on this page can be acted on the day Brandon ratifies it, and the four dimensions in P33 are the thing on it that a later session cannot revise at ordinary cost.

# S7: Onboarding, the ninety-day plan, and the learning platform

# Session 7: Onboarding, hiring mistakes, and the Chapter 3 exercises

This page is the Sŏn answer to the Onboarding and Hiring mistakes sections of Chapter 3 (Book p.216 to 227) and to the Chapter 3 exercises and templates (Book p.228 to 259), with the Chapter 3 workbook's remaining material (Workbook p.78 to 88) read for anything the book version lacks. It is written to be run from. A person who has not read the book can read this page and know what happens to someone from the day they accept a seat to the day their ninety-day plan closes: what arrives in their hands and through which tool, who stands beside them, what they are taught and in what order, what is read and what is written down, when they first hold a table or a station alone, and what the house refuses to conclude about them along the way.

Every position on this page is numbered from P1 and carries exactly one mark. (Recommended) is the team's position, ready for founder ratification. (Founder-gated) requires input the team cannot supply. (Chef-gated) is left open for the chef partner. (Team-filled) is populated once the team exists. Nothing on this page is final. A recommended position is a recommendation until Brandon ratifies it, and a founder-gated position is argued to the ceiling one founder can reach and then marked for what Dominic, the chef, or the team must close.

Vocabulary follows the ledger and Sessions 4 to 6. "Operating system," unqualified, is the human system; the software is "the stack" or "the OS surface." The customer is the customer, in every module, every module's narration, and every sentence a new person is taught. Service periods are named by time of day. A "seat" is a node in the web with a domain, a strand, and documented competency requirements; the "seat sheet" is the sixteen-field artifact that opens it (S5 P12), and its field 6 carries the entry bar and the first unlock, field 7 what the house develops, field 10 the decision-rights range, field 11 the shift shape, and field 14 the languages. "The person page" is the card on the team home Session 4 specified (S4 P18), created at the offer by recruiting with ten entries (S5 P16; carryover `86akh7qn7`). "The check-in" is the fifteen-minute conversation Session 4 fixed and the ledger binds (S4 P15, P19, P20). "The four dimensions" are the scorecard's dimensions Session 6 named and Session 13 inherits (S6 P33). "The domain lead" is the lead of the domain a seat sits in, named by seat, holding the functions Session 5 stated and not the functions it stated beside them (S5 P33). "Service-ready" is defined on this page (section 6.6) and nowhere before it.

Financials are not a context source for this program. Wage rates, training pay, mentor pay, and the pay for authoring a module are the same rule: none is stated, estimated, or implied, and where a mechanism needs one the page says the figure is not a context source and routes the gap to Session 13. Her chapter's one figure in this range, a rejected-candidate survey result on page 226, does not enter this page.

The stack is bought and this page builds into it (carryover `86ajgmm86`): Greenhouse is the applicant system; Rippling is the single sign-on, human-resources, and payroll layer; Trainual, Synthesia, and Loom are the training production stack; Google Workspace is the floor team's backbone. For every mechanism placed in a tool, this page says whether it is configuration, a build, or to confirm, and it asserts no tool feature as fact. No operating-system document names a data hub tool (`86akh5u6e`), and nothing here assumes one. Where the text says "the scheduling surface," it means whichever bought tool posts the schedule, unnamed here.

The service-period count is a parameter, said once. Onboarding is written for dinner, which is the first and for now the only configuration under a ratified charter. A period added by ratified charter adds a module set to the learning platform (the period's procedures) and a register block to the service module (the period's register, drawn from canon), and a person already in the house who takes a seat in the new period runs the shorter period plan of section 7.7, not a second ninety-day plan. Nothing on this page assumes four periods, and no lunch module exists.

## 1\. Her ask, and what Sŏn already holds

### 1.1 Her ask

Her onboarding section opens on the moment of arrival: a new person is "on high alert for context and opportunities to learn," and a company that only has them "show up, fill out some paperwork, get set up on your laptop, and start working" has missed "a huge opportunity to start inculcating new hires into the company and the culture" (Book p.216). The curriculum she asks for carries three things in order: "The 'why' of the company, including the mission and the story behind it"; "The 'what' of the business, including current priorities and goals"; "The 'how' of company behaviors, including how people work together and the operating principles" (Book p.216). She asks that "company leadership should take part in onboarding new hires," that "Stories, not bullet points, are what really get a message across," and that the curriculum be "the fastest possible ramp to success" (Book p.216). Her own house runs "a weeklong core onboarding curriculum for every new hire, no matter their level," with team programs alongside, and the manager translates "the company operating system to the team level" in a first 1:1 or a one- to two-hour session (Book p.216).

The one voice in her section from a kitchen says what this page has to answer for a cook: "people just get thrown onto the job. I think this is the wrong way to do it. Training is very important, and understanding all the layers of the company is very important. If you're getting hired as a cook, it's not just about the kitchen," and "when you train someone, it's not like, 'Now you're trained.' No. You always have to be on top of it. It's a continuation of things" (Book p.216 to 217, Dominique Crenn).

Her prep rule: "all prep work should be done asynchronously before the onboarding program starts," paperwork and equipment included (Book p.217). Her nine outcomes for a person emerging from onboarding: a community of other new hires; leadership's vision and the principles; the business and its products; the users' perspective; the operating structures and current goals; a picture of the organization; key processes such as compliance; where the team fits; and "An ability to find internal resources to self-educate and seek assistance" (Book p.217).

Internal mobility: a survey at every team change, five questions, read over time for "bad mobility" (Book p.217 to 218); and manager-to-manager transitions, with a guide in the appendix (Book p.218; p.252 to 253). New hire onboarding: her "Working with Claire" document, the first meeting devoted to mutual expectations across six headings (onboarding, operating approach, management style, communication preferences, initial priorities, the upcoming career conversation), and the invitation to the new person to write their own (Book p.218 to 219). New leader onboarding: standardize, then add; the New Leader Experience with welcome emails, prescheduled meetings and pre-reads, a leadership assessment, a coach, first-month actions, and a ninety-day 360 (Book p.219); Table 5's six objectives and tactics (Book p.220); the daily or every-other-day standup for critical roles, and the "narrow" path between listening and acting (Book p.221); and the direct report's sidebar in nine parts, from "Commit to their success" to "Share stories and histories" (Book p.221 to 224).

Hiring mistakes: most surface "a few months into the person's tenure" as performance, but some right away, even before the start date; four example signals; "anything that violates your employee handbook"; get minor feedback to the person "quickly and strongly"; "The main thing is to do something," rescind or terminate swiftly, a short note to the team (Book p.224 to 225). Closing the loop: a retrospective by the hiring manager; ATS data on time in process, funnel performance, and interviewer stats; engagement and pulse survey prompts; marrying hiring data with performance data at milestones; surveying the rejected (Book p.225 to 226). Her closing line: "Hiring is expensive, but talent is everything" (Book p.227).

The exercises appendix reproduces the workbook's Chapter 3 templates (Book p.228 to 259). Four of the eight are Session 6's and are answered there: the interview framework and rubric, the sample questions, the written exercise, and the candidate review framework (Workbook p.43 to 77; S6 P17 to P55). This page confirmed against the book's versions (Book p.229 to 251) that nothing there is absent from Session 6, and it answers them by reference (section 15). The four that are this page's: the Manager Transitions Guide (Book p.252 to 253; Workbook p.78), Working with Claire (Book p.253 to 257; Workbook p.80 to 83), the Working with Me template (Book p.257; Workbook p.84), and the New Leader Experience with its schedule (Book p.257 to 259; Workbook p.86 to 88). The workbook versions were read from page 78 onward and carry nothing the book's lack; the workbook's notes pages are blank.

### 1.2 What the record holds

This is the first session whose subject the record treats at length, and the paragraphs are quoted whole because the whole page hangs from them.

Onboarding (WP p.18). "Onboarding begins before the first shift, not when the person walks in. Before they arrive, information is delivered, expectations are set, the peer mentor is connected, the locker is assigned, and the uniform and tools are ready down to the shoes. Everything needed to succeed is waiting, because the investment in the person's success precedes their first clock-in." "Why comes before how. Orientation to the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard happens before operational training, because a person needs the reason before the mechanics. The sequence reinforces that culture is the foundation the operational work is built on, not a poster on the wall." "Every new person is paired with a mentor, a proven cultural steward rather than simply the strongest performer, someone who answers questions and makes the early experience reflect the standard. Progression is documented from the start: clear milestones, skill assessments, and feedback, so the person always knows what they are learning, why it matters, and how mastery is demonstrated. A ninety-day plan sets expectations and goals with regular check-ins and course correction, so early success is planned rather than hoped for."

Training infrastructure (WP p.18 to 19). "The industry's training model is sink or swim ... Shadow someone for two shifts, catch fragments because they are busy, get thrown in before ready, fail, quit, repeat. This is not an unfortunate reality. It is designed-in failure." "Sŏn's learning platform feeds the progression structure in Part I ... An internal education system built like the content the team actually uses, engaging and personalized and constantly expanding. Any qualified team member can create training modules and get paid for teaching everyone else. The more modules completed, the more earned ... And competency validation: no one touches a table until they are actually ready." "The platform teaches, the competency structure validates, and the invisible advocate removes the friction between wanting to grow and growing." "Cross-training is career development, not only operational insurance. A server who learns the kitchen becomes more valuable everywhere, and a lead who understands both sides of the house leads better. The goal the system builds toward is internal succession."

Performance management (WP p.19), which the ninety-day plan runs into: "Performance systems develop people rather than judge them"; "Advancement is tied to demonstrated mastery: when a person is ready, they schedule a competency conversation with the appropriate lead and are signed off"; "no surprises: continuous communication means a formal review never contains new information"; "Feedback runs both directions."

We pay for what matters (WP p.19 to 20): "Full uniforms, company provided and company paid: tops, bottoms, aprons, and shoes where appropriate"; "Smart lockers for every team member"; "A real employee area with secure lockers and a comfortable break space is not a perk. It is basic dignity, and dignity is a precondition for presence." Rippling, "chosen for what it delivers, including access to cost-effective benefits for frontline employees" (WP p.20). The transparency sheet's item 5, "the training plan with pay dates" (WP p.18).

Part I, which onboarding delivers a person into: "New people always enter at the outside edge. The web never acquires altitude, only reach" (WP p.9); "Outside edge is highest information sensitivity ... Not the bottom of a hierarchy. The most sensitive position" (WP p.9); for each employee "the web inverts. The employee is at the center of their own knowledge map. Skills branch outward in every direction" (WP p.11); "The path is explicit before they start it. Every position has documented competency requirements visible to anyone" (WP p.11); "After a set period in any role, the next skill set unlocks automatically. It is self-paced" (WP p.11); "Advancement requires preparation, not permission" (WP p.14); the server "owns the table relationship and resolves it using their authorized judgment and generosity range" (WP p.13). The failure modes onboarding is built against: memory failure, where "Training means teaching the same things repeatedly to a rotating cast" (WP p.13); skill invisibility, where "employees do not know what advancement requires because the competencies are not documented or accessible" (WP p.14); cooling failure (WP p.13, p.14). "Employees are the users" and "Blame the process, fix the process" (WP p.17). Bandwidth, then joy, then retention, then results (WP p.12, p.17).

The stack (WP p.21 to 22): "heavily deterministic software over a thin layer of AI"; "Bought where the capability is settled, built where it is the edge"; the OS surface as "the home where the software agents live"; the structured feedback channel that "syncs to the execution system" (WP p.22).

Canon governs every word a new team member is taught. The non-negotiables and the order bandwidth, joy, retention, results (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.4). The language constant, "Internal communication included" (Canon v3.0, p.5). The playground philosophy's prohibition on "training systems that measure procedure execution without building toward judgment" and its requirement of "training architecture that progresses from procedure mastery to autonomous judgment" and "service authority distributed to the closest-to-customer position" (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.14). Jeong and nunchi, "Developed through mastery, exercised through judgment," neither scripted (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.15). Mahk's requirement that "service speaks to a dish with felt knowledge, not recited description" (Canon v1.0, section 01) and its prohibition on "service delivered by script rather than felt knowledge" (Canon v1.0, section 01). Ma's prohibition on "service staff who manufacture activity because standing still feels wrong" and its requirement of "staff understanding that the empty wall is a decision, not a gap" (Canon v1.0, section 01). The service model: step-back architecture in three phases, floor authority, arrival choreography with "We have you" and "We walk, we never point," the David protocol as "system decision, never floor call," the late-night transition as "same person, same moment," the pyeong-sang as "pre-designed, not responsive" (Canon v1.0, sections 06 and 08; Canon v3.0, p.78 to 80). The uniform system, in two versions that differ (Canon v1.0, section 08; Canon v3.0, p.81), and the wear test as "the governing production gate" (Canon v1.0, section 08). The pre-service scene, "Person-triggered, not clock-automated. Visible to staff; imperceptible to customers" (Canon v1.0, section 06). The six-tier hierarchy in two versions (Canon v1.0, section 02; Canon v3.0, p.32); the difference is unresolved (`86akh3rx4`, `86akh3tjb`) and any position turning on it is marked held. The Hangul rules: Korean terminology "stands without explanation in all brand contexts from day one" (Canon v1.0, section 04; Canon v3.0, p.45). The prohibition on AI-generated imagery "on all public-facing surfaces" (Canon v1.0, sections 02 and 10; Canon v3.0, p.33, p.63). The five voice rules and six binary tests (Canon v1.0, section 09; Canon v3.0, p.53 to 54), the forbidden lexicon, and the rule that "welcome" and "enjoy" are "acceptable as in-person service language only" (Canon v1.0, section 09).

### 1.3 What Sessions 1 to 6 already decided

Session 4 built the check-in and the person page, and the ledger binds them: fifteen minutes as the first fifteen minutes of a scheduled shift in the pre-service window, paid as shift, placed by the stack when the interval elapses, three questions, an upward question, one line written on the person page and read back, every two weeks inside the ninety-day plan and monthly after, refusing verdicts, task assignment, pay, and discipline (S4 P15, P18, P19, P20). The person page holds one goal and its state, the progression state from the stack, the last three check-in lines, the next date, and the ninety-day plan while active (S4 P18); a person's first goal is the plan's, not the quarter's (S4 P42). The shift brief's readiness block is a checklist the rush cannot delete and the close carries nothing about a person (S4 P10, P12). Two cadences coexist until the last proof gate; no build meeting in the building during service hours; the room's mechanisms are frozen for dinner's first quarter except the committed class and shift-close maintenance (S4 P9). The mechanism reset runs after dinner's first quarter and after the first full year (S4 P39). The bandwidth ledger already counts, per hourly person per month, the brief, the close, fifteen minutes of check-in, one pulse question, a recognition, and the review every three to six months, and nothing else (S4 P63).

Session 5 fixed that role definition lives in recruiting and the seat sheet is the single account of a seat (S5 P11, P12, P13); that recruiting creates the person page at the offer with ten entries and writes nothing else (S5 P16); that the start date has conditions, mentor connected, uniform and locker ready, the seat's first modules on the platform, the first check-in on a pre-service window the lead works, item 6 filled, never a new period's first service, never coverage before "no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (S5 12.6); that a start date which cannot be set inside a month because the mentor or the modules are not ready is a training-infrastructure load, not a recruiting one (S5 12.6); that the cohort is hired against the seat and onboarded against the first unlock, with the unlock period fixed on every sheet and the ready-now pool existing from day one (S5 P60); that cross-period fluency is a development marker on the person page (S5 P62); that the transparency sheet's item 5 carries the training plan with pay dates and item 8 the seat's range (S5 P34); and that her work style grid does not enter recruiting and may return only as a self-awareness tool (S5 P8). Session 5's readiness row 55 already checks the ten entries, the mentor connected, and the first check-in on the schedule; row 57 the pool and the visible path; row 38 that the platform's first unlock points at the sheet.

Session 6 fixed the four dimensions and the rule that nothing appears at review that was not read at hiring, and that no scorecard ever appears on a person page (S6 P33, P34; row 71). It fixed the training form for interviewers, modules read, a live session, an observed stage, a paired stage, then solo, all on scheduled shift, recorded by the stack (S6 P38), and how the founders are trained before the platform exists (S6 P39, founder-gated). It placed the cohort's practicals in training services marked as run without load, with the first four dinner weeks as the load read recorded at the check-in (S6 P31; S5 P42). It fixed the hiring calendar as gates with the kitchen chain unskippable and the leads in the building six weeks before dinner's gate (S6 P15). It fixed the offer's content, including the start date's conditions and the mentor's seat, extended aloud by the domain lead (S6 P57, P58), and the acceptance as the seam to Rippling and the person page (S6 P58). It wrote the ninety-day calibration read from the ninety-day mark back to the interviewer (S6 P41) and routed where a hire that does not hold is read to Session 14 (S6 18.6). It found that canon's felt-knowledge requirement is not in the strand definition and that the menu does not exist (S6 18.5), that cross-training's cross-domain sign-off is unnamed (S6 18.8), and that the leads are hired into the center where everyone enters at the edge (S6 18.3).

Session 1 decided the working-with-me document: written by all three founders on one spine, exchanged among them, the chef partner's before the partnership is signed, and issued to the two leads in a shorter form when each is seated, with each lead asked to write one on the same spine (S1 6; S1 7.6; S1 8.5). Session 3 wrote readiness row 4, that every server and floor manager can state their range and escalation triggers unprompted, and named a failed row 4 "a range that was written and not delivered, which is an onboarding failure routed to Session 7" (S3 12.3). Session 3 also fixed the decision-rights form and the rule that an incomplete entry is marked rather than filled by analogy (S3 4.1).

### 1.4 How much is decided, and where she is refused

Counted honestly, her onboarding material divides in three, and the proportions are the reverse of Session 6's. About half is already held by the record, in its own words and in a form more specific than hers: prep before arrival, why before how, a mentor, documented milestones and skill assessments, a ninety-day plan with check-ins, a learning platform, competency validation before a person touches a table, cross-training as development, uniforms and lockers ready, and paid training. This page does not re-derive any of it. It builds the mechanism under each commitment, because the record states the commitment and not the mechanism, and a commitment with no mechanism is what her section calls "the companies that simply have you show up" (Book p.216).

About a quarter is absorbed for its discipline and refused for its form. Absorbed: leadership taking part; stories over bullet points; the fastest possible ramp; the first conversation as a setting of mutual expectations; standardize the process and add for leaders; the new leader's balance between listening and acting; the direct report's "give data points, not judgments"; "do something" about a mistake rather than drift; and the loop closed from outcomes back to the hiring system. Refused, each with what does its work in section 18: the core onboarding week; the monthly leadership session; the manager's one- to two-hour team translation; the internal mobility survey; the manager transitions guide and its meeting; the New Leader Experience's apparatus (welcome emails, the onboarding point person and checklist, the leadership assessment, the coach, the ninety-day 360); the daily standup; the shadow and reverse-shadow arrangement as a standing pattern; "loan your social capital"; the engagement and pulse survey prompts about onboarding; and the working-with-me document as anything required of an hourly person.

The last quarter does not apply because Sŏn does not have the thing it assumes: a running house with a team to absorb a new hire, an existing curriculum, a manager who assigns and reviews, a person being layered under a new leader, a division to introduce a leader to, an HR partner, an org development function, a learning platform with content already on it, and a menu. Section 3 works the first and last of those, mechanism by mechanism, because the pre-opening cohort meets none of the conditions her section assumes and the cohort is the first population the record's commitments are promised to.

**P1 (Recommended).** The record's onboarding and training paragraphs (WP p.18 to 19), with the commitments around them (WP p.19 to 20) and the structure they deliver a person into (WP p.9 to 14), are held as decided. This page builds the mechanism under each commitment, extends the record where it is silent, and alters none of it. Every place it extends a Session 4, 5, or 6 specification it says so by position number, and every place it would contradict one it stops and surfaces the conflict (sections 4.3, 5.5, 6.4, 11.4, 20) for Brandon rather than overwriting it.

**P2 (Recommended).** Her onboarding, hiring mistakes, and exercises material is absorbed for its discipline and refused for its forms. Absorbed: leadership taking part, stories over bullet points, the fastest ramp, mutual expectations set at the first conversation, standardize then add for leaders, the listening-to-acting balance, data points not judgments, do something about a mistake, and the outcome loop back to hiring. Refused, each with what does its work in section 18: the core week, the leadership session, the team translation session, the mobility survey, the transitions guide, the New Leader Experience's apparatus, the daily standup, shadow and reverse-shadow as a standing pattern, social-capital loans, the onboarding survey prompts, and the working-with-me document for hourly seats.

**P3 (Recommended).** Onboarding is written for dinner as the first configuration. A period added by ratified charter adds a module set and a register block to the platform and a shorter period plan to the person, never a redesign and never a second ninety-day plan (section 7.7).
