## 2\. What onboarding is for at Sŏn, what it may conclude, and what it refuses to conclude

### 2.1 The intended behavior, stated so it can be tested

The People Systems Designer's first move is to state, in behavioral terms, what the system is supposed to make people do, because a system with no statable intended behavior cannot be evaluated. Her section states an intent, "the fastest possible ramp to success" (Book p.216), and the record states a stronger one, "early success is planned rather than hoped for" (WP p.18). Neither is behavioral. This page states the behavior, and every mechanism after this section exists to produce it or is cut.

At the close of the ninety-day plan, a person in an hourly edge seat: holds their seat solo on the schedule at service tempo, reproducing the seat's entry procedures without a mentor beside them; states their decision-rights range and its escalation triggers unprompted, in their own words, and has used the range at least once inside it; speaks of the customer as the customer in every sentence, spoken and written, and of a dish with felt knowledge of the dishes that exist; has opened the learning platform and moved on it without being asked, so the invisible advocate has a record to read; has told the house, at six check-ins, what was in the way, and can say what the building did about it; and knows the seat after theirs and what it requires, from their own account on the team home, without asking anyone.

That is the whole of it. Onboarding is not for producing a person who feels welcomed, which is a mood, or one who has "been onboarded," which is a document. It is for producing the six behaviors above, and the Realist's addition is that the first of them has to hold on a Friday with a full book, not on the calm Tuesday the sequence was designed on.

### 2.2 What onboarding may conclude

Four things, and each has a record.

Whether the person is service-ready in the seat, per section 6.6: the entry procedures reproduced in a paired service and read on the practical's rows by an assessor who is not the mentor (S6 I4), the range and triggers stated, the language constant held, and the felt-knowledge block passed for the dishes that exist. The record is the readiness form (I7) and the first solo's date on the schedule.

Whether each milestone of the ninety-day plan reached its state, and on what date. The record is the plan block on the person page, written by the stack for the milestones it can see (modules, the paired services on the schedule, the form's date) and by the lead at the check-in for the rest (section 7).

What the building supplied and did not supply of what the person said they needed, which is dimension 4 read on the building at six check-ins (S6 P33). The record is the check-in lines.

What in the house's training infrastructure did not hold for this person: a module missing in their language, a mentor absent, a paired service that ran short, a felt-knowledge block that could not be passed because the dishes had not been tasted. The record is the training-infrastructure line at the leads' review (S5 12.6's trigger), and it is read as a load on the infrastructure, never on the person.

### 2.3 What onboarding refuses to conclude

A verdict on the person. The review is not a verdict (WP p.19) and the check-in refuses one (S4 P15); the plan cannot be a verdict on the way to a review that is not.

A level, a placement, or a pay outcome. Everyone enters at the seat's entry point (S6 P62) and the architecture is Session 13's; the plan's close changes nothing about pay and says nothing about it.

Nunchi or Jeong. Neither is a ninety-day expectation (ledger; S5 P6). Nunchi is "Developed through mastery, exercised through judgment" (Canon v3.0, p.15), and ninety days is the beginning of mastery; Jeong "requires time, repetition, and memory" (Canon v1.0, section 01) and the plan is too short to have accumulated any. A plan that named either as a milestone would be scoring at ninety days what recruiting refused to score at entry.

Month-six performance, cross-strand fluency, or a person's ceiling. The plan reads the entry horizon of field 6 and nothing past it.

Whether a hire was a mistake. The plan reads states; where a hire that does not hold is read, and what is concluded from it, is Session 14's (S6 18.6; section 13). The plan may say a milestone did not reach its state and by which link. It may not say what that means about the person.

Whether the person "fits." There is no such dimension at hiring (S6 6.2) and none at onboarding.

Anything about the person that the person has not heard. The person page is written in the room and read back (S4 P18), and the plan block is part of the page.

**P4 (Recommended).** Onboarding's intended behavior is the six behaviors of 2.1 at the close of the ninety-day plan. It may conclude service-readiness per seat with a readiness form, the state and date of each plan milestone, what the building supplied against what the person said they needed, and what in the training infrastructure did not hold. It refuses to conclude a verdict, a level or pay outcome, nunchi or Jeong, month-six performance or a ceiling, whether a hire was a mistake, fit, or anything the person has not heard.

### 2.4 Who runs it, and the departure from her manager

Her onboarding has one owner, the manager, who understands the curriculum, adds team content, holds the first 1:1, sets expectations, and later runs the career conversation (Book p.216 to 219). At Sŏn nothing is assigned, reviewed, or escalated by a person standing above another person (ledger), so her manager's functions are distributed across five runners, each with a stated range, and no runner holds all of them.

The domain lead, by seat. Holds the person's check-in and reads and writes the person page there, and only there (S4 P20). Names the mentor from the pool (section 11). Places the paired services and the first solo on the schedule, the first solo only on a passed readiness form (section 6.5). Reads the training-infrastructure line to the leads' review. Does not teach the modules, does not run the readiness read, does not write a verdict, does not assign tasks, does not hold advancement (S5 P33). For floor seats on the outward-facing strand the domain lead is the Maitre d, who owns "Team development, training, and the invisible advocate function" (WP p.10); for the inward-facing floor strand, and for runner and host seats, the lead is held (S5 P64; `86akh7r10`) and every entry on this page that names the domain lead for those seats is incomplete until it closes; for beverage the Head of Beverage; for the kitchen, chef-gated.

The mentor. A proven cultural steward from the person's strand, named by the lead from the pool, paid as shift, beside the person at the live session and the paired services, answering questions, carrying the house's ways and the standard, and writing nothing on the person page (section 11).

The assessor. A trained assessor from the seat's strand who is not the mentor and does not decide, scoring the readiness read on the practical's rows (S6 I4; S5 P41). The same separation hiring uses: the person who taught is not the person who reads.

The founder, for the why. Pre-opening and through dinner's first quarter, a founder delivers the why block of orientation in person (section 5.4). After that, the holder of the concept's voice internally, which is an open question the ledger carries (`86akh2qq0`; spec `86akh3u2y`).

The stack. Creates the accounts at acceptance, delivers what arrives in the person's hands, places the check-ins, records module completion and paired services, refuses a start date without its conditions and a solo without a form, and writes the milestone dates it can see. Onboarding runs without a lead's memory, or it is a node-overload failure by the ledger's rule.

**P5 (Recommended).** Her manager's onboarding functions are distributed across five runners with stated ranges: the domain lead (check-in, mentor named, paired and solo placed on a passed form, the infrastructure line), the mentor (beside the person, teaching the house's ways, writing nothing), the assessor (the readiness read, not the mentor, not the decider), the founder and later the voice-holder (the why block), and the stack (accounts, delivery, placement, refusals, records). No runner holds all of them, and no mechanism depends on a lead remembering.

### 2.5 The four-part entry test, run on every mechanism

The ledger's rule: any mechanism states its bandwidth cost, what it buys, who runs it, and where its record lives, or it does not enter the cadence. The table runs the test on every mechanism this page adds. Mechanisms Sessions 4 and 5 already entered (the check-in, the person page, the start-date conditions) are not re-tested.

| Mechanism | Bandwidth cost | What it buys | Who runs it | Where the record lives |
| ---| ---| ---| ---| --- |
| The arrival note (I1) | None to the person; generated by the stack at acceptance | The record's "information is delivered, expectations are set" (WP p.18) with nothing required before the first paid hour | The stack; the Operations Lead for its legal content | Rippling's onboarding record and the person page |
| The orientation block (I3) | One scheduled block on the first shift per person, paid; a founder's or voice-holder's presence for the why block | Why before how as a mechanism rather than a poster | The domain lead; a founder for the why | The person page's first milestone, dated by the stack |
| The range card (I4) | Read once at orientation, taught in one module, rehearsed at paired services | Row 4 as an output rather than a hope | The domain lead; the mentor | The seat sheet's field 10 version on the person page |
| The seat's module set (I5) | Taken on scheduled shift, in the check-in's unit of time per module | The platform's teaching, in the person's language, before any table | The person, self-paced; authored under I11 | Trainual's completion record, copied to the person page |
| The mentor (I6) | The mentor's shift hours beside the person at the live session and the paired services, placed by the stack | The record's mentor with a range and a refusal list | The domain lead names; the mentor holds | The mentor's name and pool eligibility on the person page |
| The readiness read (I7) | One assessor as a placed extra body for one paired block per person | "No one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19) with a form behind it | The assessor; the lead reads the form | The readiness form on the person page; the first solo on the schedule |
| The four-week load read (I8) | One line per week at the check-in, inside the fifteen minutes | The load the training services could not read (S6 P31) | The domain lead at the check-in | The person page |
| The felt-knowledge block (I9) | The tastings in training services; one module per dish set | Mahk at service rather than recited description | The chef partner for content; the assessor reads it | The readiness form's felt-knowledge row |
| The plan's six check-in reads (I10) | Inside the fifteen minutes already funded | The plan carried by its check-ins rather than by a lead's memory | The domain lead | The person page's check-in lines |
| The onboarding read (I12) | One line at the monthly domain read, computed by the stack | The record's "planned rather than hoped for" measured, with no target | The Maitre d at the domain read | The domain read's record |
| The lead's plan and pre-reads (I13) | The lead's first six weeks are build time already scheduled | A lead who has read the operating system before running it | The sponsoring partner | The lead's person page |

Nothing in the table adds a meeting, a form the person fills, or a minute off the clock. The bandwidth ledger's per-person count (S4 P63) is unchanged: the modules and the paired services are shift, the orientation block is the first shift, and the six reads sit inside the check-in already funded.

**P6 (Recommended).** The eleven mechanisms this page adds pass the four-part entry test as tabled, and none adds to the hourly person's monthly count in the bandwidth ledger beyond the scheduled shift on which training already runs.

## 3\. The pre-opening cohort and the steady-state hire, mechanism by mechanism

Her onboarding is written for a person joining a running house: a curriculum exists, teams exist to absorb them, a manager has context to translate, and "internal resources to self-educate" (Book p.217) already exist to be found. Sŏn's first cohort joins a building that is not open, has no menu until the chef chain reaches it (S6 P15), has no team to absorb them because they are the team, and has no learning platform content until someone builds it. The record's commitments are written in the steady state and do not say which of them assume a running house. This section says so, and writes the pre-opening form of each beside the steady-state form, so that neither is quietly used for the other.

| Mechanism | Assumes a running house? | Steady-state form | Pre-opening form |
| ---| ---| ---| --- |
| The person page at the offer (S5 P16) | No | Ten entries at the offer | Same. The page exists on the team home before the OS surface does; where the team home lives pre-surface is to confirm (section 8.2) |
| The start date's conditions (S5 12.6) | Partly: "the training platform carries the seat's first modules" assumes modules exist | The stack refuses a date without them | The first modules are built by the leads and founders before any cohort start date (section 8.4); a date that cannot be set because they are not built is a training-infrastructure load on the partners' review, not on recruiting |
| The mentor connected before arrival (WP p.18) | Yes: "a proven cultural steward" assumes someone has proven it | Named from the pool (section 11) | The cohort arrives in two waves; the first wave's mentors are the leads, the chef partner or station leads for the kitchen, and the founders for the why; the first wave mentors the second once the training-service record shows the non-negotiables held and the procedures reproduced (P8) |
| Orientation and the why block (section 5) | No, but assumes a charter | Individual, on the first shift, with the voice-holder for the why | The cohort's orientation runs as one block per wave, in the building, with a founder; the community her section wants (Book p.217) is the cohort itself and needs no mechanism |
| The module set (section 8) | Yes: content exists | Taken on the platform, self-paced, on shift | The first set is built before the cohort and is the interim platform on Trainual; the cohort's completion records are the first the platform holds |
| The live session (section 6.1) | No | The mentor walks the section or station with the person outside service | Same, in the building, before training services begin |
| The observed and paired services (section 6.1) | Yes: real services exist | Observed beside the mentor in a real service; paired on the schedule in real services the leads' review has not flagged | Training services are the only floor there is (S5 P42); observed and paired run in them, marked as run without load, and the readiness read in a training service reads procedure and not load |
| The readiness read and the first solo (section 6.5) | Partly | The form in a real paired service; the solo placed after | The form in a training service; the first solo is, for most of the cohort, dinner's first service, which the ledger already forbids as anyone's first shift and this page reads as no one's first solo either (P10) |
| The four-week load read (S6 P31) | Yes | The person's first four solo weeks | The cohort's first four dinner weeks, one line per week at the check-in |
| The six check-ins (section 7.4) | No | Placed by the stack on pre-service windows the lead works | Same; training services have pre-service windows and the stack places the check-ins on them; the cohort's plans straddle dinner's gate and the first-quarter freeze does not touch them because the check-in's interval is frozen, not stopped (S4 P9) |
| The felt-knowledge block (section 9) | Yes: a menu exists | The block for the current dishes, revised when the menu changes | The block cannot exist until the chef chain reaches the menu; the cohort tastes in training services after the menu is fixed; the count of tastings needed is chef-gated (P43) |
| The range card (section 12) | No | Read at orientation, rehearsed, stated at the readiness read | Same, except that the threshold values in the range are unset (S3 4.2, instance 3) and the card states the hold in words |
| Cross-training tracks visible from day one (S5 P60) | No | Every inventory seat's requirements posted | Same; the early-morning sheets are drafted and visible (S5 P10) |
| The onboarding read (section 8.6) | Yes: volume | Monthly, at the domain read | First run at the mechanism reset after dinner's first quarter, on the cohort's record |
| The lead variant (section 6.4) | Yes: a co-lead, a domain, a running cadence | The co-lead as mentor; the domain's check-ins reading the lead upward | The first two leads have no co-lead to learn from and no domain to run; their onboarding is the partners' review from arrival, the pre-reads, and each other (P25) |

Three positions fall out of the table.

The cohort in two waves. The record's mentor is "a proven cultural steward" (WP p.18), and on the cohort's first day no one below the leads has proven anything. The industry's answer is to let the strongest performer mentor, which the record refuses in the same sentence. The team's answer is sequencing: the cohort arrives in two waves, the first wave small enough for the leads and the chef's kitchen owners to mentor directly, trained through the training services, and the second wave mentored by the first once the training-service record shows, per person, the procedures reproduced on the readiness form and no non-negotiable line on the person page. The first wave's mentor mark is provisional and converts at the mechanism reset (S4 P39) against the record. This is a hiring-calendar choice and it interacts with the pre-opening hiring burst, which is founder-gated (`86akh7qnb`; S5 P49), so it is marked founder-gated with the team's recommendation stated. What the team does not recommend: a single wave mentored by the leads alone, which is node overload by construction (WP p.14) at the moment the leads are also standing up their domains; or hiring an outside "trainer" seat, which the record's leadership count has no room for (WP p.22) and which would teach the industry's floor.

Who builds the first modules. Section 8.4 holds the mechanism. The position here is only that the first module set exists before any cohort start date is committed, that its authors are the leads for the floor, the chef partner or the kitchen's domain owners for the kitchen, and the founders for the why and the system modules, and that until the first cohort completes them there is no completion record on the platform and the record's "constantly expanding" (WP p.19) has not started. A cohort start date committed before the seat's first modules exist is a refusal the stack already holds (S5 12.6), and pre-opening the refusal is read against the partners' page, where the module set's state is a readiness row (row 78).

The first solo, pre-opening. The ledger forbids a first shift on a new period's first service. It does not say whether a cohort member's first solo, meaning their first service holding a section or station without a mentor beside them, may be dinner's opening night. The team reads the record's "no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19) with the Realist's rule that "opening night is not month six" (profile) as forbidding it: the training services are where the cohort's readiness forms are passed and where the first solos happen, so that on dinner's first service every section and station is held by a person who has already held it alone in at least one training service. The training-service count that makes this possible is a hiring-calendar item (S6 I14) and is not a figure this page sets.

**P7 (Recommended).** The pre-opening form of every onboarding mechanism is as tabled beside its steady-state form, and no mechanism written for a running house is used on the cohort without its pre-opening form: the training services stand in for real services and read procedure without load, the first four dinner weeks are the load read, the felt-knowledge block waits on the menu, and the onboarding read first runs at the mechanism reset.

**P8 (Founder-gated).** The cohort arrives in two waves, the first mentored by the leads and the kitchen's domain owners through the training services and the second by the first wave once the training-service record shows procedures reproduced and no non-negotiable line, with the first wave's mentor mark provisional until the mechanism reset. The founders close it with the pre-opening hiring burst (`86akh7qnb`), because it is a calendar and a count.

**P9 (Recommended).** The first module set for every dinner seat exists before any cohort start date is committed, authored by the leads for the floor, the kitchen's domain owners for the kitchen, and the founders for the why and the system modules; the stack's refusal of a start date without the seat's first modules (S5 12.6) is read pre-opening against the module set's state on the partners' page.

**P10 (Recommended).** No cohort member's first solo is dinner's first service. Readiness forms are passed and first solos are held in training services, so that every section and station on dinner's first service is held by a person who has already held it alone at least once. The training-service count is the hiring calendar's and is not set here.

## 4\. Before the first shift

### 4.1 The seam: acceptance

Session 6 fixed that the written offer's acceptance "is the seam to Rippling and the person page" (S6 P58). At that moment three things happen and the stack does all three: the person page is created with recruiting's ten entries (S5 P16); Rippling's onboarding opens, carrying the legal and payroll content the Operations Lead sets with counsel, which this page does not write; and the person's accounts are created by single sign-on through Rippling into Google Workspace, Trainual, and the team home, in the language the person chose at the fourth read (S6 P23). Whether Rippling's onboarding task list can carry the house's own items (the uniform fitting, the locker, the arrival note's acknowledgement) beside the legal ones is to confirm; if it cannot, the house's items live on the person page and the legal ones in Rippling, and nothing is duplicated.

Between acceptance and the first shift the person is in Greenhouse's accepted state and on Rippling's pre-start record, and they are not yet on the clock. Everything the house does in this window is the house's work, not the person's. That rule is the one the record's paragraph implies and does not state: "Everything needed to succeed is waiting" (WP p.18) describes what the house has done, and nothing in it describes what the person must have done, read, or completed before their first clock-in. This page makes it a rule (4.6).

### 4.2 The person page's ten entries, and the plan block added

Carryover `86akh7qn7` holds the ten entries whole: the seat and sheet version; the strand; the domain lead by seat; the decision-rights range as accepted; the service periods; the start date; the mentor, connected before arrival; the ninety-day plan's start; the first unlock the sheet names; and what the candidate said they need from the building, in their own words. No scorecard travels to the page (S6 row 71). This page changes none of the ten and adds one thing beneath them: the plan block (section 7.2), which is the record's "ninety-day plan while they are on one" (S4 P18) given its form. The plan block is written by the stack at acceptance from the sheet, and its milestones are empty states until they are reached.

Two things the ten entries need from this page that recruiting could not supply. First, the mentor entry is a person's name, and section 11 says who may be named and who may not, so recruiting's "mentor connected" now has a pool to name from. Second, "the ninety-day plan's start" is the start date, not the acceptance date and not the first solo, because the record's plan "sets expectations and goals with regular check-ins" (WP p.18) and the first check-in is two weeks after the start date (S5 4.5); a plan that started at acceptance would run its first two weeks off the clock.

**P11 (Recommended).** The person page's ten entries are held whole and unchanged; the plan block of section 7.2 is added beneath them, written by the stack at acceptance from the seat sheet with its milestones as empty states; the ninety-day plan starts on the start date, not at acceptance and not at the first solo.

### 4.3 The start date's conditions, held, and one condition surfaced

Session 5 wrote the conditions and this page runs under them: the mentor connected; the uniform and locker ready; the training platform carrying the seat's first modules; the plan's first check-in falling on a pre-service window the lead works; item 6 filled; not a new period's first service; not coverage before "no one touches a table until they are actually ready" can hold (S5 12.6). The stack refuses a date without them. Nothing here loosens any of them.

One condition this page would add, and surfaces rather than adds. The record commits that "Orientation to the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard happens before operational training" (WP p.18), and the mission sentence and principles version one are unratified (`86akh3tdr`, `86akh3tg0`). A person whose first shift is an orientation block with no ratified mission or principles to orient to has had the record's commitment unmet on their first day, and no later delivery is "before operational training." The team's position is that charter ratification is a condition of the cohort's start dates in the same list as the mentor and the modules, and that it is not a condition of the two leads' start dates, because the leads arrive six weeks before dinner's gate to run the cadence and their orientation to an unratified charter is a known incomplete they help close (section 6.4). This adds a condition to S5 12.6, which is a Session 5 position, and it is surfaced as an extension for Brandon to ratify alongside S5 12.6 or refuse. Section 5.5 argues it.

**P12 (Recommended).** The start date's conditions in S5 12.6 are held whole. The team recommends one extension, surfaced and not made: charter ratification (the mission sentence, principles version one, and the non-negotiables) as a condition of every cohort start date, and not of the two leads' start dates. Brandon ratifies the extension with S5 12.6 or refuses it.

### 4.4 The mentor connected

"The peer mentor is connected" before arrival (WP p.18) is a verb the record does not define. This page defines it. Connected means: the mentor is named on the person page from the pool (section 11); the stack sends the person, in their language, the mentor's name, seat, and a way to reach them through the team home; the mentor sends one message, on shift, in their own words, saying who they are and that they will be beside the person at the live session on the first shift; and the mentor's shifts for the person's first two weeks are placed on the schedule to overlap the person's. Nothing is required of the person in return. A conversation before the first shift, if the person wants one, is at the person's initiative, is answered by the mentor on the clock, and is not a condition of anything.

What connected does not mean: a checklist the mentor works through by phone; a pre-arrival "buddy" call the person is expected to make; the mentor delivering paperwork, the schedule, or the range; or the mentor learning anything about the person from the packet, which stays in Greenhouse and which the mentor never sees (S5 P16). The mentor meets the person as the house does, from the seat sheet and the person page's ten entries, and not from an interviewer's evidence lines.

**P13 (Recommended).** "Mentor connected" means named from the pool on the person page, introduced by the stack in the person's language, one message from the mentor on shift, and the mentor's first two weeks of shifts placed to overlap the person's. Nothing is required of the person before the first shift; the mentor never sees the packet.

### 4.5 What arrives in the person's hands, and through which tool

Her rule is that "all prep work should be done asynchronously before the onboarding program starts," from paperwork to equipment (Book p.217). The record's is that "information is delivered, expectations are set" and "the uniform and tools are ready down to the shoes" (WP p.18). This page lists what arrives, in what order, through which tool, and what each is for. The list is the arrival note (I1) and the physical items beside it.

Through Rippling, on acceptance: the legal and payroll onboarding the Operations Lead sets with counsel; benefits enrollment where the record's commitment applies (WP p.20); the single sign-on that creates the other accounts. This page writes none of the content and fixes only that it is in the person's language where the law and the tool permit, and that no house item is hidden inside a legal task.

Through the team home, on acceptance: the arrival note, generated by the stack from the sheet and the person page, in the person's language, in the correspondence register (Canon v1.0, section 09). It carries: the start date and the first shift's hours, stated as a paid orientation block with no table and no station; where to arrive and what the first hour is; the mentor's name and seat; the seat sheet, current version, which the person has held since the first interview (S5 P34); the transparency sheet, current version, unchanged from the offer; the range card (I4) as the sheet's field 10 rendered for the person, marked as something that will be read aloud together on the first shift; the schedule for the first two weeks, with the check-in visible on it as the ledger requires (S4 P15); a link to the seat's first modules on Trainual, visible and not assigned; the person page itself, which the person can already read; the languages the house speaks; and one line stating that nothing in the note is required before the first shift. It carries no "welcome," no exclamation point, no founder's story, and no line that names its own effect (Canon v1.0, section 09).

Through the building, before the start date: the uniform, fitted at a scheduled block that is paid as shift, in the garments canon specifies for the seat's role once the uniform tables are reconciled (section 19, finding 19.4), with shoes where the record says "shoes where appropriate" (WP p.19); the locker, assigned and named on the person page (WP p.19); and the tools the seat sheet's field 13 implies, ready at the station or section on the first shift and not handed across a desk. The fitting is the one pre-start block that is on the clock, because it is the house's work done on the person's body and it is not asynchronous.

Through Trainual, before the start date: the seat's first module set, visible, with the person's account already inside it, and no module assigned, due, or tracked before the first shift. A person who opens a module before their start date has done so on their own time and the record shows it as opened, not as required.

What does not arrive: a handbook. The handbook is the HR Systems Designer's document (profile, people systems designer), gated on the document methodology (`86ajgn2z5`), and this page specifies nothing about it except that when it exists it arrives through Rippling and is read on shift. Her employee handbook, which her hiring-mistakes section makes the reference for a violation (Book p.224), is at Sŏn the non-negotiables (Canon v1.0, section 01) until the handbook exists, and the arrival note says so.

**P14 (Recommended).** What arrives before the first shift, and through which tool: Rippling's legal and payroll onboarding and the single sign-on; the arrival note on the team home with the items listed, in the person's language and the correspondence register; the uniform fitted at a paid block, the locker assigned, the tools at the station; and the seat's first modules visible on Trainual and not assigned. No handbook exists yet; the non-negotiables stand in for it and the note says so.

### 4.6 Nothing is required before the first paid hour

The rule, stated once and applied everywhere on this page: nothing is required of a person before their first paid hour. Not a module, not a reading, not a call, not a form beyond what the law requires through Rippling. The record's onboarding paragraph describes what the house has ready; it does not describe homework. No Exploitation Ever (Canon v1.0, section 01) closes the door before any schedule does, and the ledger's rule that the check-in is on the clock by construction (S4 P15) is the same rule one step earlier. Her "all prep work should be done asynchronously" (Book p.217) is held for the house's prep and refused for the person's. Section 19 files the record's own silence on this as a finding (19.10), because "information is delivered" (WP p.18) does not say whether it is to be read before the first clock-in, and a house that assumed it would have built unpaid work into its first sentence to a new person.

**P15 (Recommended).** Nothing is required of a person before their first paid hour: no module, reading, call, or form beyond the law's through Rippling. What arrives before the start date is delivered, not assigned, and the arrival note says so in one line.

## 5\. Why before how: the charter delivery, and the blocking dependency stated

### 5.1 The record's commitment, and what it needs

"Why comes before how. Orientation to the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard happens before operational training, because a person needs the reason before the mechanics" (WP p.18). Carryover `86akh3w9a` is exact about the source: the content is drawn from the charter, not from a version this page writes, and if the charter is unratified the page records that the record's own commitment is unmet and names the charter as the blocking dependency rather than filling the gap with brand language. It is unratified: the mission sentence (`86akh3tdr`) and principles version one with the long-term commitments (`86akh3tg0`) are open in the ledger.

Her version of the same commitment is the "why" first, then the "what," then the "how" (Book p.216), delivered by leadership through "stories, not bullet points" (Book p.216). The record's order is the same and its three terms are narrower and better: the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard. This page uses the record's three.

### 5.2 What the charter holds now, and what it does not

The behavioral standard is ratified. It is the three non-negotiables, No Exploitation Ever, No Toxicity Ever, No Disposable People, and the order bandwidth, then joy, then retention, then results (Canon v1.0, section 01; Canon v3.0, p.4), and it is what the candidate was already handed as the transparency sheet's item 9, "the house's commitments to the candidate before they are the candidate's to the house" (S5 P34). The language constant, "The word is customer" (Canon v3.0, p.5), is ratified canon and is part of the standard as this page reads it, because it is a behavior every person in the house performs in every sentence.

The structure is the record. The web with no top and no bottom, the outside edge as the most sensitive position, growth outward, strands not levels, the domain lead as a systems function and not a rank, the invisible advocate, blame the process (WP p.9 to 14, p.17). These are decided, and orientation delivers them as they stand.

The mission sentence and the principles are not ratified. Orientation's why block has a first sentence it cannot yet say and a set of principles it cannot yet read aloud. Session 6 met the same gap in the third read's principle-embedded questions and held them (S6 P22); Session 4 met it in the goal page's commitment field, which "points at a placeholder until they land" (S4 P41). This page holds the why block's first two parts the same way: the block has a slot, the slot is empty, and an empty slot is not filled with brand positioning ("Korean restraint. Texas warmth. Polished but playful," Canon v3.0, p.3), which is a brand's account of itself to a customer and not a house's account of why it exists to a person who works in it. Positioning is delivered in orientation as positioning, in the brand module, and never as the mission.

### 5.3 The why block's content, in the record's order

The why block is the first content of the first shift, after the walk of the building and before any module, station, or section. It is spoken, in person, by the person section 5.4 names, in the languages the cohort speaks, with an interpreter where one is needed, and it is not a slide deck. Its order:

1. The mission, as ratified. The sentence, said once, and what it was chosen against. Empty until `86akh3tdr` closes.
2. The principles, as ratified, each with one moment from the record or the house's own captures in which it decided something. Empty until `86akh3tg0` closes. When the house has run, the moments come from the shift-close captures and the post-mortems, which is where Session 4 said the principles are tested (S4 P39); pre-opening, from the record's own stories.
3. The behavioral standard: the three non-negotiables, read as the house's commitments to the person first; the order bandwidth, joy, retention, results, with the record's own account of why the order is the decision (WP p.12, p.17); and the language constant, with the record's reason for it, that "customer keeps the transaction visible" and "You cannot truly belong somewhere that is performing for you" (WP p.25).
4. The structure the person has entered: the web, drawn on paper or on the wall from the person's own node outward (S5 P32); the outside edge as the most sensitive position, in the record's words (WP p.9); what the domain lead is and is not (S5 P33); the invisible advocate and the seat after theirs, opened on the person's own account so they see it (WP p.11; S5 P60); and blame the process, with the record's own worked example of the server, the incident, the shift close, and the next server inheriting the fix (WP p.13).
5. The stories. Her rule is right and canon sharpens it: "Specificity is the mechanism of memory" (Canon v1.0, section 01). The stories are the record's own and they are told as what happened: the room in New York that added lunch and brunch and both stayed flat, and what that taught about structure (WP p.2); the coffee shop on the wrong side of the road (WP p.3); the broken computer everyone has used (WP p.12); the fourteen leadership lines around one dinner service (WP p.22). None is a founder hero narrative; each is an argument about structure told as an event, which is what "stories of those principles in action" (Book p.216) means when the principle is structural.

What the why block refuses: a video in place of a person; a synthesized presenter of any kind (section 8.3); a printed values poster, which the record names as the thing culture is not (WP p.18); a quiz; a signature acknowledging the values; any content that names its own effect; positioning presented as mission; canon's forbidden word for the customer in any story, including quoted ones, which are paraphrased; a daypart code name; any figure.

### 5.4 Who delivers it

Her ask is that "company leadership should take part in onboarding new hires" (Book p.216). At Sŏn "Brandon Acuña-Cardona is the public voice and the origin of the operating concepts" (WP p.3), and the ledger holds open who carries the concept's voice to the team internally (`86akh2qq0`; spec `86akh3u2y`). The why block is exactly that function at its first and most consequential moment.

The team's position: pre-opening and through dinner's first quarter, a founder delivers the why block in person to every wave and every later hire, because there is no one else who holds the concept and because the first quarter's freeze (S4 P9) is not a reason for the founders to be absent from the one block that is theirs. After the mechanism reset, the holder of the concept's voice internally delivers it, and if that question has not closed by the reset, the founder continues and the reset records it as a load on the founder's seat. A domain lead delivers the fourth part, the structure, from the second quarter, because the structure is the lead's daily object; the lead never delivers the first three, because the lead is a systems function inside the structure and not its author. The mentor is present at the block and delivers none of it.

**P16 (Founder-gated).** The why block's first two parts, the mission and the principles, are empty until the charter is ratified (`86akh3tdr`, `86akh3tg0`). The record's own onboarding commitment, that orientation to the mission and the values precedes operational training, is unmet until then, and the charter is the blocking dependency. The team does not fill the slots with brand language and marks them. With it, who carries the concept's voice internally after the first quarter (`86akh2qq0`) is founder-gated and the team recommends the founder continues until it closes.

**P17 (Recommended).** The why block runs in the record's order, mission, principles, behavioral standard, structure, stories, as the first content of the first shift, spoken in person by a founder pre-opening and through dinner's first quarter, in the cohort's languages, with the structure delivered by the domain lead from the second quarter and the stories drawn from the record as events. It refuses video, a synthesized presenter, a poster, a quiz, an acknowledgement signature, positioning as mission, and any figure.

### 5.5 The blocking dependency, argued

The argument for making charter ratification a start-date condition (P12) is the record's own sequence rule: "a person needs the reason before the mechanics" (WP p.18). A cohort onboarded to the non-negotiables and the structure alone has received the behavioral standard and the web, which is most of the why, and a house that had to choose would rather have that than nothing. But the record does not say "most of." The commitment is the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard, in that order, and a cohort onboarded without the first two would be told the mission later, after their operational training, which is the sequence the record forbids. The leads are the exception because the leads are the people who will close the charter with the founders, and their orientation to an unratified charter is a known incomplete on their own plan (section 6.4) rather than a commitment unmet.

What this costs: if the charter is not ratified by the time the hiring calendar wants the cohort's first start dates, the start dates wait, and the gate slides. That is the same shape as Session 6's P16 on the compensation architecture, and the team's recommendation is the same: ratify ahead rather than slide. The charter's ratification is already a readiness row (S3 row 5) and the gate cannot open around it; this position only moves it earlier, to the cohort's start dates, which precede the gate by the training-service count.

## 6\. The first shift, the first week, the first ninety days

### 6.1 The sequence, and why it is the interviewer's sequence

Session 6 fixed the training form for interviewers: modules read, a live session, an observed stage, a paired stage read side by side, then solo, all on scheduled shift, with the record written by the stack (S6 P38). The brief asks whether operational training uses the same sequence and why.

It does, and the reason is not economy of design. The sequence is the one canon's training requirement produces when it is taken seriously: "training architecture that progresses from procedure mastery to autonomous judgment" (Canon v1.0, section 01). Modules carry the procedure as knowledge; the live session carries it as demonstration; the observed service carries it as the procedure seen at tempo; the paired service carries it as the procedure done at tempo with a person beside you; the solo is the procedure done alone, and judgment begins there. Her section's own kitchen voice describes the industry's alternative, "thrown onto the job" (Book p.216), and the record describes it as "Shadow someone for two shifts, catch fragments because they are busy, get thrown in before ready" (WP p.19). Two shifts of shadowing is the observed step with the other four missing. The sequence is what the record's paragraph is asking for, and the interviewer training is the first place the house wrote it down.

Two things differ from the interviewer's sequence, and they are stated. The paired step, for a floor or kitchen seat, is not one paired service but as many as the seat's entry procedures need, and the count is on the seat sheet's training plan (item 5) and not a house constant, because a runner's entry procedures and a server's are not the same length. And the solo step is gated by the readiness read (section 6.5), scored by an assessor, where the interviewer's solo is gated by the paired read of two scorecards; the difference is that an interviewer's solo produces a scorecard the Maitre d reads afterward, and a server's solo produces a customer's evening, which no one reads afterward.

The steps, defined once:

Modules read. The seat's first module set (section 8), on Trainual, taken on scheduled shift in the check-in's unit of time per module, self-paced within the first week, in the person's language. Modules are read before the live session and never in place of it.

The live session. The mentor walks the section or station with the person, outside service, in the building: the setup, the sequence, the positions, the surfaces the seat uses on the stack, the close. For a floor seat this is the section's setup and the step-back positions walked on the floor with no customer in the room; for a kitchen station, chef-gated in every specific; for the bar, the well. One block, on shift, in the pre-service window of a service the person then observes, or in a training service.

The observed service. The person is on the schedule beside the mentor for a service, carrying nothing: not a table, not a station, not a runner's tray. They attend the brief and do not speak at it, they stand in the step-back coverage position beside the mentor, they watch the pass, and they attend the close and watch the capture. The customer is never told a person is observing. One observed service for an edge seat; more where the seat sheet says so.

The paired services. The person works the section or station with the mentor or the seat holder beside them, carrying what the mentor hands them, on services the leads' review has not flagged short, placed by the stack with the mentor as a teaching body (S6 P31's rule for practicals, applied). The count is the seat sheet's. The person never carries a recovery, a generosity decision, or a David flag alone during a paired service; those are the seat holder's range until the solo (S5 P41's rule for candidates, applied through the paired step).

The readiness read. In the last paired service, or a separate one, an assessor who is not the mentor scores the seat's entry procedures on the practical's rows (S6 I4), the two people rows, the range stated, the language constant, and the felt-knowledge block, and submits the readiness form (I7). Section 6.5.

The solo. The first service the person holds a section or station without the mentor beside them, placed on the schedule by the domain lead only on a passed form, never a new period's first service, never dinner's first service (P10), never a service the leads' review flagged short. The mentor is in the building, on their own section, and reachable. The four-week load read starts here.

**P18 (Recommended).** Operational onboarding uses the interviewer training's sequence, modules read, a live session, an observed service, paired services, then solo, because it is the sequence canon's procedure-to-judgment requirement produces and the record's sink-or-swim paragraph describes by its absence. Two differences: the paired count is the seat sheet's, and the solo is gated by an assessor's readiness form.

### 6.2 The hourly edge seat, first

Written for a server on the outward-facing strand, because the server is the seat the customer feels and the seat whose range the record has already written (WP p.13; Canon v1.0, section 08). The runner, the bar, and the host follow as variants, and the kitchen is section 6.3.

The first shift. An orientation block, paid, scheduled, with no table. In order: the building walked, from the south drop-off through the nine beats (Canon v1.0, section 06) to the service threshold, the employee area, and the person's locker, walked and not narrated beyond what a person needs to find their way, because "We walk, we never point" (Canon v1.0, section 06) is the house's own rule and orientation is the first place it is kept; the uniform, already fitted, and canon's aging rule for it, that "evidence of honest use" is acceptable and "visible neglect, loss of structure" is not (Canon v1.0, section 08); the why block (section 5); the stack, which is the person's accounts opened on their own phone, the schedule with the check-in on it, the person page read together, the seat after theirs found together on the team home (S5 P60), and the feedback channel shown as the door the record built for "what is in the way" (WP p.22); the range card read aloud together, the range first and the triggers after, with the person saying it back (section 12); the mentor, met in person, and the first two weeks' schedule read against the mentor's; and the non-negotiables, again, as what the person may raise and where (S4 P20's trigger). The first shift ends there. It is one block and the Realist's rule is that it is placed on a day with no service in the building, or before a service the person then observes, and never inside a pre-service window a lead needs.

The first week. The seat's first modules, on shift; the live session with the mentor on the section; one observed service; the first paired service by the end of the week where the seat sheet's count allows. The first check-in is not in the first week; it is two weeks after the start date, placed by the stack, and the first week's questions go to the mentor.

Weeks two to six. The paired services at the seat sheet's count, on the schedule with the mentor as a teaching body. The first check-in at week two (section 7.4). The felt-knowledge block, once the dishes have been tasted (section 9). The readiness read in the last paired service. The first solo, placed on a passed form. The second check-in at week four.

Weeks six to thirteen. Solo services. The four-week load read, one line per week at the check-in (S6 P31). The range used, and the first escalation the person makes read at the fourth check-in. The platform opened beyond the first set, which is dimension 2's record beginning (S6 P33). The fifth check-in reads the path: the first unlock's date from the sheet, and what the person wants to learn next. The sixth closes the plan (section 7.4).

The runner, on the inward-facing strand. The same sequence, with the seat sheet's own procedures: the pass, the tray, the sequence to the table, the hand-off to the server, the clear, the station's close. The runner's observed service watches the pass more than the floor. The runner's range is smaller than the server's and the card says so; the runner's domain lead is held (S5 P64) and the runner's plan carries the hold in words. Canon's uniform for the runner, in Version 3.0 only, is "Quiet layer, no logo. Never the subject" (Canon v3.0, p.81); Version 1.0 has no runner line, and the fitting waits on finding 19.4.

The bar. The same sequence at the well, with the Head of Beverage as the domain lead (S5 P33). The bar's felt-knowledge block is the beverage program's and it is the Head of Beverage's content in the same form as the kitchen's (section 9); the coffee program's procedures, batched espresso, the undercounter installation, the automatic frother (WP p.4 to 5), are the early-morning period's module set and do not enter a dinner bar seat's plan until that period's charter is ratified (P3).

The host. Whether the Lead Host seat exists is open (S6 18.9), canon removes the host stand (Canon v1.0, section 08), and canon's arrival choreography places the Maitre d at the top of the porch steps (Canon v1.0, section 06; Canon v3.0, p.68). No host plan is written on this page. A host seat, if the inventory carries one, runs the same sequence with the arrival choreography as its procedures, and its domain lead is held (`86akh7r10`).

**P19 (Recommended).** The hourly edge seat's first shift is a paid orientation block with no table: the building walked, the uniform, the why block, the stack on the person's own phone, the range card read aloud and said back, the mentor met, and the non-negotiables as what the person may raise. The first week is modules, the live session, one observed service, and the first paired service; weeks two to six are the paired services, the felt-knowledge block, the readiness read, and the first solo; weeks six to thirteen are solo services with the load read, the range used, and the path opened. Runner, bar, and host variants as stated, with the runner's and host's domain leads held.

### 6.3 The kitchen seat

The sequence stands and every specific is the chef partner's. The record's kitchen has "Station Leads" as domain owners and "Chef on the line and Chef on prep" as domain execution, "neither a promotion from the other," and the Steward who "owns the continuity of the kitchen environment" (WP p.11). No kitchen seat sheet, module, live session, paired count, readiness row, or felt-knowledge content exists before the chef chain reaches the menu (S6 P15; S5 P44), and the chain's order is fixed: ruling, chef seated, canon's Session 1B, menu, kitchen seat sheets, kitchen practicals, kitchen hires, their training, dinner's gate. The kitchen's training therefore starts later than the floor's on the calendar and must still finish before dinner's gate, which is the sequencing problem section 9 states as a gate condition.

What this page fixes for the kitchen without the chef: the sequence's five steps and the solo gated on a readiness form; the assessor as someone other than the mentor; the check-in's holder for the kitchen as chef-gated (S4 P16); the Steward's seat as a seat with its own sheet, sequence, and plan, "not a support role" (WP p.11), never onboarded as an afterthought to the line; the kitchen's why block delivered by the founder like every other seat's, because "If you're getting hired as a cook, it's not just about the kitchen" (Book p.216) is the record's own "understanding all the layers" said by a chef; and the language rule, that a cook is onboarded in the language they chose at the fourth read (S6 P23) and the kitchen's modules exist in it.

**P20 (Chef-gated).** The kitchen seats' module content, live session, paired count, readiness rows, felt-knowledge content, and mentor pool are the chef partner's, written in this page's forms, after the chef chain reaches the menu. Fixed without the chef: the five-step sequence, the solo on a readiness form, the assessor distinct from the mentor, the Steward as a seat with its own plan, the founder's why block for every kitchen hire, and the modules in the cook's chosen language.

### 6.4 The lead variant

Her leadership onboarding standardizes the core and adds for leaders (Book p.219). This page does the same: the lead is onboarded on the same five steps and the same plan, and the variant is in what each step contains, who stands beside the lead, and what the plan's goal is. Written so it does not depend on what a lead enters at (S6 18.3), which is not resolved here; the one place it would depend is marked.

The two leads pre-opening. They arrive at least six weeks before dinner's gate (S6 P15; S5 row 56), into a building with no service, no cohort, and no cadence running. Their onboarding is: the pre-reads (I13), which are the record whole, both canon versions, the ratified pages of this operating system document from Session 1 onward, the founders' working-with-me documents issued on seating (S1 7.6), and the seat sheet for their own seat with the record's definitions as its fields (S5 P55); the why block from a founder, with the charter's unratified parts stated as the incomplete they will help close; the partners' review from the day of arrival, as the hires "as they arrive" the pre-opening rhythm already seats there (S4 P3), which is where her "daily or every-other-day standup" (Book p.221) is refused as a mechanism and its function, "quickly answer questions, capture the new leader's impressions, and align" (Book p.221), lands without a new meeting; the leads' review run by the two leads from their first full week, because row 21 needs six consecutive weeks of it before the gate and the leads' review is the leads' own observed and paired step in one; and the training services, where each lead's domain first exists. The Maitre d's live session is the floor walked with a founder; the Operations Lead's is the stack walked with Dominic, who owns "the technology build" (WP p.3). The two leads' mentors are each other and the founders; the record has no one else, and this page does not invent a coach.

The lead's plan. The plan's goal is not an unlock, because the record gives the leads no unlock and no word for what they enter at (S6 18.3); the goal is a state: the lead's domain running on the cadence, which for the first two leads is row 21 held, six consecutive leads' reviews with records, and every seat in their domain filled and its holder past the readiness read. The plan's milestones are the cadence's own rows for the lead's domain. Its check-ins are with a partner: the Maitre d's with Brandon's seat, whose domain holds experience and team health, and the Operations Lead's with the partner whose domain holds the disputed outcome under S3's Class C rule, which for a plan check-in means Dominic for the systems and cost outcomes and Brandon for the operating systems; where a lead's plan crosses both, both partners hold the check-in together, once, at the sixth. This is the check-in the record's "Team members weigh in on management effectiveness" (WP p.19) does not reach for a lead, and section 19 files it (19.7). The interval is the ledger's, every two weeks; the partners' review weekly already has the lead in the room and is not a check-in.

Later leads, after opening. A later lead hired from outside runs the leadership loop with the co-lead as second interviewer (S6 P67), and their onboarding adds what the first two could not have: the co-lead as mentor, the domain's own check-ins reading the new lead upward from the first week (S6 P67), the person pages of the domain read with each person at that person's next check-in (section 14.3, in place of her transitions meeting), and the working-with-me document written inside the plan (section 14.1). The pre-reads are the same set plus the domain's captures and the last two house reviews. The lead's first six weeks run on the in-service cadence, and a later lead's first solo is the first leads' review they run without the co-lead carrying the agenda.

Where the variant would depend on 18.3. The transparency sheet's item 7, the advancement path, for a lead; the lead's "first unlock" entry on the person page; and the entry pay rule for a lead (S6 P63). The plan's goal above avoids all three by being a state of the domain rather than a state of the lead. Nothing else in the variant needs the answer.

What the variant refuses: a leadership assessment of any kind, which reads a person for a seat and is refused for the same reason the work style grid was (S5 P8); a coach, which is a spend this program does not price and is founder-gated as such; a ninety-day 360, whose function is done by the upward question at every check-in the lead holds and by the employee NPS the record already commits (WP p.22); welcome emails, whose function is the brief's one thing carrying the seat's new holder as a fact (S6 P71) and the documented build with consent (S5 P19); an onboarding point person, which is the stack; and "loan your social capital," because a lead's authority "lives in the domain" (WP p.7) and is not borrowed from a person above them.

**P21 (Recommended).** The lead variant runs the same five steps and the same plan with the pre-reads as its modules, the partners' review as its standing forum from arrival, the leads' review as its observed and paired step, and the training services as its floor; the plan's goal is the domain running on the cadence and its milestones are the cadence's rows for that domain; the plan's check-ins are with a partner under S3's Class C rule; later leads add the co-lead as mentor, the domain's check-ins reading them upward, the domain's person pages read with each person, and the working-with-me document inside the plan. The variant depends on finding 18.3 only for item 7, the first-unlock entry, and the entry pay rule, all of which the plan's goal avoids.

**P22 (Founder-gated).** Whether a coach is engaged for a lead's first months. The team recommends none: the partners' check-in under P21 does the work the record can name, and a coach is a spend this program does not price. The founders close it.

### 6.5 The first solo, and the readiness read

"Competency validation: no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19) is the record's one gate inside onboarding and the record does not say who reads readiness, against what, or in what form. Two accounts of the advancement gate sit in the record, the system auto-scheduling a practical assessment and the person scheduling a competency conversation with a lead who signs off (S6 18.2), and this page does not resolve them. For the first solo it does not need to: the readiness read is not an advancement and it is not the first unlock. It is the entry horizon of field 6 read once, at the end of the paired services, by a person trained to read it.

The readiness read. In a paired service the leads' review has not flagged short, an assessor from the seat's strand, trained under the assessor module (S6 P37, module 9), placed on the schedule as an extra body for the block, who is not the person's mentor and did not run any of the person's paired services, scores: the seat's entry procedures on the practical's rows, reproduced, reproduced with correction and the count, or not reproduced (S6 I4); the two universal rows, asked before guessing and cleaned as they went; the three people rows, with an evidence line and a non-negotiables mark; the language row, every sentence heard to a customer and to a colleague, with "customer" held and no forbidden word; the range row, the person asked, off the floor before or after the block, to state their range and its triggers unprompted, with the answer recorded in the person's words; and the felt-knowledge row (section 9), for the dishes that exist, in the chef's or the Head of Beverage's form. The form carries the block's start and end, the mentor's name, the assessor's name and training record, and the assessor's recommendation: ready, or not yet with the rows named. No composite, no score, no verdict, no row for presence, speed, nunchi, or how the section felt about the person (S6 P29 applied). The form goes to the person page as a milestone with its rows, which the person reads, and it is the one form on the person page, because it is a milestone and not a scorecard: it carries no dimension marks and no recommendation beyond ready or not yet, and Session 13 does not score against it.

Not yet. A "not yet" names the rows and the rows are what the platform teaches; the person takes the module for each row again and one more paired service, the assessor reads again, and nothing about it is on the person page but the rows and the next read's date. A second "not yet" on the same rows is the training-infrastructure line at the leads' review (S5 12.6's trigger), read first as a question about the module, the mentor's load, and the paired count, and only after that as anything else, which is blame the process (WP p.17) applied where the record's own training paragraph says the industry fails. What a third "not yet" concludes is not this page's; the plan may extend once (section 7.6), and past that the question is Session 14's (section 13).

The lead reads the form and places the solo. The domain lead may not place a solo without a passed form, may not pass a person on their own read, and may not run the readiness read themselves, because the lead decides on the packet and the lead holding the person's check-in cannot also be the one who read them, for the same reason the assessor and the decider are separate at hiring (S5 P41). The Realist's condition on the solo: it is placed on a service the leads' review has not flagged, with the mentor in the building, and never as the only coverage for the section.

Pre-opening the readiness read runs in a training service and reads procedure without load, and the form says so, exactly as the cohort's practicals do (S5 P42). The first four dinner weeks are the load read (S6 P31), and a cohort member whose load lines in those weeks do not hold is a training and slack question, never a readiness failure, because the form said in writing that it did not read load.

**P23 (Recommended).** The first solo is gated on a readiness form scored in a paired service by a trained assessor who is not the mentor and did not run the paired services, on the practical's rows plus the language row, the range row, and the felt-knowledge row, with a recommendation of ready or not yet and the rows named; the form is a milestone on the person page and not a scorecard. The lead places the solo only on a passed form and never reads readiness themselves. Not yet is rows and one more paired service; a second not yet is a training-infrastructure line read on the process first.

### 6.6 Service-ready, defined once

The phrase appears in the session task and nowhere in the record, and this page uses it only in the sense defined here. A person is service-ready in a seat when their readiness form reads ready: the seat sheet's entry procedures reproduced in a paired service, the people rows held, the language constant held, the range and triggers stated unprompted, and the felt-knowledge block passed for the dishes that exist. Service-ready is per seat and per period; a person service-ready at dinner is not service-ready at the early-morning window until that period's plan (section 7.7) has run. Service-ready is the entry horizon of field 6 and nothing past it: not the first unlock, not cross-strand fluency, not nunchi, not "trained," in Crenn's sense that "it's not like, 'Now you're trained'" (Book p.216). The word the record uses is "ready," and this page's definition is the record's word with a form behind it.

**P24 (Recommended).** Service-ready means a readiness form reading ready in the seat, for the period, at the entry horizon of field 6, and nothing past it. It is the only sense in which the phrase is used in this operating system.
