## 16\. Decision rights for onboarding

Every entry is in the ledger's form: owner; range stated as may and may not; triggers, each naming a destination. An entry the record cannot furnish an owner for is marked incomplete and named as an open question, never filled by analogy (S3 4.1). Session 5's entry for committing a start date (S5 12.6) and Session 4's for the check-in (S4 P20) are cross-referenced, not repeated; the entries below are the ones onboarding adds.

### 16.1 Naming a mentor

Owner. The domain lead of the seat, at the offer; pre-opening, for the first wave, the founders under P8.

Range. The lead may name any person on the strand's pool in the domain who has said yes, matching for language and overlapping shifts. The lead may not name themselves; may not name the assessor who will run the readiness read; may not name a person not on the pool; may not name a person with an open plan already; may not name for temperament or for who would get along; may not name a person whose page carries a non-negotiable line.

Triggers. No eligible person on the pool goes to the leads' review as a training-infrastructure load and the start date is not set (S5 12.6). A mentor stepping back goes to the lead, who names another with no line on either page. A mentor found to have written on a person page or given a verdict goes to the Maitre d as a team-health entry and returns the mentor to the mentor module before mentoring again.

Complete for outward-facing floor seats and beverage; incomplete for runner and host seats until their domain lead is named (S5 P64; `86akh7r10`); kitchen seats chef-gated.

### 16.2 Placing the first solo

Owner. The domain lead of the seat.

Range. The lead may place the first solo on the schedule on the day the readiness form reads ready or any day after, on a service the leads' review has not flagged, with the mentor in the building, never as sole coverage for the section or station. The lead may not place a solo without a passed form; may not run the readiness read; may not pass a person on their own read; may not place a solo on a new period's first service or on dinner's first service (P10); may not place a solo as coverage for a short night.

Triggers. A solo placed without a form, which the scheduling surface should refuse and which row 79 checks, goes to the Operations Lead's record as a system failure and to the leads' review. A form reading not yet twice on the same rows goes to the leads' review as a training-infrastructure line. A first solo on a flagged service goes to the leads' review as a slack reading.

Complete for floor and beverage; kitchen chef-gated.

### 16.3 Running the readiness read

Owner. The assessor, a trained person from the seat's strand who is not the mentor and did not run the paired services; the Maitre d for the standard and the assessor pool; kitchen assessors the chef partner's.

Range. The assessor may score the seat's entry rows, the people rows, the language row, the range row, and the felt-knowledge row, in the block, and recommend ready or not yet with rows named. The assessor may not score presence, speed, nunchi, fit, or how the section felt; may not score from memory after the block; may not score a person they mentored; may not score load on a training-service read; may not pass a felt-knowledge row before the tastings; may not carry the form anywhere but the person page.

Triggers. A form with a composite, a verdict, or a refused row goes to the Maitre d and returns the assessor to the assessor module. A form on a person the assessor mentored is void and goes to the Operations Lead's record. A not-yet form goes to the person at the next check-in with its rows.

Complete for floor and beverage; kitchen chef-gated.

### 16.4 Authoring and approving a module

Owner. The author, any team member holding the validated competency the module teaches; the approver, the domain lead for the domain, the chef partner for the kitchen, the Operations Lead with counsel for compliance and food-safety content, and canon's owner for content carrying brand facts, the arrival line, the register, or the uniform.

Range. An author may write a module for a competency they hold and submit it for approval in the languages they hold, with the standard's fields complete. An author may not publish without approval; may not write a script beyond the house's one arrival line; may not gloss a Korean term; may not use a synthesized presenter before the canon ruling; may not record a customer. An approver may approve or refuse against the standard's items and may not refuse on taste; may not approve their own module; may not revise a live module except by versioned decision.

Triggers. A module the floor contradicts at a week-four check-in goes to the author through the feedback channel with the person's knowledge and to the approver for a version. A module found live without approval goes to the Operations Lead's record. A module refused twice on the same item goes to the Maitre d as a question about the standard's wording.

Incomplete on canon's owner for brand-carrying content until the concept's voice holder is named (`86akh2qq0`); Brandon's seat holds it until then, as the team's reading, and the entry says so.

### 16.5 Extending the ninety-day plan

Owner. The domain lead, with the person, at a check-in.

Range. The lead may extend once, to a stated date, for a building-caused block with the fix named. The lead may not extend for a person's not holding without a fix named; may not shorten; may not extend twice; may not label the extension or the plan a probation; may not extend outside a check-in.

Triggers. An extension goes to the leads' review as a training-infrastructure line. A second extension request goes to the partners' review as a node-overload or infrastructure entry. A plan ending with its goal not held after one extension goes to the destination Session 14 names, with the plan block, and until Session 14 names it the plan's record stays on the person page and the lead raises it at the leads' review as an open item.

Complete, with the destination past one extension held to Session 14.

### 16.6 Delivering the why block

Owner. A founder, pre-opening and through dinner's first quarter; after the mechanism reset, the holder of the concept's voice internally.

Range. The founder may deliver the block in the record's order, with the unratified parts stated as unratified, in the cohort's languages with an interpreter; the domain lead may deliver the structure part from the second quarter. No one may deliver the mission or the principles before ratification, substitute positioning for them, deliver the block by video or synthesized presenter, or add a signature or a quiz.

Triggers. A why block delivered by anyone but the owner goes to the partners' review. A cohort start date arriving before the charter is ratified goes to the partners' review as the gate item P12 names. The reset arriving with the voice holder unnamed goes to the partners' page as a load on the founder's seat.

Incomplete after the first quarter until `86akh2qq0` closes.

### 16.7 Opening a cross-domain track, and signing a cross-domain competency

Owner. The person, for opening any module on any track from the first day; the receiving domain's lead for scheduling a cross-domain practical assessment, as the team's reading; the signer of a cross-domain competency, held (finding 18.8; P40).

Range. A person may open and complete any module on any track at any time on shift. The receiving lead may schedule a cross-domain practical assessment only after the person's own plan has closed with its goal held; may not schedule one during the plan; may not read a person's own-domain readiness. The person's own lead may not block a track.

Triggers. A cross-domain assessment scheduled inside a plan goes to the leads' review. A sign-off disputed between two leads goes to the partners' review under S3's Class B rule until the signer is named.

Incomplete on the signer (18.8); kitchen chef-gated.

### 16.8 Writing on the person page during the plan

Owner. The stack, for the milestones it can see; the domain lead, at the check-in only (S4 P20).

Range. The stack may write milestones 1 to 5, 7 (the form's date and rows), 8, and 11 from the schedule, Trainual, and the form; the lead may write milestones 9, 10, 12, and 13 and the supplied lines at the check-in, read back. Neither may write a dimension mark, a rating, a verdict, or a probation state. The mentor and the assessor may not write; the assessor's form is written by the stack from the assessor's submission. No one may write between check-ins.

Triggers. A line written outside a check-in goes to the Maitre d as a team-health entry (S4 P20). A scorecard field found on any page goes to the Operations Lead's record and is removed (S6 row 71).

Complete.

### 16.9 Placing a module with a synthesized presenter

Owner. Canon's owner, for the ruling; the approver under 16.4, after it.

Range. Before the ruling, no one may publish one. After a permitting ruling, an approver may approve one for procedural narration only, with the disclosure line first, never for the why block or any content about the customer.

Triggers. A synthesized-presenter module found live before the ruling goes to the partners' review and is unpublished the same day.

Held on the canon ruling (finding 19.12).

### 16.10 Incomplete entries, named

The runner and host seats' domain lead (16.1, 16.2, 16.3): held on S5 P64 and `86akh7r10`. Kitchen seats, every entry: chef-gated on the chef ruling (S5 P57). Canon's owner for module content (16.4) and the why block after the first quarter (16.6): held on `86akh2qq0`. The signer of a cross-domain competency (16.7): held on finding 18.8 with Session 8, the founders, and the chef. The destination of a plan whose goal is not held after one extension (16.5): held to Session 14. The threshold value and known limits inside every server's range (section 12.1): set with Dominic's domain and not this page's, so every range card states them as unset. The synthesized presenter (16.9): held on canon's ruling. The floor manager and the Maitre d as one seat or two (`86akh5u9g`): every entry above that names the Maitre d for a floor seat is read against that question and is incomplete if the floor manager is a separate seat that holds the floor's check-ins.

**P55 (Recommended).** The onboarding decision-rights entries 16.1 to 16.9 as written, complete where marked complete: naming a mentor, placing the first solo, running the readiness read, authoring and approving a module, extending the plan, delivering the why block, opening a cross-domain track, writing on the person page during the plan, and placing a synthesized-presenter module.

**P56 (Founder-gated).** The incomplete entries: the runner and host seats' lead; every kitchen entry; canon's owner for module content and the why block after the first quarter; the cross-domain signer; the destination past one extension (Session 14); the threshold and limits in every range card; the synthesized presenter; and the floor manager question. None is filled by analogy.

## 18\. Instrument specifications

Specifications, never instruments. Nothing here is built, and no session builds any of it until the document methodology exists (`86ajgn2z5`). Each specification states what the instrument is, whether Sŏn uses it, what it must contain, what it must do, what it must refuse to do, where it lives and whether that is configuration, a build, or to confirm, who owns it and on what revision rhythm, and what it is gated on. Numbering is this page's own, I1 onward; earlier sessions' instruments are cited by session and number. The instruments come in the order a person meets them: what arrives, the plan block, the first shift, the range card, the modules and their standard, the mentor, the readiness form, the load read, the felt-knowledge block and the tasting record, the check-in reads, the onboarding read, the lead's plan and pre-reads, the lead's document, the period and domain plans, the infrastructure line. The instruments her material proposes that Sŏn refuses come last, each with what does its work.

**I1. The arrival note.** What it is: the message the stack sends a person on acceptance, carrying what arrives before the first shift (4.5). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the record's "information is delivered, expectations are set" (WP p.18) as one document. Must contain: the start date and the first shift's hours as a paid orientation block with no table or station; where to arrive and the first hour; the mentor's name and seat; the seat sheet, current version; the transparency sheet, current version; the range card (I4) marked as to be read together; the first two weeks' schedule with the check-in visible; a link to the seat's first modules, marked visible and not assigned; the person page; the languages the house speaks; the line that nothing in it is required before the first shift; and a line naming the non-negotiables as the standard until a handbook exists. Must do: be generated by the stack from the sheet and the person page on acceptance; go in the person's chosen language in the correspondence register; match the offer in every term; carry no house item hidden in a legal task. Must refuse: "welcome," "enjoy," "excited," an exclamation point, a founder's story, a line naming its own effect; a module assigned or due; a figure; canon's forbidden word for the customer; a promise about a service period without a ratified charter; any term not on the sheet. Where it lives: the team home, generated by the stack, a build; its trigger on acceptance in Greenhouse or Rippling, to confirm. Who owns it: the Maitre d for the standard; the Operations Lead for its legal lines; Brandon's seat reviews the copy against canon until the voice holder is named; revised with the sheet. Gated on: S6 I11 (the offer); S5 I15's register.

**I2. The plan block.** What it is: the ninety-day plan's form on the person page (7.2). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the record's plan with "clear milestones, skill assessments, and feedback" (WP p.18) given its form, and the "ninety-day plan while they are on one" Session 4 placed on the page (S4 P18). Must contain: one goal as a state with a binary measure; thirteen milestones as states with a date or "not yet" and the writer of each; the fourth-read baseline with one supplied line per check-in; the six check-in dates; for a lead, the domain's cadence rows as milestones and the goal as the domain running (P21). Must do: be written by the stack at acceptance from the seat sheet; be the same for every person in the seat except in dates, baseline, and lines; be readable by the person at any time on a phone in their language; be written by the stack for what it can see and by the lead only at the check-in, read back; tell the lead which read each check-in is; close at the sixth check-in with the goal's state; feed the onboarding read (I12); extend once under 16.5. Must refuse: a dimension mark, rating, verdict, or free-text assessment; a probation label or state; a milestone about nunchi, Jeong, presence, or fit; a wage or rate; a line written by a mentor or assessor; a line written outside a check-in; a scorecard field; a second ninety-day plan for a period or domain move (I15 instead). Where it lives: the person page on the team home, a build; pre-OS-surface on the interim backbone, to confirm against S4 P18's write rules. Who owns it: the Maitre d for the form; the domain lead per person; revised at the mechanism reset. Gated on: S4 P18; S5 P16; the document methodology.

**I3. The orientation block.** What it is: the first shift's content in order (6.2), including the why block (5.3). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is why before how (WP p.18) as a scheduled, paid block. Must contain: the building walked through the nine beats to the employee area and the locker; the uniform's aging rule; the why block in the record's order with the unratified slots stated as unratified; the stack on the person's own phone (accounts, schedule with the check-in, person page, the seat after theirs, the feedback channel); the range card read together and said back; the mentor met and the two weeks' schedules read together; the non-negotiables as what may be raised and where. Must do: be one paid block on the schedule with no table and no station; be delivered in person, the why block by a founder pre-opening and through the first quarter; run in the person's language with an interpreter where needed; be placed on a day with no service or before a service the person then observes, never inside a pre-service window a lead needs; record on the plan block who delivered it and the charter version. Must refuse: a video, a synthesized presenter, a poster, a quiz, an acknowledgement signature; positioning presented as mission; canon's forbidden word for the customer in any story, including quoted ones; a daypart code name; a figure; a table or station touched; a module assigned as homework afterward. Where it lives: the schedule as a block, configuration; its content as a document under the methodology, a build. Who owns it: a founder for the why block; the domain lead for the rest; revised when the charter is ratified and at the reset. Gated on: P16 (the charter); `86akh2qq0` after the first quarter.

**I4. The range card.** What it is: the seat sheet's field 10 rendered for one person, with the range first and the triggers after, each with its destination (12.1). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is how row 4 becomes an output. Must contain: what the holder decides without asking, in the record's and canon's own words for the seat; what the holder may not decide; each trigger with its named destination; for a server, the bottle, routine recovery inside known limits, and the three canon triggers with S3's destinations; the threshold and the known limits stated as unset where they are; the field 10 version; the person's own words saying it back, recorded at orientation. Must do: be read together at orientation; be re-read at the readiness read's range row and the fourth check-in; match field 10 exactly and change only when field 10 changes by versioned decision; exist in the seat's languages; name "escalate" as no destination. Must refuse: a number this program generated; a trigger without a destination; "manager"; a range taught as permission; under-use taught as safe. Where it lives: the person page beside the plan block, a build; generated from field 10 on the team home. Who owns it: the domain lead from the sheet; the Operations Lead for compliance triggers; revised with field 10. Gated on: S5 P12; S3 4.2's destinations; the threshold and limits (Dominic's domain).

**I5. The seat's first module set and the training path.** What it is: the modules a person completes before the readiness read, ordered as a path per seat on Trainual (8.2, 8.4). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the platform's first content. Must contain, per seat: the system modules (the stack's surfaces, the person page, the feedback channel, the range card's form), shared across seats; the seat's procedure modules for every field 6 entry row, each under I11; the language module (the constant, the lexicon, the arrival line as the house's one line); the range module with its two written examples; the service module for the period's register, from canon; the felt-knowledge block (I9) as the last module, held until the tastings; the mentor and assessor modules as separate paths; the interviewer modules (S6 I5) as paths once the platform exists. Must do: exist in every field 14 language before the seat's first start date; be completable on shift in the check-in's unit of time per module; record completion per module per person and copy it to the plan block; be revised by versioned decision on the week-four line; show the version each person completed; be visible before the start date and assigned only after the first shift. Must refuse: any module that fails I11; a module on the first unlock, cross-training, or another period in the first set; a module assigned before the first paid hour; a due date; a completion recorded by a lead from memory. Where it lives: Trainual, configuration for the paths, with four items to confirm (8.2); the content as documents under the methodology, a build; the completion copy to the person page, a build. Who owns it: the domain lead per seat; the founders for the system modules; the chef partner for the kitchen; pre-opening the authors under P34; revised at the reset and on the week-four line. Gated on: the document methodology; P9; the chef ruling for the kitchen; the Trainual items to confirm.

**I6. The mentor module and the mentor pool.** What it is: the module a person completes before mentoring, and the list per strand per domain of eligible mentors (11.2). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is the record's "proven cultural steward" (WP p.18) given a test. Must contain, the module: the mentor's carrying list and refusal list (11.3) with the refusals first; the live session's form; how to be a teaching body on a paired service; the feedback channel's use; what to do with a question about pay, a grievance, or a non-negotiable (route, never answer); the rule that the mentor never writes and never gives a verdict. The pool: per strand per domain, each person's eligibility conditions with dates (plan closed with goal held or pre-opening ready form; no non-negotiable line; module complete; seat or strand in domain; yes), current open plans mentored, languages, and the provisional mark pre-opening. Must do: be readable by the domain leads and the Maitre d, with each person's own entry on their own page; refuse a name to a lead outside the pool; record when a mentor steps back with no line on any page; be read by the stack when the lead names at the offer. Must refuse: a ranking; a temperament field; a "strongest performer" field; a mentor with two open plans; a mentor who is the assessor; a lead as their own domain's mentor after the first wave; a mentor's note on any person page. Who owns it: the Maitre d; the chef partner for the kitchen's pool; revised at the reset. Gated on: S5 I24's form; P8 for the first wave; the document methodology.

**I7. The readiness form.** What it is: the assessor's form for the first solo (6.5), filling Session 6's practical rows (S6 I4) for a person in the seat rather than a candidate. The training-infrastructure line.** What it is: the standing item at the leads' review carrying every extension, every second not-yet form, every load line that did not hold, every missing mentor, and every start date that could not be set for a training reason (S5 12.6's trigger, given a form). Whether Sŏn uses it: yes; it is blame the process with a place to go. Must contain, per line: the person's plan, by plan and not by verdict; the link that did not hold; the fix named, as a module, a mentor load, a paired count, a schedule, a supply, or a sequence item; the owner of the fix and its date. Who owns it: the Maitre d; revised at the reset. Gated on: S4 P22's agenda; S5 12.6.

**I17** is the tasting record, specified with I9.

The instruments her material proposes that Sŏn refuses, each with what does its work. Specified as refusals so that a downstream cluster does not build them by habit.

What does the job: the orientation block (I3) for the why and the stack, and the seat's path (I5) on shift for the rest. Gated on: nothing; refused.

What does the job: the seat sheet, the range card, and the person page, which existed before the person did (7.1). Gated on: nothing; refused.

Whether Sŏn uses it: no; it reads a person for a seat (S5 P8's reasoning). What does the job: the lead's working-with-me document as self-awareness (I14; S1 8.5). Gated on: nothing; refused.

**I24. The coach.** What it is: "access to a coach for six months" (Book p.258). Whether Sŏn uses it: no, as the team recommends, and founder-gated as a spend (P22). What does the job: the partner's check-in on the lead's plan (P21). Gated on: P22.

What does the job: the upward question at every check-in the lead holds, read at the leads' review as a load reading on the lead when it stretches (S4 P19), and the employee NPS (WP p.22). The welcome emails, the onboarding point person, and the new leader checklist.** What it is: the recruiter's and manager's welcome emails, the point person "(could be admin support)," and the checklist they populate (Book p.258 to 259). The onboarding pulse prompts and the manager milestone survey.** What it is: "New people on my team are being onboarded quickly and effectively" and its siblings (Book p.226), and "a quick performance survey to managers at certain milestones" (Book p.226). **P58 (Recommended).** The seventeen instrument specifications I1 to I17 as stated, each carrying what it must contain, do, and refuse, where it lives and whether that is configuration, a build, or to confirm, who owns it and on what rhythm, and what it is gated on. None is built here; all are gated on the document methodology (`86ajgn2z5`). * * *

## 19\. Findings inside Sŏn's record

Twelve findings, each a conflict, a silence, or two accounts of the same thing, found by reading the white paper and both canon artifacts against each other and against the bought stack with her onboarding section as the question. Each is written as what the record says in one place, what it says elsewhere or fails to say, why it bears on onboarding, and who closes it. Sessions 5 and 6's findings and the ledger's open questions are not counted again; where one touches a finding below it is named as adjacent. None is resolved here. Where a section above supplied a working answer, the finding says which position holds it and marks it as the team's reading.

**19.1 Anyone qualified may author a module, and the record names no approver and no test.** In one place: "Any qualified team member can create training modules and get paid for teaching everyone else. The more modules completed, the more earned" (WP p.19). Elsewhere: canon governs every word on every surface, Mahk forbids "service delivered by script rather than felt knowledge" (Canon v1.0, section 01), Ma forbids "Filling a surface because it reads unfinished" (Canon v3.0, p.10), and the record itself says the platform is "constantly expanding" (WP p.19) with no word on who says a module may join it or what "qualified" means. A payment for volume and a prohibition on filling sit one page apart with nothing between them. Why it bears on onboarding: the first modules a new person reads are the house's voice, and an unapproved module is a script by another route. Who closes: the founders on the standard (P33, I11, the team's reading), Session 13 on the payment's shape (P35). Silence.

**19.2 The mentor is "proven," and the record's first cohort has no one who has proven anything; and mentoring is teaching, which the record pays, and the mentor's pay is unstated.** In one place: "a proven cultural steward rather than simply the strongest performer" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: the house opens with a cohort hired from outside (S5 11.2), teaching is paid (WP p.19), and the mentor "answers questions" (WP p.18) with no word on their hours, their pay, or their limits. Why it bears on onboarding: the first mentors cannot be proven and the record's sentence excludes the industry's substitute; and a mentor who is unpaid is a favor and a favor is the first thing a Friday deletes. Who closes: the founders on the first wave (P8), Session 13 on recognition beyond shift (P35). Two accounts, and a silence.

**19.3 No one touches a table until ready, and the paid practical puts a candidate on a table in a real environment.** In one place: "competency validation: no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19). Elsewhere: "For roles with a physical skill component, the second interview is a paid practical in a real environment" (WP p.18), which is a person who has not been validated working a section in service. Session 5 reconciled it by rule, the candidate never alone on a station or the only person a table has and never serving a customer who is told (S5 P41), and this page's paired step inherits the rule. Why it bears on onboarding: the same sentence gates the first solo, and the record does not say whether "touches a table" means alone or at all; this page reads it as alone, with a person beside them until the readiness form (P23). Who closes: the founders, ratifying S5 P41 and P23 together as one reading. Two accounts.

**19.4 The two canon versions carry two different uniform tables, and onboarding fits a uniform.** In one place: five roles, floor manager in "Business suiting, Korean fashion sensibility," hosts in "Blazer + button-up shirt," servers in "Fluid structured jacket + structured shirt + wide-leg pant + chunky loafer," bar in "Elevated button-up shirt," daytime in "Chore coat + cargo pant + tee + hat + designated shoe" (Canon v1.0, section 08). Elsewhere: five roles, Maître d' in a "Tailored jacket," server in a "Structured overshirt, apron," floor manager in a "Full jacket," bartender "Fitted, sleeve rolled," runner in a "Quiet layer, no logo" (Canon v3.0, p.81). The roles differ (hosts and daytime in one; Maître d' and runner in the other), the garments differ for the same role, and the version rule says a living document changes "by versioned decision, never by drift" (Canon v3.0, p.94) without saying which version's table stands. Why it bears on onboarding: the uniform is fitted before the start date (P14) and taught on the first shift (P19), and the fitting cannot know which garment. Who closes: canon's owner, with the founders. Adjacent to S6 18.9 for the host role. Contradiction.

**19.5 The training plan carries "pay dates," and the record does not say what training pay is.** In one place: the transparency sheet carries "the training plan with pay dates" (WP p.18). Elsewhere: compensation is "a point system weighted by the days each person works," "calculated daily" (WP p.20), and the record never says whether a person on a paired service, a module, or an orientation block earns as a seat holder does, as a trainee does, or on some other rule; and "no one touches a table until they are actually ready" (WP p.19) means the first weeks are weeks the person does not hold a section that fills the room. Why it bears on onboarding: item 5 is handed at the first interview, item 6 gates the offer, and this page's sequence is weeks of paid time whose pay rule is unstated. Who closes: Session 13, with the founders. Financials are not a context source and this page states no rule. Silence.

**19.6 Korean terminology stands without explanation in all brand contexts, and a training module explains.** In one place: "Korean terminology stands without explanation in all brand contexts from day one. No parenthetical translations, no footnotes, no italicized definitions" (Canon v1.0, section 04; Canon v3.0, p.45). Elsewhere: the record promises training in the candidate's chosen language (WP p.17; S6 P23), and a module that teaches a new server what nunchi asks of them on the floor is, on its face, an explanation of a Korean term to a person who may not hold Korean. The rule says "all brand contexts" and does not say whether a training module is one. Why it bears on onboarding: every module that touches the service philosophy either explains a term or does not, and the standard (I11) holds the gloss prohibition while marking it. Who closes: canon's owner, under the deferred Korean Terminology Deployment Rules (Canon v1.0, What Remains), with the candidate-facing question the ledger already carries (`86akh7r2t`). Adjacent. Silence.

**19.7 Feedback runs both directions, and no one holds a lead's check-in.** In one place: "Team members weigh in on management effectiveness, operational improvements, and culture" (WP p.19), and the ninety-day plan has "regular check-ins" (WP p.18) for every new person. Elsewhere: the check-in is between a person and the lead of their domain (S4 P15), the two leads are parallel and "Neither reports to the other" (WP p.10), and the record names no one who holds a check-in for a lead; Session 4's bandwidth ledger gives each lead "one conversation with a partner" per month (S4 P63) without calling it a check-in. Why it bears on onboarding: a lead on a ninety-day plan has six check-ins to be held by someone, and the record does not say by whom. Who closes: the founders; P21's reading (a partner under S3's Class C rule) is the team's. Silence.

**19.8 The why is delivered before the how, and the record names no one who delivers it.** In one place: "Orientation to the mission, the values, and the behavioral standard happens before operational training" (WP p.18). # Session 8: Chapter 4, Team structures

Book pp. 261 to 281 (the Chapter 4 introduction and Team structures). Workbook Chapter 4 holds nothing on team structures; the unblocking process (Workbook pp. 98 to 102) is answered in section 17 and routed to Session 11. Session task `86ajgmhxx`. Profiles at the table: the Organizational Systems Architect (owner) and the Hospitality Operations Realist. Her chapter is written for a company whose structure changes as headcount rises: solid and dotted lines, functional and business-unit and hybrid charts, a hinge team, business leads, spans of control, and new layers of authority introduced under a leader. Sŏn is one house at one address whose record says the web "never acquires altitude, only reach" (WP p.9), that new people "always enter at the outside edge" (WP p.9), that "nothing is assigned, reviewed, or escalated by a person standing above another person" (ledger, S3 3.4), and that roughly eight leadership lines run the whole day (WP p.22). Most of her mechanisms are refused for their form and absorbed for their discipline. The page is written so that a person who has not read the book knows what the structure is, who holds what, what each seat may and may not do, and what the structure refuses to become.

One founder ruling governs this session and is recorded in section 2. It is Brandon's, not the team's, and it is designed from, not re-argued.

## 1\. Her ask against the record, and how much is decided

### 1.1 What she asks

Start from strategy and arrange teams to serve it; decide how much solid-line and dotted-line leverage to give a strong leader; keep the structure flexible and reexamine it at least yearly; distinguish teams (persistent mission, at least a year) from projects (weeks or months, a subgroup) and working groups (under three months, cross-functional, a directly responsible individual, a spin-down); use a Code Yellow for one-off existential threats; choose functional or business-line structure and orient teams vertically or horizontally; place a hinge where the focus turns from product to customer; run business leads with dual reporting, ring-fenced headcount, forums, goal setting, and calibration; watch the number of direct reports and introduce a layer when it grows; and communicate a structure change person by person with a narrative first (Book pp. 262 to 281).

### 1.2 What the record already holds

The record holds more of the structure than her chapter would suggest, scattered across Part I, Part II, Part V, and both canon artifacts. It holds the model: a web with a center and an outside edge, neither superior, growth outward not upward (WP p.9). It holds the management layer: two parallel co-leads, the Operations Lead owning the strategic what and the Maitre d owning the coordinative how, "co-leads of different systems serving the same center" (WP p.10). It holds the level below the leads as functional designations that "mark accountability in the moment, in the domain" and "are not permanent elevations above anyone" (WP p.10). It holds strands, not levels: an outward-facing strand whose output is the experience at the table and an inward-facing strand whose output is the operational sequence, "different jobs requiring different types of intelligence" (WP p.10 to 11). It holds the kitchen's shape in outline: Station Leads as domain owners, Chef on the line and Chef on prep as domain execution "neither a promotion from the other," and the Steward as "the tension that holds the kitchen sequence together" (WP p.11). It holds beverage: the Head of Beverage owns the program and its execution maps to the same two strands (WP p.11). It holds progression as connections rather than altitude (WP p.11), the invisible advocate (WP p.11), and the failure-mode reference whose second entry, node overload, is the test this page runs on the ruling (WP p.14). It holds the leadership delta as a claim: eight lines across the day against fourteen around one dinner service, and a kitchen of two title tiers (WP p.22). It holds the brand architecture's service periods: dinner the heart, late night dinner's own later register, the early morning the lowest-friction door, lunch and brunch held in reserve (WP p.35 to 36). And it holds the open items that bind structure: role naming, the compensation architecture for cross-strand fluency, and the web rendered as a designed artifact (WP p.15).

Canon holds the floor's authority: "server owns the table," "Floor manager owns the room, coverage, pattern recognition, backs up without intercepting," with routine recovery pre-authorized and three escalation triggers (Canon 1.0, section 08; Deck 3.0, p.79). It holds the threshold: the Maître d' "at the top of the porch steps before the customer crosses" (Canon 1.0, section 06; Deck 3.0, p.68), the host stand removed (Canon 1.0, section 08). It holds two uniform role lists that do not match (Canon 1.0, section 08; Deck 3.0, p.81). It holds the service periods as four (Canon 1.0, sections 01 and 02; Deck 3.0, p.6), which the white paper states as three with lunch removable, an open disagreement (`86akh5ubn`).

Sessions 1 to 7 hold, and this page does not re-open: the departure from her hierarchy (S3 3.4); the four goal-bearing units, company, service period, domain, and person (S3 P3.2); the decision-rights rule in owner, range, triggers form (S3 4.1); the daypart charter with nine fields as the form no period opens without (S2 11, S4 P66); the period count as a parameter (S3 13.2, S4 P52); gates, not dates (S4 P47); the seat sheet as the single account of a seat (S5 4.2); the domain lead as the node with the most connections to a seat and not a manager above it (S5 P33); no hiring committee and no runner (S5 8.6, S6 P9); the invisible advocate's clock on the sheet (S5 P60); the mentor pool and the assessor (S7 P41, P23); the lead's plan with the domain running on the cadence as its goal (S7 P21); and stability as a property of the system (ledger).

### 1.3 The gap

What the record does not hold, and this page supplies: what "team" means at Sŏn and whether the service periods are one team or several (section 3); the structure drawn in one place rather than scattered (section 4); the leadership-line list and the variety pass the ledger has held since Session 3 (section 5); who holds a service period (section 7); the inward-facing floor strand's lead, the runner, the host, and whether the Lead Host is a seat (section 8); the seat inventory's structure and the three seat lists reconciled (section 9); levels, ladders, what a lead enters at, and which seats are salaried structurally (section 10); cross-strand fluency defined so it can be demonstrated, and cross-period fluency placed (section 11); the advancement gate's two accounts and the cross-domain signer (section 12); work style demand by period, answered without the grid (section 13); temporary structures and Code Yellows (section 14); spans, layering, and the structure at each gate (section 15); the kitchen's structure marked and its packet list (section 16); how a structure change is made and reaches the team (section 17); and the decision-rights entries for structure (section 18).

**P1 (Recommended).** Her team structures chapter is answered from the record's web and the two-lead management layer, which Sessions 1 to 7 hold as decided. ## 2\. The founder ruling on the Maitre d

### 2.1 The ruling, recorded

On 2026-09-13, in the Session 8 chat, on founder decision `86akh5u9g` (carryovers `86akh5utd` and `86akh2r3e`), Brandon ruled that the floor manager and the Maitre d are the same position. In his words, lightly cleaned: instead of a floor or service manager and a Maitre d, the Maitre d role is reverted to its origins as the master of the house, holding both roles, rather than saturating the floor team with two managers or leaders. Its source in the record is the white paper's management layer: the Maitre d "is not a floor role locked to the host stand with a French title. It is a consolidated role that combines what most operations split between a service director and a maitre d manager, two positions with so much inherent crossover that splitting them is the structural error. The Maitre d at Sŏn is freed from the host stand entirely to hold the floor and the team" (WP p.10). The ruling is Brandon's. It is not a team recommendation, it is not marked, and it is not re-argued on this page.

One note on spelling. The program has written "Maitre d" since Session 1, following the white paper. Canon writes "Maître d'" (Canon 1.0, sections 06 and 08; Deck 3.0, pp. 68 and 81). Canon's form governs any surface a customer or a candidate reads. This page uses the program's form for the seat and canon's when quoting canon.

### 2.2 What the ruling closes

There is one seat that owns the room and the floor team: the Maitre d. There is no floor manager seat and no service manager seat, now or at any gate. "The owner of the room," which every earlier decision-rights entry carried as an incomplete owner, names a seat. That closes `86akh5utd` (one role or two), `86akh2r3e` (the naming difference between the record's halves, closed for the operating system and routed to canon for canon's own wording), and the owner half of `86akh5u94` for the room's transitions and for emergency authority during a service. It closes the hold on hosts' domain lead in S5 P64, because the reading S5 marked held, hosts as the Maitre d's domain, no longer waits on a floor manager who might hold them instead. It closes the reading in S7 16.10 that every onboarding entry naming the Maitre d for a floor seat was incomplete if a floor manager held the floor's check-ins: the Maitre d holds them.

What the ruling does not close, and this page works: the domain lead for the inward-facing floor strand and for runners (section 8); whether the Lead Host seat exists (section 8); the three seat lists (section 9); and the seat's load (section 2.5).

### 2.3 The entries the ruling completes

Each entry is restated in owner, range, triggers form. Where the record states the range and the triggers, the entry is complete. Where it does not, the owner is complete and the entry stays incomplete for its missing part, named. Section 18 carries the full register for structure; the four entries the ruling touches are here.

**The server's escalation destination (S3 4.2, instance 3).** _Owner:_ the server for the table; the Maitre d for the room. _Range:_ the server calls attunement, approach timing, and the spoken note or silence, and executes routine recovery inside known limits (Canon 1.0, section 08); the Maitre d holds coverage and pattern recognition and backs up without intercepting, which means the Maitre d does not take a table from a server inside the server's range (Canon 1.0, section 08). _Triggers:_ financial recovery above threshold, from the server to the Maitre d; kitchen failure affecting multiple sections, from the Maitre d to the Chef Partner as the kitchen's owner of execution during service (WP p.10), with the Operations Lead informed; genuine emergency, to the Maitre d as the room's emergency authority (this section, below). _Status:_ complete on owner, range, and trigger destinations. Incomplete on the threshold's value and the known limits, which are set with Dominic's domain and are not a context source for this program (S3 4.2; ledger).

**The transition trigger (S3 4.2, instance 2; S4 14.1).** _Owner:_ the Maitre d, as the owner of the room for the service, and where the Maitre d is not in the building for a service, the person named at that service's brief as holding the room (section 2.5). _Range:_ the owner triggers the pre-service scene, "person-triggered, not clock-automated" (Canon 1.0, section 06), and the dinner-to-late-night transition, "same trigger as lighting and sonic, same person, same moment. Not announced. Register loosens. Last turn table held, transition moves toward them. Nothing cleared prematurely" (Canon 1.0, section 08); the transition is "table-state dependent, not clock-dependent" (Canon 1.0, section 08). The owner may not trigger by clock, may not announce it, may not clear the last turn table ahead of it, and may not delegate the trigger to the stack. _Triggers:_ a transition that did not follow the table state is captured at the shift close and read at the leads' review; a scene that fails to run when triggered goes to the Operations Lead as a stack failure. _Status:_ complete on owner and range. The record names no trigger destinations for the transition itself; the two above are the team's and the entry says so. Incomplete on the record's side for triggers.

**Emergency authority during a service (S3 4.3, Class D).** _Owner:_ the Maitre d for the room; the Chef Partner for the kitchen; each may close their side of the building without asking. Closing the building for a service period is the Operations Lead's call with the Maitre d consulted; closing for longer than one service period is a founder decision. _Range:_ the record holds "genuine emergency" as a trigger (Canon 1.0, section 08) and no range. The range stated here is Session 3's Class D recommendation, now with its owner named: the Maitre d may stop service, stop seating, evacuate the room, and call outside help without asking anyone; may not close the building for a following service; may not decide the kitchen's side. _Triggers:_ a safety event, a weather event on the patio, a stack outage the floor cannot run through, a kitchen failure the Chef Partner calls, each to the Maitre d for the room's response; any closure to the Operations Lead the same day and to the partners' page. _Status:_ complete on owner. Range and trigger list are the team's (S3 P4.4, extended here), not the record's, and the entry stays marked accordingly until ratified.

**The live cross-domain call (S4 P61).** _Owner:_ the Maitre d for the room's side of any live failure that spans both domains mid-service, with the Chef Partner owning the kitchen's side. _Range and triggers:_ absent from the record. Section 18.8 supplies a recommended range and triggers as the structural half Session 4 routed here, and the entry stays incomplete until ratified.

**P2 (Recommended).** The four entries above as restated: the server's escalation destination complete except for the threshold's value; the transition trigger complete on owner and range with the team's two trigger destinations; emergency authority complete on owner with the team's range and triggers; the live cross-domain call complete on owner with its range and triggers in section 18.8. None is filled by analogy, and each states which part is the record's and which is the team's.

### 2.4 The canon change, routed

The ruling does not reconcile canon. Canon, Version 1.0, gives the room to "the floor manager" (section 08), lists "Floor manager" and "Hosts" among five uniform roles with no Maitre d (section 08), and places the Maître d' at the top of the porch steps (section 06). Canon, Version 3.0, lists Maître d' and Floor manager as two distinct uniform roles, the first who "sets the register at the steps," the second who "reads as the owner of the room" (Deck 3.0, p.81), and names the floor manager as the room's owner in the service model (Deck 3.0, p.79). Canon also assigns sonic governance to "management sign-off" at tier 2 and "floor management" at tier 3 (Canon 1.0, section 07; Deck 3.0, p.75). Canon still says what it says until its owner versions it. The change canon needs, stated once for the reconciliation item: one floor seat, named the Maître d' in canon's form, holds the room, the threshold register, and the sonic tier that "floor management" held; the "floor manager" role leaves both uniform tables and the service model's floor-authority paragraph; and the two sonic tiers that assumed two management strata on the floor are re-read against a floor with one (finding 21.2). Routed to `86akh3tjb` as an extension, alongside the uniform-table reconciliation Session 7 filed (`86akhb2jj`).

**P3 (Recommended).** The canon change is routed to the reconciliation item `86akh3tjb` as stated and is not written here. Until canon is versioned, this page cites canon's floor manager as canon's word for the seat the ruling names, and every surface a customer or candidate reads uses canon's form.

### 2.5 The seat's load, tested

The ledger binds every session to "stability is a property of the system": a lead who produces stability by hand is a node-overload failure, and the fix is to restore the system, not to praise the lead. The record's own failure-mode reference names node overload as "one domain owner is absorbing load that belongs to adjacent domains, usually a manager doing too much operational work because the parallel structure has blurred" (WP p.14). The ruling puts in one seat what three accounts in the record spread across up to two: the white paper's Maitre d (service culture and the emotional standard of the room; team development, training, and the invisible advocate function; customer relationship systems and recovery standards; accountable to experience quality and team health, WP p.10), canon's floor manager (the room: coverage, pattern recognition, backing up without intercepting, the server's escalation destination, the tableside spirit, Canon 1.0, section 08; WP p.26), and the deck's Maître d' (the register at the steps, Deck 3.0, p.81). To that the earlier sessions had already attached: the floor's check-in rotation, which Session 4 named as the one cost on its page that can exceed its budget (S4 P63); the candidate-experience standard (S5 8.6); the mentor pool and the assessor pool's standard (S7 P41, 16.3); the module standard (S7 I11); the David flag as its recommended owner (S3 4.2, instance 4); and, now, the transition trigger, emergency authority for the room, and the room's side of the live cross-domain call. This section tests the load and does not reverse the ruling.

**What the seat holds across the service periods that hold charters.** A leadership line at Sŏn is a domain, and the record says the eight lines run "the full span of the day" (WP p.22) without saying how a seat spans hours its holder does not staff (finding 21.4). The answer the record itself supplies is one level down: "functional designations describe who owns what on a given night" (WP p.10). So the Maitre d's seat holds the floor domain across every open period, and the room at any given hour is held by the seat's holder when present and by a per-service designation when not. Under dinner alone, the Maitre d holds the room on every dinner service the Maitre d works; on the Maitre d's days off, the room is held by a named person from the floor's seats, named at that service's brief, and the readiness test (row 95) reads whether that name was given. When the early morning opens by ratified charter, the morning's room is the window and the patio (WP p.33; Canon 1.0, section 06), and it is held by the morning's designation from the morning's seats; the Maitre d's seat still owns the domain, holds the morning seats' check-ins and opens their seats, and does not stand at the window at seven and on the floor at seven. When late night opens, it is dinner's own later register in the same room (WP p.35), and the person who held the room through dinner holds it to close; the transition trigger passes only if the brief named a different holder for late night. The seat's shift shape is field 11 of its sheet, and that field, not the seat's title, is what says which services the holder works.

**What the stack and the structure carry so the seat is not the integration layer.** The stack posts the schedule, surfaces preferences at the brief, captures incidents at the close, places the check-ins when their interval elapses, holds the David flags, and runs the pre-service scene (WP p.21; S3 row 15; S4 P15). The structure carries the rest: the server's range absorbs every table-level disturbance inside known limits before it reaches the seat (Canon 1.0, section 08); the door designation holds the threshold so the seat is not walking every table (section 8); the sequence designation on the inward-facing strand holds the floor's side of the pass so a kitchen failure is first felt and first answered by the strand built for timing (section 8); the Head of Beverage holds the bar seats' check-ins and opens the bar seats (section 4); the mentor carries the first weeks' questions so they do not arrive at the seat (S7 P42); the assessor pool scores every readiness read so the seat scores none (S7 P23); the invisible advocate unlocks and schedules so the seat never holds advancement (WP p.11); and the leads' review with its interface read carries every cross-period question off the floor and onto a record (S4 P22). Every one of those is a mechanism the earlier sessions specified, and the readiness test already reads whether each is running rather than being done by hand (rows 8, 9, 13, 15, 30, 77, 80).

**What the requisite-variety pass shows.** Section 5 runs the pass in full. Its result for this seat: four of the eight disturbance classes converge on the floor domain, customer-side, floor-side, people-side, and transitions, and under the ruling all four have the Maitre d's seat as their lead-level regulator. Three of them have a regulator beneath the seat only if the designations in section 8 exist: the door for arrival disturbances, the sequence for pass-side timing, and the room designation for the seat's absent hours. One, people-side, has the check-in load, which grows with the count of floor seats and has no regulator beneath the seat at all; the count is a gap, and the reading is that the floor's check-in load is the first thing to read at the mechanism reset, per S4 P63.

**The load findings for Brandon, stated plainly.** Three, none of which is a recommendation to reinstate a second seat.

1. _The room is unheld during the Maitre d's absent hours unless a designation names who holds it._ Canon's floor authority paragraph assumes the room has an owner on every service. A seat cannot be in the building for every service of every open period. What carries it: a room designation named at every brief, defaulting to the Maitre d, otherwise a named person from the floor's seats who holds coverage, pattern recognition, the transition trigger, and emergency authority for that service, and nothing else the seat holds. Section 8 specifies it; section 18.10 writes its entry.
2. _The Maitre d at the threshold is a room with no one reading it._ Canon has the Maître d' at the top of the steps before the customer crosses and seating every table (Canon 1.0, sections 06 and 08). The Realist's read: a walk below street pace for every table, from the porch to the seat and back, is the room's owner off the floor for the length of every arrival. What carries it: the record's own Lead Host designation, "the door and the host-stand function" (WP p.10), carried by a host seat, so that the threshold register canon wants is set by whoever holds the door that service and the Maitre d holds it personally only when free to. This reads canon's threshold sentence as a register, not a fixed post, and that reading is routed to canon's owner with the change in 2.4 (finding 21.1).
3. _A kitchen failure affecting multiple sections reaches the seat with nothing between the pass and the room._ The trigger names the Maitre d as the floor's owner who escalates to the Chef Partner; the first place the failure is felt is the floor side of the pass, on the inward-facing strand, which has no designation and no lead in the record. What carries it: the sequence designation on the inward-facing strand (section 8), named at the brief, holding the floor's side of the pass and calling the floor's re-sequencing before the disturbance is a room problem.

A fourth is a stack finding rather than a seat finding and is stated in section 5: a stack outage mid-service has no regulator in the record, and without a degraded-mode procedure it lands on the Maitre d's memory, which is the ledger's exact definition of node overload.

**P4 (Recommended).** The Maitre d's seat holds the floor domain across every period that holds a charter, and the room at any hour is held by the seat's holder when present and by a per-service room designation named at the brief when not. The stack and the structure carry the integration work as listed, and the readiness test reads whether they do. The three load findings are carried by designations named at the brief, the room, the door, and the sequence, and by no second seat.

**P5 (Founder-gated).** The reading of canon's threshold sentence as a register set by whoever holds the door that service, with the Maitre d at the steps when free to be, rather than a fixed post. Brandon, with canon's owner, in the reconciliation item. Until ruled, the door designation holds the threshold on every service and the Maitre d holds it when present.

## 3\. What "team" means at Sŏn, and whether the service periods are one team or several

### 3.1 Her definitions

A team is "a group with a shared long-term mission," lasting "at least one year," working "on a collection of persistent jobs to be done," with lasting structures, norms, and culture invested in it. A project is "a subgroup with a shorter-term goal" inside a team. A working group is "a group with a short-term mission, usually comprised of individuals from multiple teams and functions," "a collection of individuals, not a team," with a directly responsible individual and a spin-down (Book pp. 265 to 268, Table 6). Her introduction adds the distinction that matters: most of what people call teams "are actually just groups of individuals parallel processing their way through work," and the milestone is when people "work as an integrated entity rather than as a set of individuals operating alone" (Book p.262).

### 3.2 What Sŏn holds, and the one sense the word carries

Session 3 settled the goal-bearing units: the company, the service period, the domain, and the person, which "intersect rather than nest," with her division and team units "not used" (S3 P3.2). Session 2 refused her team charter at the team unit because "domain ownership and the founding seat descriptions do that work at eight leadership lines" (S2 P11.1). What neither session did is say what the word "team" means when the record uses it, and the record uses it constantly: "the team," "team development," "team health," "the culinary team," "the whole team" (WP pp. 10, 20). Sessions 9 to 11 inherit whatever this page says.

The team's position is that Sŏn has exactly one team in her sense, and it is the whole house. It has a shared long-term mission (the charter's, when ratified), a collection of persistent jobs that are never complete, and lasting structures invested in it, which is this operating system. Her integrated-entity test is the record's description of a great night: "distributed intelligence rather than coordinated direction," "every element in relationship with every other, information moving laterally without routing through a chain of command" (WP p.8). That is one integrated entity, not several, and it is what the web is a drawing of.

Nothing smaller than the house is a team in her sense. A domain is not a team: it is a set of seats with one owner, and its "structure" is the seat inventory's rows and the domain lead's functions (S5 P33), not norms and a culture of its own. A strand is not a team: it is an intelligence and a primary output (WP p.10 to 11). A service period is not a team, for three reasons this page states and section 3.3 tests: it has no people of its own, because one labor pool staffs the periods (S5 P10) and a person's periods are a field on their sheet; it has no lead of its own, because a period adds no leadership line (section 3.4); and its goals are "one set across both strands and the kitchen" (S3 P7.1), which is her own rule against organizing goals by function, with the unit translated.

So when her Chapter 4 says "team" and the later sessions must translate it, there are three readings, and each sentence of hers takes one: when she means the collective that achieves more as a unit than alone, the word is the house; when she means a manager's reports, the people one person develops and holds check-ins with, the word is the domain, and the "manager" is the domain lead in Session 5's sense; and when she means who is on tonight, the word is the service roster, the people the brief named for that service across every domain, which exists for one service and dissolves at the close. The record's "the floor team" and "the culinary team" are domains. The record's "the team" is the house.

**P6 (Recommended).** Sŏn has one team in her sense, the house. A domain, a strand, and a service period are not teams. Her word is translated three ways for Sessions 9 to 11: the house for the collective, the domain for a manager's reports, and the service roster for who is on tonight. The record's "floor team" and "culinary team" are read as domains.

### 3.3 One team or several, answered for any ratified set, with the interfaces as the test

Carryover `86ajgmmc3` asks whether the service periods are several teams or shifts of one, and says everything about scheduling, cross-training, and identity follows from it. The task note's thesis is that periods compound rather than reset. The record says the same in three places: "one restaurant and one brand, one brand texture, met at different times of day" (WP p.33); a bolted-on period "becomes a worse version of dinner no matter who bolts it on, because the restaurant underneath was built to do one thing at one hour" (WP p.2); and canon's "No daypart is a reset, each is a continuation" (Canon 1.0, section 02).

The answer, stated for any ratified set and not for four: the service periods are one team met at different hours, and the structure makes that true by construction rather than by assertion. A period is a period of one restaurant, and not a second restaurant at the same address, exactly when its daypart charter's dependent interfaces field is not empty and its provided interface is consumed by another period or by the connective layer. The ledger already binds this: "A period whose dependent interfaces are empty is a separate restaurant, not a period of one" (S4 P66). This page adds the structural consequence. A period that passed that test shares the labor pool, the kitchen, the customer record, the leadership lines, the inventory, and the readiness test with every other period; it adds seats, a designation set, a register block, and a period plan; it adds no lead, no line, and no second web.

Drawn for dinner first. Under dinner alone there is one period and the test has nothing to compare it against; dinner's dependent interfaces are the connective layer and the kitchen, and its provided interface is what it hands to the layer (the customer record, the servers' books, the cohort's fluency). When the early morning is drafted in dinner's first quarter (S4 P49), the test runs for real: the morning draws from dinner's kitchen for its prep, from the customer record for the standing order, and from the dinner cohort for its people (the morning's seats are held first by dinner's people through the period plan, S5 P10, S7 P30); it hands on the customer who "is enrolled in the layer on the first visit" (WP p.36) and the person who is at the window at seven and knows the room at seven. If that charter can be drafted with the dependent field blank, the morning is a coffee shop that shares a lease, and the structure refuses to open it, which is the same refusal the record's own diagnosis of the peer makes (WP p.33 to 34). Late night draws from dinner's room in its last turn and hands on nothing to a following period, only to the layer, which is why canon writes it as the same room loosened and not a service of its own (Canon 1.0, section 08). Lunch is not drafted before the first full year, and its charter attempt is the decision instrument (S4 P51).

The scheduling, cross-training, and identity consequences the carryover names all follow from "one team." Scheduling: one schedule across periods from one pool, posted by the stack, with a person's periods drawn from field 4 of their sheet (S5 P12) and their period plan (S7 I15). Cross-training: cross-period fluency is a development marker on the same person page as cross-strand fluency (section 11), not a transfer between teams. Identity: one uniform arc, one register that "loosens" rather than changes (Canon 1.0, section 08), one team home, one readiness test.

**P7 (Recommended).** The service periods are one team met at different hours, for any ratified set. A period is a period of one restaurant when its charter's dependent interfaces are non-empty and its provided interface is consumed by another period or the layer; a charter that fails the test is not opened. Dinner is the first configuration. The early morning's charter is where the test first runs against another period, and late night is dinner's own later register in the same room.

### 3.4 How a period added by ratified charter changes the structure

Stated once, so no later gate re-derives it. A period added by ratified charter:

*   Adds seats to the inventory: the seat rows the charter's count calls for, each for that period, marked drafted at the ruling and open at the build (S5 I1). It may add a seat class the house does not yet hold, in which case Session 6's rule applies: a seat class that would produce a one-scorecard packet needs a runner named before it opens (S6 P9).
*   Adds a designation set for the period's services: a room designation, and where the period has a threshold and a pass, a door and a sequence designation, each named at the period's brief (section 8).
*   Writes the interfaces: its own charter's dependent and provided fields, and a line in every open period's charter that its provided interface is now consumed by the new period. The weekly interface read at the leads' review begins the day two periods are open (S4 11.2).
*   Adds the period's register block to the module set, the period plan for people already in the house (S7 P30), and the period's block to the brief and the close.
*   Adds a line to the variety test record: the pass in section 5 is re-run at the period's gate against the new configuration (S3 I: requisite-variety test record).

It does not add a leadership line, a lead, a check-in holder, a second labor pool, a second web, or a second readiness test. The only way a period adds a line is that the variety pass at its gate shows a disturbance class resolving to nothing or to a founder by default, and a line is then argued at the gate review, marked, and ratified before the period opens. No period adds a line by assumption.

**P8 (Recommended).** A period added by ratified charter changes the structure as listed: seats, a designation set, interfaces, a register block and a period plan, and a re-run of the variety pass. It adds no leadership line unless the variety pass at its gate requires one, and then only argued and ratified before the period opens.

## 4\. The structure, drawn

The web is drawn in words and once as a text diagram. It has a center and an outside edge and no altitude; the diagram is read from the center outward, never from top to bottom, and nothing in it is above anything else. The record's own open item is the web "rendered as a designed organizational artifact rather than a chart" (WP p.15), and the owner of that render is open (`86akh7ru5`); what is drawn here is the structural content the render must carry, not the render.

### 4.1 The center

The center is "information convergence," "a systems function, not a rank" (WP p.9). It holds the culinary and conceptual vision the leads serve (WP p.10), which is written into the record and canon so that it is code-bearing rather than a person's charisma (S1 section 3). Three founding seats own it as domains: Brandon's seat owns the concept, the operating systems, and the experience; Dominic's seat owns the capital, the financial architecture, and the technology build; the chef partner's seat owns the culinary vision, under whichever account of the seat the ruling chooses (WP p.3; `86akh2qrp`). The founders' cadence is the partners' review, the domain read, and the gate review (S4 P53). The founders assign, review, and escalate no person (S4 P58). Their presence on the floor runs on the service metronome (ledger).

Two leads sit at the center as co-leads of different systems: the Operations Lead, "accountable to the operational outcomes: labor efficiency, cost targets, compliance, vendor performance, and facility integrity," who "oversees those systems and is accountable to their outputs, not their manual production"; and the Maitre d, who "owns the how of the experience," "accountable to experience quality and team health" (WP p.10). "Neither reports to the other" (WP p.10). Each pairs monthly with a partner: the Maitre d with Brandon, the Operations Lead's pairing founder-gated with Dominic recommended (S4 P59, P60).

### 4.2 The domains, and their leads

A domain is a set of seats with one owner, and its lead is "the node with the most connections to it: holding the check-in, opening the seat, deciding the hire; not assigning, not reviewing from above, not holding advancement" (ledger; S5 P33). The domains, with their leads as the record names them and as this page completes them:

*   **The floor.** Two strands, outward-facing and inward-facing (WP p.10 to 11). Domain lead: the Maitre d, for both strands (section 8). Seats: server, host, runner, and any further floor seat a charter calls for. Per-service designations: the room, the door (the record's Lead Host), and the sequence.
*   **Beverage.** "The Head of Beverage owns the program, and outward-facing and inward-facing execution map to the same two-strand logic as the floor" (WP p.11). Domain lead: the Head of Beverage, a seat (section 4.4). Seats: bartender and any further bar seat a charter calls for.
*   **The kitchen.** "Domain owners are Station Leads, and domain execution is Chef on the line and Chef on prep, neither a promotion from the other. The Steward owns the continuity of the kitchen environment" (WP p.11). Domain lead: the chef seat, under either branch of the ruling (S5 P57, P58). Everything below the spine in section 16 is chef-gated.
*   **The operating architecture.** The stack, the schedule, compliance, vendors, the facility, the record's maintenance (WP p.10). Owner: the Operations Lead. This domain has, in the record, no seats beneath it: the back-office administrator is removed by software (WP p.22). Whether it ever holds a seat is a structure change under section 17.

The Operations Lead and the Maitre d are domain leads for their own domains and for no seat in the other's. The check-in of a lead is held by a partner under Session 3's Class C rule, as Session 7 read it (S7 P21, finding 19.7, `86akhb2jg`).

### 4.3 The outside edge, and the strands

Every seat that is not a lead's sits at the outside edge, "the primary receivers of the operation," "the most sensitive position" (WP p.9). Within a domain the seats are strands, not levels. On the floor: the outward-facing strand's primary output is the experience at the table, its intelligence "relational and expressive and emotionally attuned under load," and the customer feels it; the inward-facing strand's primary output is "the operational sequence that makes the outward strand possible," its intelligence "architectural and coordinated and timing-precise," and the customer "never feels this strand, they feel that everything arrived right" (WP p.10 to 11). Server and host are outward-facing seats; runner is an inward-facing seat (section 8). Beverage maps the same way: the bartender is outward-facing, "Bartender always in proximity" (Canon 1.0, section 06), and any bar seat whose output is the program's sequence is inward-facing. The kitchen's strands are chef-gated.

### 4.4 The Head of Beverage, as a seat

The record carries the Head of Beverage three ways: as a functional designation that "owns beverage program execution for this shift," "not permanent elevations above anyone" (WP p.10); as the owner of the program, "In beverage, the Head of Beverage owns the program" (WP p.11); and as the seat that inventory, costing, and purchasing in software "collapse a wine manager and a bar manager into" (WP p.22). The second and third are a seat; the first is what the seat does on a given night (finding 21.3). The team reads it as a seat and a leadership line, because a program is owned across periods and a designation exists for one service, and because the bar seats need a domain lead who opens them, holds their check-ins, and decides their hires, which a nightly designation cannot do (S5 15.7's reasoning, applied here). The Head of Beverage's own check-in is held by the Maitre d, as the lead whose outcomes, experience quality and team health, the program's execution serves, with the Operations Lead holding the program's inventory, costing, and purchasing outputs through the stack. This is one seat with two leads reading two different things, and it is not dual reporting in her sense, because neither lead assigns or reviews the Head of Beverage; each reads a record (section 6.1).

**P9 (Recommended).** The structure is: a center holding the vision, three founding seats owning domains, two parallel leads; four domains, the floor, beverage, the kitchen, and the operating architecture, each with one lead; strands within domains; every non-lead seat at the outside edge. The Head of Beverage is a seat and a leadership line, the domain lead for bar seats, with its check-in held by the Maitre d and its program outputs read by the Operations Lead.

**P10 (Chef-gated).** The kitchen's domain below its spine: stations, the Station Leads' count and which stations they own, the pass owner per service, the line and prep split, the Steward's count, and the kitchen's strands. Section 16 holds the list.

### 4.5 The diagram, read from the center outward

```
                         the outside edge
              (highest information sensitivity: every non-lead seat)

   server . host . runner . bartender . chef on the line . chef on prep . steward
        \      |      /          |               \          |          /
         \     |     /           |                \         |         /
        THE FLOOR domain      BEVERAGE domain        THE KITCHEN domain
        lead: Maitre d        lead: Head of Beverage  lead: the chef seat
        strands: outward,     strands: outward,       strands: chef-gated
                 inward                inward          domain owners: Station Leads
        designations per      designation per        designations per service:
        service: room, door,  service: the program's  the pass owner (chef-gated)
        sequence              execution
              \                   |                        /
               \                  |                       /
                \        THE OPERATING ARCHITECTURE      /
                 \       owner: Operations Lead         /
                  \      (the stack, schedule,         /
                   \      compliance, facility)       /
                    \             |                  /
                     -------- the center -----------
                     information convergence, not rank
                     Operations Lead  ||  Maitre d   (parallel; neither reports to the other)
                     the vision: Brandon's seat . Dominic's seat . the chef partner's seat
```

The diagram carries no arrow pointing down. The lines are connections, and a seat's "further along" is the count of them (WP p.11). The center is drawn last because it is where the lines converge, not where they start. New people enter at the edge, leads included in the sense section 10.3 gives.

### 4.6 Pre-opening, at dinner's opening, and at each later gate

**Pre-opening.** The founders hold every domain. The hiring partner, recommended as Brandon's seat (S4 P4, `86akh7qnb`), opens every seat and decides every packet until a lead is in the building. The chef seat is unruled and gates the kitchen chain (S5 P58). The two leads are in the building at least six weeks before dinner's gate (S6 P15). Once a lead arrives, that lead opens their own domain's seats first, and the leads hire their domains (S5 4.4). The Head of Beverage is hired by the Maitre d as the beverage domain's first seat, or pre-opening by the hiring partner, and then hires the bar. The pre-opening cohort arrives in two waves under S7 P8. Designations run from the first training service, so that the brief has named a room, a door, and a sequence before there is a customer.

**At dinner's opening.** Two leads, the chef seat filled under the ruling, the Head of Beverage, the dinner seats on the inventory filled or held at the bar, every kitchen seat under the chef's sheets, every brief naming its designations, the room designation the Maitre d on every service the Maitre d works and a named person otherwise, and the variety test record run once against the actual line list.

**At each later gate.** Section 3.4 states the change per period. Dinner steady and the early morning added: the morning's seats, a morning room designation from the morning's seats, the interface read begins, the Maitre d's seat spans by designation and the seat's check-in load grows by the morning's seats. Late night added: no new seat unless its charter calls for one, the register block, the transition trigger's owner reading as the room's holder through close. The first full year and the lunch ruling: a charter attempt and nothing built before it. At every gate, the variety pass is re-run and the inventory is versioned.

**P11 (Recommended).** The structural positions that hold pre-opening, at dinner's opening, and at each later gate, as stated. Pre-opening the founders hold every domain and the hiring partner opens every seat; at dinner's opening every domain has its lead and every brief its designations; each later gate changes the structure only as section 3.4 allows.
